"My meditative concentration is such that it could fill everything from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven with fire."
This serves to manifest purity.
For example, when Śubhavyūha was slandered by others, he declared of himself:
"In a single thought-moment, I am able to know the events of five hundred kalpas."
This serves to manifest his purity.
Because Dabba was slandered by Cālī, he constantly emitted radiance to manifest his purity. Furthermore, it is to eliminate the mind of contempt;

for example, as a bhikṣu devoted to study might despise one who practices meditation or assists in communal affairs, a bhikṣu who practices meditation might likewise despise those engaged in these two activities, and a bhikṣu who assists in communal affairs might likewise despise those who practice meditation or study.

Therefore, by the power of his meditative concentration, Dharmapāla constantly manifested radiance; furthermore, he managed bedding and requisites and assisted in communal affairs, because he had extinguished the signs of disparagement and the mind of competitiveness.

Third, it was to subdue the prideful minds of bhikṣus dwelling in mountain forests and under trees, who constantly claimed that city-dwelling bhikṣus—being distracted, talkative, and preoccupied with worldly affairs—were incapable of accomplishing anything through their practice of the Path or cultivation of their studies, while they themselves considered that no one could surpass them in secluded retreats.
Therefore, although Dabba was amidst the chaos of the assembly, he attained great supernormal power; by emitting light from his hands to divide the bedding, he subdued those with arrogant hearts.

Fourth, it was to manifest the fruit of diligence, showing that such supernatural powers are obtained through the power of diligence, thereby exhorting those who are indolent, conceited, and self-indulgent.
Fifth, it was to cause the donor and patron to increase their roots of goodness.

Sixth, it was to manifest the dharma of non-retrogression: although Dharmapāla’s prior conduct had been perfectly pure, he was later slandered by Maitrībala; at that time, people doubted and claimed he had retrogressed, so [the Buddha] emitted light to clarify that he had not, in fact, retrogressed.

If even the monk who distributed the bedding possessed such divine power because he manifested the great majesty of the Sangha, how much more so for other venerable ones whose fame is far-reaching and exalted?

Eighth, out of reverence for right action so as not to let it be deficient or empty, he remains constantly in a state of meditative concentration while also sharing out bedding and furniture; thus, he ensures that the affairs of the Sangha are accomplished without neglecting his own practice of dhyāna. For these reasons, he constantly emits radiance.
The community of monks performed a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to appoint him as the distributor of meals; because he served as the distributor of meals, he was slandered by Maitrībala.

Subsequently, they appointed him as the distributor of bedding and requisites; because he had been slandered, light issued from his hands, causing all sentient beings to extinguish all unwholesome dharmas.
Because the matter of bedding and requisites is also more important, it has been moved to the front, while the appointment for the assembly is placed afterward.
As for why the bhikṣu Cīra always receives coarse and inferior food, it is due to the power of his past karma.
Furthermore, this person lacks a pure mind day and night; devas, nāgas, and spirits create the conditions to cause their undertakings to be contrary to their wishes.
If the World-Honored One knows me, he cannot say it is so because of my actual purity;
yet he cannot say it is not so because of the power of my past karma.
For what reason does the Buddha not declare that *dravya* (substantiality) is pure?
First, because the Buddha’s mind of equanimity is free from partiality and attachment, he does not immediately state that one is right and the other is wrong.
Second, because the karmic fruit of his past actions had matured:

in the time of the past Kāśyapa Buddha, he served as a distributor of food. At that time, there was an Arhat among the monks dwelling in a cemetery who was walking along the road with a dignified and handsome appearance.
A certain woman saw him and conceived a lustful attachment, gazing after him without ceasing.
When the man who provided his food saw her thus, he assumed she had previously had an affair with him and immediately said:
"This bhikṣu must have committed an illicit act with this woman."
Because he slandered the noble ones and the sages, he fell into hell.
Once his retribution was exhausted and he emerged, he encountered a Buddha and attained the Way due to his original wholesome karma;
yet, by the power of residual karma, he received this evil retribution.
Because this bhikṣuṇī Mitrā has herself confessed her commission of an offense, the *nihsargika-karman* (act of reconciliation) should be performed against her.

Regarding "confessing one's own offense": if a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī confesses having committed an offense and does not reform or repent, the *nihsargika-karman* should be performed against them.
If one does not perform the *nihsargika-karman* (act of banishment) but simply expels them outright, if the person subsequently reforms and repents, they incur a *sthūlātyaya*;
if they do not reform and repent, they incur a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu has violated the precepts and is internally rotten, such that the entire community knows of it, there is no need for him to speak of it himself; he should be expelled immediately.
If a formal ritual (karmavācanā) is performed to announce this to all those in the four directions, his transgression will be subdued and he may act without further fault.
Whenever any of the five assemblies confesses having committed a grave offense—whether before a single person or before many—they must all be expelled.
A bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī must be present in person, while the other three assemblies need not be present.
The Bhikṣu Dravya was granted the *smṛtivinaya* (the verdict based on mindfulness) as described among the seven methods for settling disputes. Regarding the legal procedure for such a settlement:

he is not permitted to participate in any communal monastic affairs; he may not join the assembly in any of the one hundred and one formal acts (*karmas*); nor may he be included in the Saṃgha’s invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*), nor in the distribution of the robes at the end of the *varṣā* retreat.
If he dies, the Sangha may not perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to take his property; it should be given to his close lay relatives.
He himself may not receive the Dharma from another, nor may he teach the Dharma to anyone else.
One must not accept the prostrations, offerings, recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), or any formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*) from others, nor may one give consent or purity (*chanda-śuddhi*).
There are three types of persons who will inevitably fall into hell due to the sin of slandering [the Dharma].
He spoke simultaneously of the offenses for which these two men fell into hell; the Buddha does not wish to call out the evils of individuals by name.

Since such evil persons were present among the assembly, the Buddha therefore used this occasion to speak of their transgressions, so as to cause those offenders to subdue their evil minds and feel profound shame and remorse.
Now, when a person is born into this world, an axe is born within their mouth.
Regarding this, the Buddha himself spoke of a past cause:
"Incalculable eons ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Arira. During that Buddha's teaching, there were two brothers who left the household life to become bhikṣus."
Because the elder brother practiced dhyāna, he attained arhatship with the three insights and six supernormal powers;
the younger brother mastered the Tripitaka and propagated the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the fourfold assembly of the world venerated both men, yet because of his attainment of the noble path, the elder brother received a greater share of offerings and sustenance.

At that time, a donor brought a piece of fine cotton cloth and gave it to the elder brother but not to the younger; likewise, in all matters of food, drink, clothing, and medical treatment for illness, they were treated with partiality and inequality.
The younger brother, who was a bhikṣu, conceived a mind of resentment and malice, desiring to harm and slander [his brother].
At that time, a female lay devotee was sent by a donor to the place of a Tripitaka Bhikṣu. The Bhikṣu said to the woman:
"Give me false testimony against that Bhikṣu.
The woman said:
"This is a noble one;
how could one slander him?
Thus, through various skillful means, that bhikṣu seduced her mind, and the woman consented.
The bhikṣu said:
"I shall go and retrieve that cotton cloth and give it to you to serve as evidence for his crime.
Just say:..."
"Have sexual intercourse with me.
She immediately sought him out and gave herself to him, then returned home.
When asked the reason for her actions, she was questioned why it had taken so long.
He immediately said, "The bhikṣu there detained me for sport; that is why it took so long.
He spoke again:
"Give me this cotton cloth.
At that time, all the people of the world were filled with doubt and suspicion.
Seeing these two individuals committing such great evils, the arhat bhikṣu immediately fled to another region.
The Buddha said:
"The younger brother bhikṣu at that time was myself;
the woman was Sundarī."

"Because I slandered those who had exhausted their outflows and were beyond training in my previous lives, now that I have exhausted my outflows and am in the stage of one beyond training, I am once again subjected to slander.

The reason for establishing these precepts for the bhikṣus is so that the Dharma may endure for a long time; it is to stop slander and defamation, and to ensure that those practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) may dwell in peace and security, without hindrance to their recitation of the scriptures or their practice of the Path.

This is a common precept: if a bhikṣu violates it, he incurs saṃghāvaśeṣa; if a bhikṣuṇī violates it, she also incurs saṃghāvaśeṣa; and if those in the three lower assemblies violate it, they incur duṣkṛta.
Regarding "unfounded *pārājika*": there are four types of unfounded slander.
First, slandering with an unfounded *pārājika* offense results in a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
second, slandering with an unfounded *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense results in a *pāyattika*.
Third, if one slanders [a monk] by falsely claiming he has shed the blood of a Buddha or caused a schism in the Saṃgha without basis, he incurs a sthūlātyaya;
fourth, if one slanders [a monk] with a groundless pāyattika offense, he incurs a duṣkṛta.
There are three types of speaking of another's grave offense:
first, to speak of another's *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one incurs a *pāyattika*;
to speak of another's shedding of the Buddha's blood or causing a schism in the Saṃgha, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the offenses of *pāyattika* and *dukkaṭa*:
there are three types of concealing another's grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
First, if one conceals another's *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
Concealing another’s act of shedding the Buddha’s blood or causing a schism in the Saṃgha constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
concealing a *pāyattika* offense is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is only one category for slighting or reviling the precepts: slighting any of the five classes of offenses all constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Even to revile or disparage the very last article [of the precepts] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Groundless slander, speaking of another’s grave offense, and reviling the precepts—these three matters constitute disputes, for they disturb the Dharma.
Because concealing another’s grave offense and hiding their evil deeds defiles the Buddha-dharma;
furthermore, because groundless slander and speaking of another’s grave offense obstruct and cause the abandonment of reciting the scriptures and practicing the Path.
To disparage the precepts is to destroy the Dharma-body of the Buddha.
To conceal gross offenses causes the Buddha-Dharma to become impure and fosters unwholesome dharmas.
Regarding "without basis," there are three kinds of roots:
First, seeing; second, hearing; third, doubting.
Based on these three types, it is called "having a basis" (*sāmulaka*);
not seeing, not hearing, and not doubting is called "lacking a basis" (*amūlaka*, literally "rootless"). Thus, doubt is said not to constitute a basis.

Regarding the faculty of the eye: it must be kept pure and free from disease so that what is seen is examined with precision and can be relied upon and trusted; however, only the physical eye is permitted, not the divine eye, for one who possesses the divine eye does not speak of the faults of others.
Furthermore, if one were to listen to those who report the transgressions of others by means of the divine eye, who among people would be without fault?

There are only differences in the degree of their divine vision, such that there is nothing they do not see. If one allows for the reporting of transgressions, then matters of interference and confusion will be many.

As for the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*), it must necessarily be pure, free from error, precise, and trustworthy; furthermore, one must not rely on the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), as its nature is the same as that of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).

Because doubt cannot be relied upon—if one describes a transgression yet speaks of it as having a fixed characteristic, such a doubtful state is not definitive—whether one considers it a committed offense or a non-offense, or whether it is deemed unreliable, it therefore cannot constitute a faculty (*indriya*).
5. The Tenth Precept on Schism in the Saṃgha. Regarding the schism in the wheel of the Dharma and the schism in the saṃgha through formal ritual (karmavācanā), what is the difference between them?
The answer is:
“There are various differences.”
To cause a schism in the Wheel of the Dharma and to cause a schism in the Saṃgha through formal ritual (karman) both constitute thullaccaya offenses.
However, causing a schism in the Wheel of the Dharma constitutes a thullaccaya that is a heinous crime (ānantarya), which cannot be expiated;
causing a schism in the Saṃgha through formal ritual constitutes a thullaccaya that is not a heinous crime, which can be expiated.
Furthermore, one who breaks the wheel of the Sangha enters the Avīci Hell to undergo retribution for one kalpa;
one who breaks the Sangha through ritual (karmavācanā) does not fall into the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, breaking the wheel of the Sangha requires a minimum of nine persons, whereas breaking the Sangha through ritual requires a minimum of eight persons.
Furthermore, in the case of breaking the wheel of the Saṃgha, one person claims for himself to be a Buddha;
in the case of breaking the Saṃgha through formal ritual (karmavācanā), one does not claim to be a Buddha.
Furthermore, in the case of breaking the wheel of the Saṃgha, it is broken entirely within and without the boundary (sīmā); [in the other case, it is not].
To split the *saṃgha* through formal procedure (*karmabheda*), it is essential that a separate formal procedure be performed within the same boundary (*sīmā*).
Furthermore, the breaking of the wheel of the *saṃgha* (*cakrabheda*) must be carried out by a man;
however, the breaking of the *saṃgha* through formal procedure can be accomplished by both men and women.
Furthermore, to break the wheel of the Saṃgha is to break the Saṃgha of conventional truth;
to break the Saṃgha of ritual action (karmavācanā) is to break both the Saṃgha of conventional truth and the Saṃgha of ultimate truth.
Furthermore, while the schism of the Wheel of the Dharma (*dharmacakra*) affects only Jambudvīpa,
the schism of the Saṃgha through ritual action (*karmasaṃghabheda*) extends throughout the three continents.
Devadatta enticed the young bhikṣus with five points, causing them to give rise to heterodox views.
The essentials for causing a schism in the Sangha have the five points as their foundation.
A question was asked:
"Since the Buddha himself always praised these five points, why are they called 'unlawful'?"
He replied:
"The reason the Buddha praised them was that the four noble lineages can lead one to attain the eightfold noble path and achieve the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.

Now Devadatta has spoken perversely, saying that the eightfold noble path leads toward nirvāṇa but is instead slow and difficult, whereas practicing five dharmas to seek liberation makes the path to it very swift."
Therefore, it is said that this is "unrighteousness" (*adharma*).
To speak of unrighteousness as righteousness means to claim that the five factors which are unrighteous are righteousness.
To speak of righteousness as unrighteousness means to claim that the Noble Eightfold Path, which is righteousness, is unrighteousness.
Regarding "those who preach what is not the Vinaya as the Vinaya": there are five things that are not the Vinaya which they claim to be the Vinaya.
Regarding "those who preach the Vinaya as not the Vinaya": the Noble Eightfold Path is the Vinaya, yet they claim it is not the Vinaya.

Regarding "claiming one has committed an offense when one has not": the Buddha did not establish precepts for the mind, yet he stated that the arising of the three poisons within the mind constitutes a violation of the precepts.

Regarding "claiming one has not committed an offense when one has": although the shaving of hair and clipping of nails were not prohibited, the Buddha declared this to be a violation of the precepts; yet others say that hair and nails possess life, and ask: "Is there anyone who does not shave or clip them?"

To describe a minor offense as grave is like the case of the Utpala Dragon, whose sin became irredeemable because he plucked a tree leaf; for this reason, some claim that killing plants and trees is always a grave offense.

Regarding the statement that "heavy offenses are light": seeing that Sūdena, Dhanika, and others did not incur heavy offenses because they acted previously, one then claims that sexual misconduct and theft are light offenses.
To say there is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense where there is none is to claim that an offense against any of the four minor categories of precepts constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, when in fact it does not.
To say there is no *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense where there is one is to claim that committing any of the four grave offenses (*pārājika*) does not constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, when in fact it does.

Regarding "the Dharma that is always taught and the Dharma that is not always taught": the Eightfold Noble Path is the Dharma that is always employed, yet it is said to be the Dharma that is not always employed.

Regarding the statement that "dharmas which are not of the nature of permanence are taught as dharmas of the nature of permanence": there are five dharmas that are not of the nature of permanence, yet they are taught as dharmas of the nature of permanence.
To claim that the four prohibitions are minor while the other sections are grave is not the true teaching, yet it is called the teaching;
to claim that the four prohibitions are grave while the other sections are minor is the correct teaching, yet it is called not the teaching.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Scroll Three;
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Scroll Four.
Translator’s name lost; now appended to the Qin Records.
6. The twelfth [offense], defiling a family. Regarding the twelfth offense of defiling a family:
those born when the two lunar mansions Aśvinī and Bharaṇī arise are given names derived from those mansions.
These are families of noble lineage who are deeply attached to worldly pleasures and cannot relinquish their minds; for this reason, they violate the precepts.

Being heedless and committing evil deeds, they defile the families of others by performing various kinds of unwholesome karma and destroying the virtuous faith and respect of others; this is called "defiling the family."
One who performs evil conduct engages in such impure karma; because it is defiled, filthy, and turbid, and because it results in evil fruits, it is called "evil conduct.

Furthermore, regarding "defiling the families of others": if a bhikṣu makes any request—whether on behalf of the Triple Gem or for his own sake—involving various articles of faith given to kings, ministers, elders, householders, and all other laypeople, as well as those who have left the home life, this is all termed "defiling the families of others."

Why is this? For all those who have left the household life, they should remain free from conditioned activity and desire, maintaining purity for themselves, taking the cultivation of the Path as their primary concern.
If one engages in the exchange of letters and messengers with worldly people, it will disrupt and disorder one's correct practice; such is not appropriate for one who has left the household life.
Furthermore, if one presents gifts to laypeople, it violates the former's spirit of equanimity and good will;
instead, it causes the recipient of the gift to feel joy, attachment, and reverence.

Regarding the failure to receive material offerings: even if one is a worthy or holy person, if one lacks a heart of love and respect, one loses the profound merit and benefit of those who preceded them.

Furthermore, it subverts and confuses the Buddha-dharma; for while all laypeople ought to provide food, drink, and clothing as offerings to monastics, monastics instead make offerings to white-robed laypeople. Thus, they lose the hearts of the sages above and bring disorder to the True Dharma.
All householders constantly seek the pure field of merit within the Triple Gem, sacrificing their own flesh and blood to plant roots of goodness.

Yet, because of the circumstance of giving gifts to renunciants as objects of faith, they instead give rise to expectations toward those renunciants; this destroys the pure faith and reverence that others previously held toward the Triple Gem and causes them to lose all the various offerings and sustenance due to renunciants.

If one were to give small gifts to laypeople, even if they were to erect a stupa made of the seven treasures and adorned in every way, it would not be as good as sitting in quietude and maintaining pure precepts; this is truly making offerings to the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.

If one were to give even a small gift to a layperson such that they could establish a vihāra as magnificent as Jetavana, it would not be as meritorious as sitting in quietude and maintaining pure precepts; this is the true pure offering to the Triple Gem.

If one were to give small gifts to laypeople, even if one were to fully provide the four requisites to all the noble ones throughout Jambudvīpa, it would not equal the merit of sitting in meditation and maintaining pure precepts; this is the true pure offering to all the noble ones.

If there are those with great power who wish to destroy a stūpa or damage an image, and it can be fully preserved through the means of a gift, one should sell the flowers and fruits from the stūpa grounds.
If there is money in the stūpa, or if goods are obtained through other circumstances, one should manage the matter as appropriate.

If there are those with great power who wish to cause dissension, disruption, or reduction within the Saṃgha, they may sell whatever items are found upon the Saṃgha’s land to obtain money, according to the circumstances.

Whether it be according to the seniority of the Saṃgha or according to the seniority of the face-to-face assembly, if there are those with forceful power who wish to effect a reduction, one should adjust it according to whatever goods are produced within that specific locality.
If one's parents are fields of merit, then providing for them is permitted.
If they are persons belonging to the *saṃgha*, because they perform service for the *saṃgha*, then this [gift] should be given to them.

If a donor wishes to provide food for the community of monks and desires to know the proper rule, this should be given to all who are solitary, destitute, and begging; out of a heart of compassion, it should be given.
All non-Buddhists constantly act as great enemies toward the Buddha-dharma, seeking out its flaws and shortcomings; it is appropriate to give to them.
If they beg for robes and bowls according to circumstances for the sake of their own bodies and lives, one should give to them to avoid calamity and hardship.
Regarding "sitting on the same bed with a woman": a bhikṣu must not sit on the same bed as a woman; if he does so, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
He must not share the same mat or the same bedding; in all such cases, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

Long beds may be joined together, provided that they have separate seats, separate mattresses, and separate rugs, leaving a gap between them so that each rug and mattress remains distinct for sitting.

As for women, this applies to all women; whether mother, daughter, sister, or any other relative, regardless of how close the kinship, it is strictly forbidden, because it would destroy one's dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
If one applies scented paste to the body or perfumes one's robes, the four assemblies incur a *duṣkṛta* offense;
for bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *pāyattika*, because women possess deep-seated attachments.
None of the five groups of practitioners are permitted to sprinkle scented water on the ground, except for the sake of the Triple Gem.

Regarding the act of stringing flower garlands oneself or having others string them: the reason this is not permitted is that the evil conduct performed therein—whether previously committed or occurring after the precepts were established—obstructs and hinders the practice of the Path.
It is likewise not permitted to do so even for the sake of the Three Jewels.
Furthermore, it is said:
"If one uses flowers, incense, necklaces, or other articles of adornment, they must not be placed upon the body of the Buddha; rather, they should be scattered on the ground as an offering."
If a bhikṣu offers flowers to the Saṃgha, he must not scatter them upon their bodies.
If he places flowers on top of a beverage, it is likewise not permitted for him to drink from it.
If one causes elephants to fight, or even causes chickens to fight, it is forbidden for all five assemblies.
If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to kill, causes them to fight so that they die, it is a *pāyattika*;
if they do not die, [it is likewise].
A *duṣkṛta* offense.
Causing the three groups [of monastics] to fight is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For all five groups, running away is not permitted, except in the case of urgent or difficult circumstances.
None of the five assemblies are permitted to weep, not even upon the death of their own parents; all such instances are forbidden.
Should they do so, the four assemblies incur a *duṣkṛta* offense, while the bhikṣuṇīs incur a *pāyattika* offense, because their hearts are bound by deep attachment.
None of the five groups of monastics shall shout loudly, as this destroys dignified deportment, except in cases of urgent distress.
None of the five groups of monastics shall whistle or speak with distorted pronunciation, as this destroys dignified deportment.
At that time, regarding Ānanda, someone asked:
"Ānanda is the Buddha’s attendant; why has he left the Buddha to travel about?"
He replied:
"Ānanda followed along because there were sentient beings with whom he had a karmic connection who were ready to be transformed. He asked:
“When will Ānanda be able to leave the Buddha and travel about?
He replied,
“If the Buddha enters into meditative concentration, he will be able to leave and travel about.”
Furthermore, when the Buddha went to other regions, Ānanda was unable to go with him, and thus he obtained his release at those times.
Moreover, by receiving the Buddha’s mission, he was able to leave and travel about.
Ānanda entered with an empty bowl and emerged with an empty bowl.
Question:
"Ānanda is the Buddha’s attendant and possesses great merit; moreover, these are his native lands and all his kinsmen. For what reason did he go out empty-handed after begging for alms?"

He replied, "The constellations Aśvinī and Maghā have committed great unrighteousness therein, engaging in various evil deeds such as aggression and defilement. That we have escaped harm is already a great fortune; how much more so to obtain food."
Furthermore, because Ānanda entered the monastic life at a young age and many years have passed, they did not recognize him.

Chapter Seven: The Thirteenth Precept on Contrary Speech. If it is as described, the assemblies of all Tathāgatas will attain increasing benefit, for by speaking together and instructing one another, they shall collectively emerge from transgressions.
Question: "The sutras state that one should simply observe one's own bodily conduct and clearly discern what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.
How is it that this does not contradict the teaching that one should instruct others in turn?"
He replied:
"The Buddha established his teachings according to the circumstances; though the words may differ, their intent is consistent, and they do not contradict one another.
Because the hearts of people in former times were possessed of love and hatred, and their speech caused harm, the Buddha therefore said: 'One should simply observe one's own bodily conduct.'"
If one possesses a compassionate mind and can be of benefit to others, one should therefore engage them in conversation and instruct them.
If, however, one has dull faculties and lacks wisdom such that speech would be of no benefit, it is said that one should simply observe oneself.
But if one is intelligent, wise, and of sharp faculties, such that one’s words are beneficial, then one should indeed provide mutual instruction.
If one has heard little and seen little, one's speech will be of no benefit; therefore, it is said that one should "only observe one's own conduct.
If, however, one has heard extensively and seen broadly, such that there is something to propagate and benefit others, then one should teach them in turn.
It is further said:
If one speaks for the sake of gain, offerings, fame, or renown, it is for this reason that it is said one should "only observe one's own bodily conduct";
however, if one expounds the Buddha-dharma for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace to sentient beings, then one should teach and exhort others in turn.
It is further said:
"For the sake of happiness in the present life, one should merely observe one's own bodily conduct;
however, if one wishes to transform and benefit sentient beings through the Dharma so that the whole world may become like oneself, then one should teach others in turn."

Furthermore, because those who have newly left the household life still harbor attachments to their parents, siblings, wives, and children, it is said that they should "only observe their own bodily conduct.
However, once they have long been immersed in the power of the Buddha-dharma and are able to assist others, they should then teach one another in succession.
4. The Two Aniyata Dharmas. Regarding the first of the two Aniyata Dharmas: At that time, Viśākhā went directly to the house of Ghoṣita.
She asked, "Viśākhā is wise, of sharp faculties, and a person of great virtue and respect; knowing that a bhikṣu was sitting with a woman in a secluded place, for what reason did you go there?"
He replied:
"This person has already entered the path and deeply delights in the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha himself has always said: "
"There are five benefits to listening to the Dharma:

first, hearing the Dharma never heard before; second, purifying and strengthening what has already been heard; third, eliminating false views; fourth, attaining right view; and fifth, understanding the profound Dharma."
"For this reason, Viśākhā’s devotion to the Dharma is so profound that she does not allow suspicion to hinder her.
When the Buddha taught various dharmas, for laypeople who had not yet entered the path of the fruits of the spiritual life, he mostly spoke on the merit of giving.
For those renunciants who have already entered the path, he frequently speaks of the merit of observing the precepts.
He establishes the precepts for the bhikṣus for one primary reason: to stop slander.
Second, it is for the sake of eliminating strife and contention.
Third, it is for the sake of increasing the sublime Dharma.

A bhikṣu who has left the household life has severed his ties to worldly defilement and is revered by humans and devas; he transforms sentient beings through the Way. Yet, if he engages in private, secret, and base conduct with women in secluded places, he violates the intent of the Sages above and loses the faith and respect of humans and devas below.
The fourth is for the sake of the sequential method for severing evil karma.
Since [the offense] begins in a secluded place and gradually becomes so habitual and entangled that it reaches all extremes, one must prevent it.

Regarding such a person, they will never speak falsely for their own sake; even if it were for the sake of another or for the sake of wealth and profit, this is one who has accomplished untainted faith and will never intentionally utter a lie.
Even if an ordinary person deeply delights in the Buddha-dharma, they would not utter false speech even for the sake of losing their life, let alone a noble one (ārya).
Suppose someone were to say:
"If you speak falsely, it shall not harm your life."
"If you do not speak falsely, I shall take your life.
He then thought to himself:
"If I do not speak falsely, I will destroy this physical body and extinguish this single life."
"If one speaks falsely, one destroys immeasurable physical bodies and simultaneously harms the Dharma-body.
Thus, he vowed not to speak falsely.
Another person then said to him:
"If you speak falsely, I shall spare your parents, brothers, sisters, and all your kinsmen.
If you do not speak falsely, I shall kill all those who are dear to you."
He then reflected further:
"If I speak falsely, I shall harm these kinsmen of mine throughout this life and the cycle of birth and death.

If I speak falsely, I will wander through the three evil realms and forever lose my kin and relatives across successive human and celestial lives; furthermore, I will lose my noble and holy companions who have transcended the world."
This is called not speaking falsely for the sake of another.
Furthermore, one might say:
"If you speak falsely, I shall give you precious jewels and various kinds of wealth and profit."
"If I do not speak falsely, I shall not give it to you.
He then reflected:
"If I do not speak falsely, I will lose this worldly wealth."
"If I were to speak falsely, I would lose the wealth of the noble Dharma.
This is called not speaking falsely for the sake of material gain.

As for "not being indeterminate," when the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment, he had already determined the gravity, lightness, accessibility, and restrictions of the five categories of precepts; there was nothing therein that remained unsettled.

The reason this is called "uncertain" is simply that a trustworthy person may not recognize the gravity of the offense's characteristics, nor know the name of the offense; even if they see [the monk] sitting in one place with a woman, they do not know what he might be doing.
Did you engage in sexual intercourse?
Did you commit physical contact?
Or did you utter evil speech?
Is it because he spoke more than five or six words that it is called "undetermined"?

This refers to the precept concerning sitting in a secluded place with a woman; whether the formal act has already been completed or not, one applies the *vibhāṣā-vinaya* (the method of seeking the truth) based on the facts. For instance, if a bhikṣu initially says "yes" but later says "no," or says "I did not go there" or "I did not commit this offense."
One should follow the words of a trustworthy person and grant the *yadbhūyaḥ-vinaya* (discipline according to what is factual).

The reason for doing so is: first, to subdue the evil mind of the offender; second, to ensure that the offender, despite their suffering, does not conceal their transgression; third, to enable fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) to dwell in peace and happiness; and fourth, to maintain solemnity for the future so that unwholesome dharmas do not arise.

Regarding one who seeks the Vinaya in earnest: if they confer full ordination upon others, act as a preceptor for dependence, or maintain new or old śrāmaṇeras, these acts are all accomplished; however, they incur only a *duṣkṛta* offense.
From not instructing in the Vinaya up to not engaging in formal legal discourse, all such acts are invalid and constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If, after a *karmavācanā* has been performed, one confesses a prior offense, the *karmavācanā* should be dissolved and the individual should be disciplined according to the gravity of the offense;
if one does not confess it, the *karmavācanā* shall not be dissolved for as long as life lasts.
The second *aniyata-dharma* differs from the two preceding *dharmas* solely in its setting; otherwise, all aspects are identical.
It is also the same as the *yathābhūta-vinaya*.
The two *aniyata-dharmas* are concluded.

5. Thirty Matters: 1. The Circumstances for the First Precept on Keeping Extra Robes (Atirekacīvara). Regarding the circumstances for the first precept on keeping extra robes among the thirty matters: as for the group of six bhikṣus, they are: first, Nanduka; second, Upananda; third, Kālodāyin; fourth, Channa; fifth, Aśvaka; and sixth, Punarvasu.
It is said that two individuals attained the destruction of the outflows and entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*:
first, Kālodāyin, and second, Cchanna;
these two persons were reborn in the heavens. Furthermore, it is said:
The two individuals committed grave precepts.
It is also said:
"They did not commit them; for if one had committed a grave offense, they would not have been reborn in heaven."
First was Nanda and second was Upananda;
these two fell into the evil realms and were born among the nāgas:
first was Aśvayuj and second was Punarvasu.
The two were skilled in mathematics and the shifting movements of yin and yang:
the first was Nantuo, and the second was Bannantu.
The two were also profoundly versed in the way of archery:
The first was Kālodāyin and the second was Cchanna.
These two were skilled in music and various forms of entertainment;
the third was Aśvajit.
The second pair were both accomplished in preaching the Dharma and engaging in debate:
first, Nandat; second, Upananda.
Two individuals deeply understood the Abhidharma:
first, Kālodāyin; second, Channa.
Both were capable in every respect, skilled in preaching the Dharma and in debate, and proficient in the Abhidharma.
The first is the constellation Aśvinī and the second is the constellation Pūrva-phalgunī.
It is further said:

"These six men were unimpeded in all they encountered; they were thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Internally, they served as the pillars and beams of the Dharma; externally, they acted as great protectors of the Buddha-dharma."
Two were excessive in desire:
first, Nanduka; second, Upananda.
Two were excessive in anger:
The first lunar mansion is Aśvinī, the second is Pūrva-phalgunī.
There are two who are particularly deluded:
the first is Kālodāyin, the second is Channa.
It is further said that three individuals were prone to excessive desire:
first, Nandika; second, Upananda; and third, Kālodāyin.
Two individuals were prone to excessive anger:
The first lunar mansion is Aśvinī and the second is Pūrṇā.
One person was particularly deluded, namely Kṛṣṇa.
Five persons were of the Śākya lineage, of royal descent:
Nantuo, Bānántuó, Mǎsù, Mǎnsù, Chǎnnà, and one of Brahmin descent, Jiālúotáiyī—
these six were all from noble lineages who influenced one another and became friends to propagate the Buddha’s teachings.
Regarding those who wear different garments: because their stores are numerous, they change what they wear according to the time and occasion.
It is also said:
one simply wears a single garment, yet it differs according to the time and place.
It is further said:
"During the course of a single day, whatever clothes one wears, once the night has passed, they shall not be worn again on the following day; thus, the garments differ from day to day.
In this manner, one maintains a variety of such surplus robes."
Question: "By what means did you obtain such various garments? Answer:
"Since you are of noble lineage, have many acquaintances, are much sought after by others, and furthermore possess great desire, it is for these reasons that you have so many robes.
He asked: "For what purpose do you thus accumulate so many robes?"
He replied:
"I was originally from a noble family; while formerly living at home, I was attached to necklaces and various kinds of finery.
Although I left the household life out of a love for the Dharma, because of my former habits, I take pleasure in fine robes and alms bowls."
Furthermore, from lifetime to lifetime, his nature has always been characterized by excessive desire; for this reason, he now accumulates wealth without satiety.
He asked: “Is this pure gift a true gift?”
"Is this a gift given as a mere designation?
He replied,
"It is a pure gift in every respect."

Among the ninety-six kinds of impure giving, the Buddha, by virtue of his great kindness, great compassion, and power of skillful means, taught and commanded that they be purified through giving; this is giving through skillful means, not true giving.
[This allows] the disciples to possess surplus wealth without violating the precepts.
A question is asked:
"Why did the Buddha not simply allow the disciples to possess surplus wealth, but instead insistently establish a formal rule and devise this expedient means?"
He replied:
"The Buddha-dharma takes few desires as its foundation; therefore, the precepts were established to prohibit the accumulation of surplus wealth.
However, the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ: there may be beings who must accumulate much before they can practice the Path and realize the holy Dharma."
Therefore, the Tathāgata first establishes the precepts and subsequently employs skillful means; thus, there is no obstruction within the Buddha-dharma, and sentient beings derive benefit.
For instance, at one time a bhikṣu came and said to the Buddha:

"Grant me a pure dwelling, adorned with banners, flags, flower canopies, silken fabrics, and bedding; let the ground be smeared with incense and decorated with various kinds of music played on strings and wind instruments."
The Buddha commanded Ānanda to seek out [the necessary materials] everywhere, and he immediately provided them for him.

The bhikṣu remained in the center of mind, practicing the Path with tranquility; the Buddha taught him the Dharma according to his needs, and thereupon, severing his fetters and exhausting his outflows, he became an Arhat, fully endowed with the noble dharmas of the three knowledges and six supernormal powers.
For this reason, the penetration or obstruction of the Buddha-dharma according to the faculties and natures of sentient beings is known only by the Buddha; one should not raise objections to this.

This bhikṣu has descended from the sixth heaven to be born among humans; he is to be delivered according to his former habitual practices. Therefore, having already made a pure gift, he may possess surplus wealth without violating the precepts.
Question: "Does the steward bhikṣu not violate the precept against possessing surplus goods? Answer:
"There is no offense.
This was a gift given through skillful means, for it was the property of another.
This is the first of the thirty matters.

The reason for establishing these precepts with the bhikṣus is twofold: first, because if one pursues worldly gain, spiritual benefit will not be realized; second, because it would cause the loss of the donors' faith, respect, and pure minds.
If a bhikṣu is insatiable and no different from a layperson, he violates the Buddha’s teaching on the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa).
This is a common precept; both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs incur a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, while śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are five kinds of superfluous items (*adhika-vastu*):

first, precious jewels; second, coins and objects resembling jewels; third, robes or materials for robes that exceed the prescribed measurements; fourth, all robes or materials for robes that do not meet the prescribed measurements; and fifth, all grains, rice, and so forth, as well as all money and treasures. A bhikṣu must not possess these.

If the items are to be assigned in order within the Saṃgha, the bhikṣu must immediately declare them as pure (*śuci*) to another bhikṣu; if he does not so declare them, he must relinquish the precious objects to a trustworthy lay attendant (*śuddhika-puruṣa*). This is as explained in the rules concerning the keeping of precious objects: he must perform a *pāyattika* confession before the Saṃgha.

If one possesses money or items resembling jewels, with the exception of the "one hundred and one" permitted articles, all such things should likewise be relinquished to a pure attendant (śuddha-puruṣa) who shares the same resolve; as explained in the precept regarding the possession of jewels, one should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
There are two ways to purify money and precious objects:
if a layperson brings money or precious objects to a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should simply say:
"This is an impure object; I ought not to possess it."
"If it is pure, you should accept it.
This is the ritual for purification (*pariśuddhi*).
If a layperson says:
"Give this jewel to the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu said,
"I should not possess it."
The attendant said,
"I shall keep it as a purified object.
This constitutes the act of purification (*pariśuddhi*).
If a layperson does not state that they are keeping a purified object, and a bhikṣu himself has not performed the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification), he may simply leave it on the ground.
If there is a bhikṣu present, he should perform the *śuddhi* for it and keep it for as long as necessary.
If there is no bhikṣu present, one must not accept [the robe]; if one accepts it, it constitutes a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
Whether one obtains a robe of proper measure or a robe of improper measure, it is better if one immediately performs the *śuddhi-viśuddhi* (purification/declaration of purity);

if one does not perform the purification, there is no fault for up to ten days. Upon reaching the tenth day, one must either give it to another person, perform the purification, or take formal possession of it.

If one does not give it away, does not perform the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*), and does not take formal possession of it, until the end of the eleventh day at the conclusion of the rainy season retreat, then for a robe of standard measurement, it must be relinquished and one should perform a *pāyattika* confession before another person;
for a robe that exceeds the standard measurement, it must be relinquished and one should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
If a bhikṣu obtains grains, rice, or similar items, he should perform the ritual purification (viśuddhi) on that very day.
If there is no layperson present, he should perform the purification before the fourfold assembly of the Saṅgha.
If he fails to perform the purification until the time for the distribution of bedding has arrived, the grain must be relinquished, and he must perform a confession for the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
A śrāmaṇera should possess two sets of robes: one is a robe to be worn constantly, which should be an antarvāsaka;
the second is an uttarāsaṅga, to be worn when entering the community of monks or when traveling. These must be kept clean.
One may possess a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, one *kaṣāya*, and one *pūro*.
Regarding items worn on the body, it is permitted to keep only one of each; all others are considered surplus property.
If a śrāmaṇera obtains money or precious objects, he must likewise perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification) immediately;
if he does not do so, he must relinquish the money or precious objects and perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
If he obtains clothing that is either of permissible measure or beyond permissible measure, the same ten-day limit applies.
If ten days pass and one has kept surplus items, one must relinquish them and perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
All grains, rice, and so forth may likewise not be kept for more than one night; this follows the same rule as for *bhikṣus*.
Among the five kinds of robes, three types incur the offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika* if kept for more than ten days:
first, a robe gnawed by cattle; second, a robe gnawed by rats; and third, a robe burned by fire.
These three kinds of refuse rags (*pāṃśukūla*), if kept beyond ten days, result in the offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

There are two kinds of robes that do not incur the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (expulsion and forfeiture): first, a robe soiled by the initial sexual union of a man and woman; second, a robe soiled by a woman’s childbirth. If these are kept for more than ten days, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Regarding the "ten-day period": the Buddha, knowing the characteristics of the Dharma, established this limit of ten days—neither lax nor hurried, neither adding nor subtracting.

If one obtains a robe on the first day, one shall not be subject to the act of *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (reinstatement), nor shall one perform such an act, nor shall one carry out the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* for those whose evil and heterodox views have not been removed.

If one’s mind is deranged, disordered by illness, or impaired, and one has not been formally expelled, nor has one regained one's original state of mind, then even until the end of one's life, one does not violate this precept;
however, if one is later expelled or regains one's original state of mind, the offense is calculated from that point forward based on the number of days elapsed.
If one obtains a robe on the first day and ascends to the celestial palaces, dwelling as far north as Uttarakuru,
no offense is committed against this precept until the end of that life;
upon returning to the original location, the offense is established according to the number of days elapsed.

If one receives a robe on the first day and it reaches the fifth day, yet the formal act of suspension has not been performed, or the evil and heterodox views have not been removed through suspension, or if the person is deranged, mentally disturbed, or their mind is impaired— such that they ascend to a celestial palace or travel north to Uttarakuru— and later returns to be released from the suspension,
or regains their original state of mind, or returns to their original location.
Some say that from the day of being subject to the act of suspension, one incurs the offense on the tenth successive day.
Others say:
One takes the first five days as the basis and counts the subsequent five days before the offense is completed.
The Vinaya masters say:
"The latter [period] is the definitive rule."
In Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha, the precepts and Dharma of the bhikṣus exist in their entirety.
These realms are likewise like the dragon palaces, where all things have owners.
Therefore, in these three places, it is not as it is in the heavens, where objects appear spontaneously upon contact.
The goods of Uttarakuru have no owners, and in those two places, there is likewise no monastic code of discipline (*śīla*) for bhikṣus.

Regarding the method of pure giving (*viśuddha-dāna*): in the case of coins or any kind of precious object, one should first seek out a layperson (*avadāta-vastra*) who understands the Dharma and speak to them so that they understand the meaning:
"According to my status as a bhikṣu, it is not the rule to store money or precious objects."
"Now, take the donor as the pure master (*śuddhādhiṣṭhātṛ*); later, when you obtain money or precious objects, give them all back to the donor.

Once a pure master has been obtained, whatever money or precious objects are subsequently acquired must all be declared as pure (*viśuddha*) before the bhikṣus; it is not necessary to state the name of the pure master.
Once the purification (*śuddhi*) has been declared, one may keep the items for as long as necessary, whether near or far.
If the master of purification (*śuddhipati*) dies or departs for another country, one should seek another master of purification.
With the exception of money and precious gems, all surplus property must be purified before the five groups of monks (*pañcavargīya*).

One should seek out a donor who maintains the precepts, is learned, and possesses virtue; subsequently, having obtained goods, one should perform the *śuddhi* (purification) rite by reciting the name of the *śuddhi*-master before a single bhikṣu.
If the *karmadāna* (purifier) dies or travels far to another country, one should seek another *karmadāna*.
This excludes those who have been suspended for not seeing their offense or for not relinquishing a wrong view;
as well as the six types of persons subject to expulsion: [the list follows].
First, shedding the blood of a Buddha; second, causing a schism in the Saṃgha. Together with these, one commits the four pārājika offenses.
Among the six [offenses], even if one commits only a single one, one is likewise ineligible to serve as the presiding master (karmavācanā-ācārya) for the purification ceremony.

A śrāmaṇera who has received the precepts; one who is deaf, mute, blind, or sightless; one whose mind is deranged, disturbed by illness, or corrupted; one who is a *pārivāsika*, a *mānatva*, or any of the five types of persons; and all those who have performed a pure donation (*śuddhadāna*).
Because one wishes to have them serve as witnesses for the sake of purification, one must not give rise to disputes; such persons would then be acting contrary to the Dharma.

If one has declared the purification (*śuci*) of money or jewels, and subsequently exchanges them for all manner of clothing and wealth, making three robes, an alms bowl, and utensils that fall within the category of the "one hundred and one items," no further declaration of purification is required;
however, everything outside of those one hundred and one items must be declared pure.
If money or precious objects are easily obtained through forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika), all clothing and wealth shall be converted into one hundred and one items.
Regarding the prior possession of money, it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense, which should be confessed face-to-face.
Regarding the prior possession of precious objects, one incurs the offense of forfeiture; this must be confessed before the Saṃgha.

If one has already exchanged the materials for clothing to make the "one hundred and one" items, they need not be relinquished again, as they have already entered the state of being purified (*śuddha*).
Regarding anything outside of these one hundred and one items—whether used to make robes or not—all must be declared pure (*śuci-vyavahāra*).

If one speaks of purified money, gems, clothing, or wealth, and someone borrows them away, then at a later time, when the gems are returned, they are returned as gems; when the money is returned, it is returned as money; and for the clothing and wealth, there is no need to speak of them as purified again.
If one borrows an item of a different kind and later returns an item that is not similar, it must be formally dedicated again (*pāriśuddhi*), because the items are different.
If all clothing and wealth have been formally dedicated as part of the "one hundred and one items" (*ekottara-śata-vastu*), there is no further need for dedication.
If one makes pure [cloth] from the remainder, it may be either cloth of proper measure or improper measure.
If there are long-lasting utensils, they must all be declared as pure again.

If one first uses an article subject to the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense that was of proper measure to make cloth of both proper and improper measure, this cloth must be entirely relinquished, and one must perform the *pāyattika* confession.

If one first possessed an article subject to forfeiture for exceeding the prescribed measure (*atireka-pācittiya*), and subsequently used it to make a robe that is both within and beyond the prescribed measure, this robe must be forfeited in its entirety, and one must perform a confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one first possessed an article subject to forfeiture for being within the prescribed measure, and later acquired cloth for a robe and made a robe that is both within and beyond the prescribed measure, this robe is not to be forfeited; one need only confess the prior *pāyattika* offense.

If one first acquires an object subject to forfeiture for exceeding the proper measure, and subsequently purchases cloth with which to make both a garment of proper measure and one of improper measure, this latter garment is not forfeited because it has already entered into the state of being purified; one need only repent for the previous *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the *saṃghāṭī*, *uttarāsaṅga*, and *antarvāsaka*: the reason for establishing these three distinct names is the desire to manifest the unprecedented Dharma.
Among all ninety-six types of [non-Buddhist] schools, none possess these three names; this distinction is made because they differ from the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
Furthermore, as for the saṃghāṭī robe: the inferior has nine strips, the middling eleven strips, and the superior thirteen strips.
Regarding the medium *saṃghāṭī*, the inferior has fifteen strips, the medium has seventeen strips, and the superior has nineteen strips.
Regarding the superior *saṃghāṭī*, the inferior has twenty-one strips, the medium has twenty-three strips, and the superior has twenty-five strips.
The lower *saṃghāṭī* consists of two long and one short [panels]; the middle *saṃghāṭī* consists of three long and one short; the upper *saṃghāṭī* consists of four long and one short.
If one possesses and wears the lower *saṃghāṭī* with three long and one short [panels] while walking about, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one wears the middle *saṃghāṭī* with four lengths and one shortness, or two lengths and one shortness, and carries it while walking about, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one wears the upper *saṃghāṭī* with two lengths and one shortness, or three lengths and one shortness, and carries it while walking about, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The robe should be measured at three or five cubits; at its maximum length it is six cubits and at its maximum width three and a half cubits.
At its minimum, it is four cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width.
If it is in accordance with the Dharma and measures three or five cubits,
when receiving it, one should say:
"This robe is now complete."
There is no fault in accepting and keeping it.
However, if one says, "It is such a robe," then the acceptance is not valid; one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense because it violates the proper decorum.
If it exceeds three or five cubits, at the time of acceptance, one should say:
"In this way, the robe is properly acquired;
there is no fault in its acceptance and maintenance.
If one says that this robe has not been properly acquired through acceptance, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense because it violates the rules of decorum."
Furthermore, because one lacks robes, there is no offense of possessing an extra robe for more than ten days.
If the robe is less than three or five cubits [in length], when receiving it, one should say:
"This robe is now complete."
There is no fault in receiving and keeping [the robe].
If one says that such a robe does not constitute valid acceptance, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense because it violates the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*).
Furthermore, because the robe is incomplete, there is no offense of possessing an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) beyond ten days.
If the robes are three or five cubits long, they may be accepted according to the Dharma, and thus constitute formal possession.
If a bhikṣu dies, his three robes should be given to the attendant who nursed him.
If they exceed three or five cubits, one should inform the Saṃgha of the amount according to its size; it is best if the Saṃgha, being in harmony, grants them [to the attendant].
Regarding the method for receiving robes: if they are of surplus length, one must perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification).
If one does not perform this purification, they are included among the category of surplus property.

Among all the various items belonging to a monk, the three robes and the alms bowl must necessarily be received and maintained; as for other items, it is permissible to receive them, yet there is no fault in not doing so.

If a bhikṣu does not accept the three robes for more than ten days, he incurs no offense of possessing extra robes and no offense of being separated from his robes overnight; however, he incurs the offense of violating dignified decorum and the offense of having a deficient set of robes.
If a new *saṃghāṭī* consists of at most three layers—where one layer is new and two layers are old—it is called "new clothing.
If the robe is made entirely of new material, it is a newly made *saṃghāṭī* consisting of two new layers; the same applies to the *niṣīdana*.
If one makes a new uttarāsaṅga or antarvāsaka from new cloth, each shall consist of a single layer.
If the old cloth is extremely abundant, the saṃghāṭī may be four layers thick, the uttarāsaṅga two layers, the antarvāsaka two layers, and the niṣīdana four layers.
If the three robes are torn, it does not matter whether the holes are large or small; as long as the seams remain intact, they continue to constitute the formal possession (*dhāraṇa*).
Even if the robes have become worn from age or have lost their color, the formal possession is not lost.
If one later applies a different color to it, the status of its being properly maintained is not lost.

If one patches the robe with other materials, yet if it is merely sewn straight [without forming a patch] and the robe cannot be completed, then if ten days pass, one falls into the offense of possessing extra cloth (*dīrghadravya*), unless one has previously performed the ritual of *śuddhika* (purification).
If the cloth is joined by reversing the hooks and needles so that it becomes a complete robe, one should apply three dots [of dye] and there is no need to undergo the formal act of acceptance again.
If the material for the robe was previously declared pure (*śuddha*), but later it is made into a robe and formally accepted as such, then the state of purity is lost.
If this robe is later relinquished, it must be formally purified (*śuddhi*) again.
If it is not purified, one incurs the offense of keeping an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*).

If a bhikṣu has re-sewn his three robes and, due to some circumstance, removes a portion and carries it away to another location, this is called "not being separated from one's robes while staying overnight."
If a bhikṣu dies, it is further said:
"The formal act (karmavācanā) concerning this robe was performed within the original boundary.
It is also said:
One should give [the robe] to the attendant, because it was originally held as a single robe together with him.
The Vinaya Master says:
"The latter is the definitive rule."
If there is a cause and condition such that a single piece of cloth may serve as three robes, provided its color is made to conform to the Dharma,
one may accept it as a single robe or accept it as two robes, receiving and maintaining it according to what is obtained.
If there is an extra cloth beyond fifteen cubits, it must be declared as pure (*śuddha*).
If it is not so declared, one falls into the offense of possessing excessive wealth (*atireka-lābha*).
[Next is] the method for receiving the three robes (*tricīvara*).
It should be recited three times.
One must not say "the second," and the same applies to the third.

Regarding the offense herein: if one obtains a robe on the first day and discards it on the second, and continues in this manner until obtaining a robe on the ninth day and discarding it on the tenth; or if one obtains a robe on the tenth day and keeps that robe for ten days without discarding it, without formally accepting it, and without performing the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*), then upon the conclusion of the day on the eleventh, it constitutes an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Regarding the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: although all robes from the preceding nine days have been relinquished and purified, because of the causal continuity of the previous sequence, one incurs the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for the single robe obtained on the tenth day.
In all these cases, what is referred to as "renouncing" (捨) constitutes a complete purification (*viśuddhi*).
Inferring from this principle, the subsequent clauses may be understood by analogy.

If one obtains a robe on the first day and renounces it on the first day, and then obtains another robe on the second day—because there is no continuity between them—one may successively obtain robes for ten days starting from those two days.

If one obtains a robe on the first day and discards it on the second, and does not obtain another robe on the second day but obtains one on the third, and continues obtaining robes in this sequence for three days up to the tenth day, because they do not form a continuous connection.
Regarding the "ten-day robe" within this context, it is defined by a continuous succession according to the sequence of days.

If one obtains a robe on the first day and discards it on the second day, and then obtains another robe on the second day, it is considered continuous with the first day; for within that same day, there is one act of discarding and one act of receiving.

If one receives a robe on the first day and relinquishes it on the first day, and receives another robe on the second day such that it is not continuous with the robe received on the first day—because they were relinquished on different days and received on different days—then these two robes shall again follow the sequence for ten days.
Subsequent phrases may be inferred by analogy; their meaning can thus be understood.

If a bhikṣu has already relinquished a robe that ought to be relinquished and has already confessed his offense, yet the continuity [of the transgression] has not been severed, and he subsequently obtains another robe, this later robe constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense in relation to the former robe.

Regarding the statement "obtaining [an item] in succession," this does not refer to a chronological succession of days. Rather, it is called "succession" because the mind repeatedly seeks [the item] without interruption.

Once the robe has been relinquished and the offense has been confessed, the mental continuity of seeking is severed. If, on that very day, the robe previously sought arrives, or if an unexpected robe arrives, it does not fall under the category of "succession," because the mental continuity has been broken.

If one relinquishes the robe on that very day, confesses the transgression on that very day, yet the intention to seek a robe does not cease for up to a month—whether the sought-after robe arrives or another comes unexpectedly—all such instances constitute a continuous succession. This robe thus incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense in relation to the previous robe; the offense is incurred on the very day the robe is obtained, without the need to wait for further days.

If one relinquishes the robe today, repents the offense, and severs the intention that very day, yet later on, due to further conditions, one again seeks and obtains a robe, this does not constitute a continuous succession of offenses, because the intention was severed in the interim.

When the ground is perceived as cleared, one relinquishes the robe; having already confessed the offense, the subsequent continuity of the mind is severed. If, toward evening, one again seeks and obtains a robe, that robe is relinquished, and one must perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.

If the robe has already been relinquished, the continuity [of the offense] has already been severed, and the transgression has not yet been confessed, even if one obtains a robe after many days, the relinquishing of that robe constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

2. The Second Section on the Causes and Conditions for Staying Apart from One’s Robe Overnight. Regarding the foreign designations for the appearance of dawn (*aruṇodaya*), there are various names: the Brahmins call it "the Sun" (*sūrya*); the wealthy and noble call it "The Easy One" (*sukara*); the mountain-dwellers and Hu peoples call it "Quashing Sand" (*kṣaya*); those who work as farmers call it "The Time of Farming" (*karṣaka-kāla*); and fishermen call it "The Manifestation" (*vyakta*).
In this way, all such characteristics are not themselves the characteristic of clarity; rather, these various names are applied upon the characteristic of clarity.
Regarding "for a minor reason": Mahākāśyapa was generally responsible for managing five great monasteries:

first, the Gṛdhrakūṭa Monastery; second, the Bamboo Grove Monastery; and there were three other monasteries. On this occasion, while he was attending to the Bamboo Grove Monastery, he came to the Bamboo Grove.
For example, Śāriputra oversaw the construction of the Jetavana Vihāra, and Maudgalyāyana managed five hundred monasteries.
A question was asked:

"Since these disciples have exhausted their outflows and fetters and have accomplished what was to be done, for what reason do they still repeatedly engage in such management and perform various meritorious deeds?"

He replied: "First, it is to repay the Buddha's kindness; second, it is to nurture and develop the Buddha-dharma; third, it is to eliminate the arrogance of ordinary and inferior sentient beings who perform minor meritorious deeds for their own self-exaltation; fourth, it is to subdue the haughty minds of future disciples; and fifth, it is to inspire the performance of meritorious deeds among future sentient beings."
Question: "Mahākāśyapa possesses great supernormal powers; for what reason did he not depart by means of his supernormal powers, but instead allow the falling rain to become an obstacle? Answer:
“Kāśyapa personally managed the monastery; he personally applied mud to the walls and personally leveled the ground.
Once he had personally leveled the ground, it rained heavily from the heavens.”
Because of the rain from the heavens, he entered into meditative concentration, vowing to arise once the rain had ceased.
The rain continued throughout the night and stopped at dawn; he then emerged from concentration as the morning light had already appeared.
It is further said:

At that time, the Buddha preached the *Kṣudrapaṇḍita-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Withered Tree) for the bhikṣus; some bhikṣus returned home to lay life, while others were filled with anxiety and distress, unable to find peace within themselves.

At that time, Kāśyapa preached the Dharma to the bhikṣus as was appropriate for them throughout the entire night without ceasing; when the preaching was finished, day had already broken, and for this reason he did not employ supernatural powers.
"I have stayed overnight separated from my saṃghāṭī robe;
what should I do now? He asked:
"Mahākāśyapa is a man of great wisdom who can thoroughly understand even profound and momentous matters; this is but a minor matter—why should he need to ask anyone about it?"
He replied:

"I wish that future sentient beings will not rely on their own meager wisdom or limited eloquence with self-assurance and self-importance, but will always maintain a sense of their own inadequacy and consult others."
"This was done to serve as a model for all beings and to manifest this trace.
As for praising the precepts and those who uphold them, the reason for praising the precepts is that the mind is thereby made virtuous.
Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa, from the very beginning, the Buddha has never rebuked him.
As with Śāriputra, the Buddha also rebuked him, saying:
"Why do you eat impure food?
As with Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Buddha also rebuked him, saying:
"Why did you confer full ordination upon one who has not yet completed twenty years?
As with Nanda, the Buddha also rebuked him:
"Why did you instruct a nun even until the time of sunset?"
As with Udāyin, the Buddha also rebuked him, saying:
"You foolish man, you engage in debate and contend for victory with Śāriputra!
As with Ānanda, the Buddha also rebuked him, saying:
“Foolish man, why do you provoke and trouble the Elder?
For Mahākāśyapa had never been rebuked by the Buddha, as his virtuous conduct was profound and he was free from any fault.

Furthermore, it is because he wishes to ensure that the Great Dharma is maintained after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; even if there should be minor deficiencies, they shall not be grounds for censure, so that sentient beings of future generations may regard it with profound respect.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa always delighted in practicing the Path; he would enter meditative concentration at the appropriate time and only arise when dawn broke.
As for Śāriputra, his mother’s name was Śārī;
"Putra" means "son of" in the language of Qin. Thus, he is called "Son of Śārī."
Because he was born from the śarīra [relics], he is named Śāriputra.
Furthermore, while his mother was pregnant, she dreamed of a man of upright appearance and dignified bearing, clad in armor and helmet and holding a great club in his hand, who entered into her body.
The physiognomist’s divination stated:
"A person of wisdom shall be born, whose intelligence and eloquence will be unsurpassed in the world; he will surely be able to defeat and subdue all masters of debate.
It further stated:

While his mother was pregnant with him, her spiritual wisdom surpassed that of ordinary people; she sought out masters of debate to contend with them for victory, leading the people of the time to wonder and say she had lost her original nature.
The Brahmins said, "This is not due to her own power;
it is simply because she carries within her a man of great wisdom."
Once it was known for certain that this was so, they provided constant attendance and protection as usual, and when the month was full, she gave birth.
As for Śāriputra’s illness, among the Buddha’s disciples, none suffered more from sickness than Śāriputra.
He was constantly afflicted by wind-cold and also suffered from the disease of hot blood. A physician said:
"For a wind-disease, one should consume barley gruel.
Another said:
"For a blood disorder, one should take barley gruel to drink.
He further said:
"One should heat stones until they are red-hot, place them in milk, and drink it."
He further said:
"One should boil garlic in breast milk and eat it.
He also said:
"You should take tree leaves, wring out the juice, and smear it upon your body.
He further said:
"Put on a meditation belt."
Śāriputra possesses great merit and wisdom; why then does he suffer from such an illness?
Furthermore, it is said:
"It is due to the karmic conditions of Śāriputra’s previous lives."
Because in past lives he troubled and disturbed his parents as well as his teachers and monks, he therefore has this illness.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Śāriputra possesses sharp faculties and wisdom."

Deeply imbued with the flavor of the Dharma, he constantly cultivated wisdom and the methods of debate; furthermore, delighting in meditative concentration, he exhorted others to perform various tasks. He was diligent in the three karmas without a moment’s slackening, and because his sleeping and rising were irregular, he contracted this illness.
It is further said:
"This is my final body; having first exhausted all the karmic retributions for the offenses of past lives, I shall then enter *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, I am frequently ill.
He wished to travel for one month.
Question:
"Śāriputra is ill; why does he wish to travel? Answer:
"Because there are sentient beings with the conditions for conversion who ought to receive it.
Just as the Buddha surveys sentient beings six times each day, never missing the opportune moment to deliver those ready to be saved,

so too Śāriputra, the second master of turning the Wheel of Dharma, constantly observes sentient beings six times each day, knowing those ready for deliverance and saving them according to what is appropriate."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, wishing to uphold the Buddha-dharma and travel through various kingdoms, he should act according to what is appropriate and adapt his conduct to suit the circumstances; for this reason, he ought to travel.

Moreover, due to the ailment of wind-cold, traveling would cause him self-inflicted suffering, as illness leads to physical decline and impairment; furthermore, it is so that he may seek out places suitable for practicing the Way.
Furthermore, in various lands, he intends to subdue those who ought to be subdued, and to inspire faith and awakening in those already subdued.
He asked: “Why does he travel for exactly one month?”
He replied:
"The sentient beings with whom he has a karmic connection will be exhausted within one month; therefore, it is one month.
Furthermore, it is said:"
Those who ought to be subdued shall be finished within one month.
Furthermore, it is said:
whatever clothing and bedding one requires shall be sufficient within one month.
It is further said:
"One should seek what is required for the illness; it shall be prepared within one month.
This refers to the heavy *saṃghāṭī*.
Question:
"Śāriputra possesses the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), by which he could turn the trichiliocosm around in his hand; why then do you say that the saṃghāṭī robe is heavy?"
He replied:

"The reason Śāriputra travels about is his desire to transform sentient beings. However, those who are to be delivered by him cannot attain awakening through supernatural powers; therefore, he does not manifest such powers. He ought to travel on foot, yet his saṃghāṭī robe is heavy."
Furthermore, it is said:

"If I were to go to subdue those who have not yet been subdued, the various masters of treatises might be defeated by my reasoning; however, if I were to manifest supernatural powers, it would only increase their arrogance. For this reason, I do not manifest my supernormal faculties. Yet, if I wish to travel on foot, my saṃghāṭī robe is too heavy."
Furthermore, it is said:
