because he manifests the aspect of great compassion, and in order that future bhikṣus who are aged or ill shall be free from all afflictions, he intends to cause the Tathāgata to establish the causal conditions for granting the *karmavācanā* of "not being separated from one's robes for one month" to aged and sick bhikṣus.
"An 'elder' is one who is seventy years of age or older.
He asked:
"For what reason did the Buddha establish the rule of not being separated from one's robe for one month?"
He replied:
"It is for the sake of the causal conditions of delivering sentient beings, and also for the sake of the causal conditions of practicing the Path.
By not wearing heavy robes, one may be free from suffering and affliction; thus, there is no hindrance to cultivating one's practice according to the season."

Furthermore, it is for the sake of seeking what is required for one's person; for the sake of seeking what is appropriate for those who are ill or emaciated; for the sake of constructing vihāras, stūpas, and monasteries; for the sake of subduing those not yet subdued; and for the sake of engendering faith and awakening in those already subdued.
It is said: "If one loses or discards the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; one must perform the confession.

This second precept regarding not sleeping apart from one's robes is common to both *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs*; it does not apply to *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, or *śrāmaṇerīs*, as they have no precept regarding sleeping apart from their robes.
When nuns establish a great boundary (mahā-sīmā), it may extend at most one krośa; this is the same as the rule for the one-month robe [retention].
However, when the Saṃgha establishes a robe boundary (cīvara-sīmā), the nuns' case is not the same.
The nuns' establishment of the robe-boundary (cīvara-sīmā) differs from that of the monks.

Generally, when establishing a great boundary (mahāsīmā), the reason for including the village within it is that, by the power of the boundary established by the Saṃgha, evil cannot find an opportunity.
Furthermore, because it is protected by the benevolent deities within the boundary and is for the sake of the *dānapati*, this constitutes the delimitation of the entire village.
If one is to establish a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), the Saṃgha must assemble in its entirety; no one may give their consent (*chanda*) by proxy.
Regarding "wearing upper and lower robes while traveling through various countries": the upper robe is the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the lower robe is the *antarvāsaka*.

Regarding "one night": it is also said that day and night are defined merely by the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); that which is bright and clear is day, and that which is dark and obscure is night.
It is further said:
the five aggregates constitute day and night.
As for "the sun setting," it is called the setting of the sun when the sun has passed beyond the boundaries of Jambudvīpa.
Regarding the "appearance of light" (*ālokanimitta*), there are various different names.

It has three kinds of colors: when the sun shines upon the Jambū tree, it appears black; when it shines upon the leaves of the tree, it appears blue; and when it passes beyond the tree and shines upon the Jambūdvīpa region, it appears white.
Among the three types of colors, white is considered the standard.
If one stays overnight separated from one's robe until the appearance of the dawn light, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

However, there are cases where one relinquishes the robe without incurring guilt; for example, if a bhikṣu goes outside the boundary to stay elsewhere, borrows a robe and maintains possession of it, and then, upon the passing of the night, relinquishes the robe and returns it to the owner—this is called relinquishing the robe without fault.

There are cases where one incurs an offense but does not relinquish the robe. For example, when a bhikṣu goes beyond his boundary to stay overnight elsewhere, he borrows a robe and accepts it; once he has passed through the designated area, he immediately returns the borrowed robe to the other person. Without performing the formal rite of relinquishment (*pratyāśraya-dharma*), he takes back his own robe. Because he has taken up his own robe again without having relinquished the previous one, his dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) is impaired, and he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is called incurring an offense while not relinquishing the robe.

There are cases where one both relinquishes the robe and incurs an offense. For example, if a bhikṣu possesses his own robe and stays overnight outside the boundary, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense at dawn; this is called both relinquishing the robe and incurring an offense.

Or, there are cases where one does not incur an offense despite not relinquishing the robe; for example, when a bhikṣu personally undertakes the practice of keeping his robe with him and does not leave it overnight—this is called "not relinquishing the robe and incurring no offense.
Regarding the exception of the *saṃgha-karman*: the Saṃgha first establishes a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), and subsequently establishes a robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*).

Regarding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), its maximum extent is ten *krośas* in length and breadth; one must ensure that no doubt arises within it during the performance of the *karmavācanā* or the *poṣadha*.

Even if there are rivers or major roads within it, they may still be included in the formal demarcation, provided that one crosses to the other bank, establishes the boundary markers (*nimitta*), and then performs the binding.
Once this has been lowered, there is no offense regarding distance, proximity, size, or magnitude.
If one performs the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to establish a robe-boundary (*cīvarasīmā*), one should state: "Excluding the village and the village boundary."
The reason for excluding inhabited areas is that such areas are characterized by distraction and instability, whereas the boundary of the robe (cīvara-sīmā) is fixed.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of avoiding slander, for the purpose of avoiding strife, for the purpose of protecting the holy life (brahmacarya), and for the purpose of removing suspicion.
Furthermore, it is said:
if there is a village, one should say "excluding the village"; if there is no village, it is unnecessary to say "excluding.
It is further said:
The nature of the *karmavācanā* procedure is such that [the boundary] is removed at all times, whether [the village] exists or not.

This is because if, at the time of establishing the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), there was no village, and after the robe-boundary has been established, a village subsequently enters within the boundary, it is unnecessary to establish it again, as it has already been established previously.

If there was originally a village and, after the robe-boundary (cīvara-sīmā) has been established, one moves out beyond that boundary, then this empty space is called "not separated from the robe-boundary.
If a village was originally small and later expands, the entire area reached by the expansion of the village is no longer part of the robe-boundary.

If a village was originally large and, after the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) has been established, it subsequently becomes smaller, then all the empty space that remains is part of the robe-boundary.

Furthermore, if a king enters within the boundary and pitches a tent to stay, the areas for preparing food and drink nearby, as well as the places for walking about and performing the necessities of life, are all excluded from the robe-boundary.

If illusionists, practitioners of incantations, or musicians enter the territory and stay at their place of residence, according to the royal law, these places are all not within the boundary of the robes.

Furthermore, regarding the exception for the *saṃgha-karman*: it is as when Śāriputra’s saṃghāṭī was heavy, and for the sake of bhikṣus who were aged or ill, the rule of not being separated from one's robe for one month was established.

If, after the *karmavācanā* has been completed, one recovers from illness and travels within that same month—provided that if the illness was severe and one did not travel immediately upon the completion of the *karmavācanā*, and subsequently, having recovered, did not travel again, but fell ill once more—one may still travel within that same month by performing the *karmavācanā* for the first time [for the renewed journey]. Thus, one is permitted to travel.

If there are sentient beings yet to be transformed and the month has already ended; or if one seeks clothing, medicine, or other necessities, or is engaged in activities for the sake of the Triple Gem, and the month has already ended before these requests are fulfilled—because such matters are difficult to accomplish, there is no offense once the circumstances have concluded.
If a bhikṣu dies, these robes should be given to the attendant who nursed him, because the robes belong to the deceased bhikṣu.
If the robes are lost and he obtains other robes—regardless of whether they are superior or inferior—he should perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) once again.
If one gives to the Triple Gem and subsequently seeks to obtain robes, one must likewise perform the *karmavācanā* again.
This applies even up to the ninth month.
It is because of specific causes and conditions that one month is established, and it is because of the causes and conditions of that month that nine months are established.
Question:
"Why is it exactly nine months, neither more nor less? Answer:
“Monks, having entered the three-month retreat in a single location to cultivate their practice, it is therefore nine months.
He asked: “Is this by means of a single *karmavācanā*?”
"Is it performed by nine karmas?
He replied, "By one karma."
As it is with the saṃghāṭī, so it is with the uttarāsaṅga and the antarvāsaka.
For specific reasons, the saṃghāṭī was permitted;
because of the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga and the antarvāsaka were permitted.
Question: "Is it permitted to be separated from one robe, or is it further permitted to be separated from two robes? Answer:
"Two robes are not permitted.
The reason three robes are prescribed is to ward off the cold; one robe cannot dispel the cold.
It is also to maintain a sense of shame and modesty; one robe cannot sustain a sense of shame and modesty."
Furthermore, the three robes were prescribed for the purpose of entering a village; it is not appropriate to enter a village with only one robe.
Moreover, the three robes were prescribed to generate a heart of joy in others; with only one robe, one does not inspire a virtuous mind in people.
The three robes were prescribed for the sake of purity in deportment; with only one robe, deportment is not pure.
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to keep only two robes, she likewise may not do so. The reason five robes are prescribed is for the sake of deportment; with only three robes, deportment is not perfected.
The rest is as previously explained.
If one wears the *uttarāsaṅga* and *antarvāsaka*, one may enter the royal palace or a village at all times without fault.

If a *māsa-kamma* (one-month formal act) is performed—whether for an elderly bhikṣu whose *saṃghāṭī* is heavy, or for one who is not actually old or ill but whose *saṃghāṭī* is heavy—the *kamma* is validly established; the Saṃgha incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, while the former person incurs no guilt because he was ignorant of the Dharma.
If the person before [the speaker] knows the Dharma, they also incur a *duṣkṛta*.

If one is not actually old or ill, and the *saṃghāṭī* robe is not heavy, yet one says "I am old and ill, and the robe is heavy," one incurs a *pāyattika* and the formal act (*karmavācanā*) is validly accomplished.
There may be a village boundary that is not a household boundary, such as when there are two villages each with only one household; this is called a village boundary that is not a household boundary.

There may be a household boundary that is not a village boundary, such as when there is one large village with no other neighboring villages but many households; this is called a household boundary that is not a village boundary.

There may be that which is both a village boundary (*grāma-sīman*) and a household boundary (*kula-sīman*), such as when two villages each consist of many households; this is what is meant by being both a village boundary and a household boundary.

There may be that which is neither a village boundary nor a household boundary, such as a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka-sthāna*); this is what is meant by being neither a village boundary nor a household boundary.
A village has both a single boundary (*ekasīma*) and distinct boundaries (*pṛthaksīma*). A contiguous village is called a single boundary; a non-contiguous village is called a distinct boundary.

A household also has both a single boundary and distinct boundaries. If it refers to the dwelling place of the rooms and buildings, it is called a single boundary; if it refers to the place where food is prepared, the place where water is drawn, the gateway, or the places for defecation and urination, these are called distinct boundaries.
The subsequent phrases may be understood by analogy.

"Not contiguous with a village" refers to a place where a rooster can fly, a place where an arrow can be shot, a place where men and women are distinguished, or a place where a person of modesty performs their bodily functions.

If there is exactly one household in a village, and one places one's robe within that single household and lies down within range of an arrow-shot, then even if one reaches the appearance of dawn, one does not lose the robe.
If the robe is located within range of an arrow-shot and the bhikṣu sleeps within a house, he does not lose the robe even if he rises at the appearance of dawn.
However, if there are many houses in a village and the robe is in one house while he sleeps in another within arrow-shot range, he loses the robe because the boundaries of each house are distinct.
If one places one’s robe outside the boundary of the inhabited area (*grāmavastu*) and lies down within range of an arrow-shot, one does not lose possession of the robe.

Regarding the boundary of contiguous villages: if there are villages on all four sides such that one can climb up onto the walls from all directions using twelve rungs of a ladder to enter or exit, and one lies down at the base of the ladder while placing the robe in the villages on the four sides, then one is not separated from the robe, because the ladders connect in all four directions.
If there is only one household in a village, the robe is not lost even if it remains inside that house.
If there are many households in a village, the robe is lost if it remains inside a house; however, if the robe is outside the boundary of the village, it is not lost.
If there is a ladder, the robe remains with one even if it is located in four separate villages;
the robe is not lost. If there is no ladder, the robe is lost if it is in four separate villages, because they are not connected.
Furthermore, there is the boundary of contiguous villages: for example, where there are two villages on opposite sides with a road between them wide enough for a carriage to pass back and forth.

If the two ends of the carriage axle reach into the two villages, and one places a robe at one end while a person stands at the other end—even if they are both upon the carriage—they do not lose their robes, because the carriage connects them.
Suppose there is a village consisting of only one household, and the robe is within that single household; even if one lies down upon a cart, one does not lose the robe.
If there is no cart, the connection is not established; it is only if there is a cart that one does not lose the robe, whereas if there is no cart, one loses the robe.

If a village is surrounded on all four sides by walls or fences, such that there is space for activities within them, this constitutes the boundary of the village; because of these enclosures, its influence does not extend far.
If a village is surrounded on all four sides by a moat, the area reached by the throwing of refuse is called the village boundary (*grāma-sīman*).

Regarding those surrounded by walls or fences and those surrounded by moats, these two types of boundaries differ from the former in that they do not connect; rather, it is the village boundary that connects to the village boundary.

Within a clan there are both a single realm and distinct realms; if parents, brothers, and sons share one meal and one occupation without having established separate distinctions, this is called a family.

If parents, brothers, and sons eat separately and engage in separate occupations, such that they are entirely distinct—even though they dwell in the same place—their affairs being each different, this is called a clan (*kula*).

A clan has both a single boundary and distinct boundaries; that which each has as its place of residence is called a single boundary, while the place where food is prepared, the gateway, the place for drawing water, or the place for performing the great and small necessities of life are called distinct boundaries.
If the robe is with one clan while the person is with another clan, then the robe is lost.
If the person is in one place while the robe is at the water source or at the food-preparation area, then the robe is lost.

From then on, when traveling through villages, the dwellings of non-Buddhists, fields, or gardens, if the owners are different and their views are different, one loses the robe; if the owner is the same and the views are the same, one does not lose the robe.
The meaning can be inferred through reasoning.
Regarding a multi-storied house: if the robe is on the upper floor and the person is on the lower floor, and the house belongs to a single owner, one does not lose possession of the robe.

If one abandons this [robe] to another master, such that the robe is in the upper layer and the person is in the lower layer, or the robe is in the lower layer and the person is in the upper layer, then one loses possession of the robe.

If the robe is in the lower layer and the person is in the middle layer, or if the robe is in the middle layer and the person is in the lower layer, or if the robe is in the upper layer and the person is in the middle layer, or if the robe is in the middle layer and the person is in the upper layer, then one does not lose possession of the robe, because the intermediate layers are joined and interconnected.
If a bhikṣu carries robes for his teacher, the distance between them—whether preceding or following—should be forty-nine *vyāma*.
The Vinaya master says:
it is also permissible for the length and breadth [of the space] to be forty-nine *vyāma*.
If a bhikṣu lies upon the boundary between two realms, with his body within both realms and his robe also in both realms, he does not lose his robe.
If there is a single wall separating two villages, and he lies upon that wall with his robe in both villages, he likewise does not lose his robe.
If a bhikṣu dies between two boundaries, the robe should be taken according to whichever direction he was facing at the time of death.
It is further stated:
"The robe shall be taken according to whichever place he first beheld."
3. The Third Account of Upasena’s Untimely Death. Regarding the account of Upasena’s untimely death: "I wish to remain in meditative seclusion for four months.
He asked:
"The Buddha established the Four Great Vows over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, desiring to deliver boundless sentient beings."
"Now that you have already attained the Way, why do you remain so tranquil and self-contained?
He replied:

"The Buddha never fails to deliver sentient beings. Sometimes he performs the work of a Buddha through silent stillness; sometimes he performs the work of a Buddha by preaching the Dharma. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, there is nothing that is not the work of a Buddha."
Generally, those who dwell in silence may be free from physical distraction, or free from mental distraction, or free from both body and mind.

During the Buddha’s four months of secluded meditation (*kāyotsarga*), he either dwelt in various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna-samādhi*), or traveled to other realms to liberate sentient beings, or entered into the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*), and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).

The reason the Buddha sits in quiet seclusion is that sentient beings might become complacent and indolent if they see the Buddha constantly; he wishes to cause them to give rise to a heart of yearning and longing, and furthermore, he does not wish to allow non-Buddhists and those with heterodox views to continue their long-standing derision and slander.

Because people commonly see the Buddha traveling through various countries, they assume he is merely wandering about without any substantial Dharma within; therefore, his quietude and silence are likewise not empty.

Furthermore, because he wishes to establish a model for future disciples, the Buddha—though fully endowed with all merit and wisdom—does not abandon meditative silence; how much more so, then, should ordinary people refrain from giving rise to indolence.

Furthermore, the Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher; when he enters meditative absorption in silence, traversing various immeasurable Dharma-gates, this is precisely the "Dharma-offering to the Teacher.
Regarding the four months of *kāyotsarga* (seated meditation), during the Buddha's lifetime there were three such periods of seated meditation:
first, after his initial attainment of the Way, he sat in meditation for fifteen days, during which time he also prohibited the bhikṣus from seeing him.
"The two-month period in the middle [of the rainy season] for sitting in meditation shall likewise be established as a regulation. He asked:
"Why did the Buddha establish [the retreats] at the beginning for one month and a half, in the middle for two months, and at the end for four months?"
He replied:
"When I first attained the Way, I began to deliver sentient beings; because the causes and conditions for transforming sentient beings were so numerous, I sat in quiet meditation for fifteen days."
At that time, because the external conditions for those beings to be converted gradually diminished, it was two months.
Later, when the time for *parinirvāṇa* arrived, the beings to be converted were nearly exhausted; therefore, it was four months.
Furthermore, when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, those among sentient beings who committed evil were few; they would recognize their transgressions merely by the fifteenth-day fast.
Later, as sentient beings gradually increased in their commission of evil, they also recognized their transgressions by practicing *kāyotsarga* (seated meditation) for two months.
At a later time, they frequently committed unrighteous acts; it was only after sitting in meditation for four months that they recognized their transgressions.
"In the past, one could go as one pleased. He asked:
“Monks, why do you not speak to Upasena regarding the regulations of the Saṃgha?
They replied, “Upasena is a man of great virtue who upholds the Buddha-dharma; out of fear of causing him difficulty, we did not dare speak to him.”

"Except for one bhikṣu who delivers food and the uposatha; for the former is an offering of food to the Buddha’s physical body (rūpakāya), and the latter is an offering of the uposatha to the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), therefore these are permitted."
This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, while for the three assemblies [of śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding "out-of-season robes": the period from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month is designated as the "robe season."
If there is a *kaṭhina* robe, the period up to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month is called the "time for robes.
From the sixteenth day of the twelfth month until the fifteenth day of the fourth month is called the "non-time."
During these four months, if a person offers robes as part of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, these are called "out-of-season robes" (*akālacīvara*).

However, if within these four months one receives robes offered by parents, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, or former spouses; or if they are received during the five-year assembly (*pañcavārṣika*) or a house-entry assembly (*gṛhapraveśa*), these are not called out-of-season robes, because each of these occasions has its own established rule.
If one seeks robes for oneself after having already requested them, it is not considered "out-of-season," because requesting when one’s three robes are complete is not permitted.

If one obtains an incomplete set of robes and sets them aside with the intention of making them complete, this may continue for up to one month; if one keeps them longer than that, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding this essence of the precept: because one has obtained an incomplete robe and wishes to make it complete, one may keep it for up to one month.
One must diligently seek to have the robe completed during that month, maintaining the intention without interruption for the duration of the month.
If at some time the expectation of obtaining [a robe] is interrupted before a month has passed,
and on the first day one obtains a robe, one should immediately form this thought:
"What I have expected for these ten days will certainly not be obtained."
This robe must not exceed ten days [of possession].

If it exceeds ten days, and if this robe—even one measuring four cubits—is made without seams or borders, yet one continues to keep it beyond ten days, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If the robe is not of the proper measure, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; this robe should be relinquished.
Even up to the tenth day, one should reflect thus:
"I fear that what I have hoped for on this first day will certainly not be obtained."
If this robe is not given away, not made into a finished garment, and not purified within one day, the same applies up to the eleventh day as previously stated.

If on the first day one acquires a robe and sets it aside, whether one obtains what was expected or what was unexpected, regarding these two types of robes, if within ten days they are not made into a finished garment, not purified, not given away, and not formally accepted, then upon reaching the eleventh day, these two robes—even if they are as small as four cubits—constitute an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

If it is not of the proper measure, this robe must be relinquished and an *dukkaṭa* confession performed; for although one has not obtained what was hoped for, that which was obtained unexpectedly must still be made into a robe.

If a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and keeps it in hopes of obtaining more, and by the ninth day he has not obtained what he expected, but instead obtains what was not expected, this robe is subject to the same rules as previously stated regarding the eleventh day.

If on the first day one obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the tenth day neither obtains what was hoped for nor obtains what was not expected, then if that robe is not made into a garment, not given away, not purified (*pariśuddha*), and not formally accepted within those ten days, the same rules apply as previously stated upon reaching the eleventh day.

4. The Fourth Case Concerning Taking Robes from a Nun Who Is Not a Relative. Regarding the nun Puṣpā:
her appearance was upright and graceful, and her complexion was the color of the blue lotus (utpala).

In a time long ago, many kalpas past, this person was a Brahmin girl. Her parents and family members went out to sea to gather treasures, leaving her behind; unable to support herself, she lived together with various courtesans in one place, selling her beauty to provide for her own needs.
This woman’s appearance was not beautiful, and no one came to visit her.
She constantly reproached herself, wondering why she alone was so unfortunate.
At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha whom everyone revered and admired.
Someone said to her, "If you can make offerings to a pratyekabuddha, you shall have whatever you desire in every lifetime, according to your wishes.
At that time, the woman followed those words; she prepared delicious food and drink, covered it with *utpala* flowers, and presented it to the pratyekabuddha.
She immediately made this vow:
"May I, in every successive life, always be born as a woman, peerlessly beautiful and respected by all, such that none can surpass me.
Furthermore, may I attain the merits and virtues realized by these śramaṇas."
For this reason, she remains a woman even in this present life, yet her physical appearance is foremost;
because of her original vow, she has now attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
As for the Andhavana Forest, it is called the "Forest of Daytime Darkness"; this forest is vast and luxuriant, and beneath its trees the sun does not shine.
Furthermore, there was a guild-president named Ānanda; it was for this reason that he was given that name.
He wrapped a piece of meat in expensive cloth and hung it upon a tree.
He asked:
"If someone were to take this piece of meat,
from whom would they incur an offense— from the thief or from the nun?
He replied:
"One incurs an offense against a nun.
Regarding why her robes are tattered and worn-out,
it is asked:
“Puṣpacitra possesses great merit and renown, and is well-known to many people; why is it that his clothing is not sufficient?
He replied:
“In this world there are two kinds of people who are neither weary nor satisfied:”
First, whatever he obtained he accumulated; second, whatever he obtained he gave to others.
Because Puṣpavarṇa gave everything he acquired to those who asked, his basic necessities for sustaining life were constantly in short supply.

"Regarding those filling the long robes: this refers to when the Buddha entered his private chamber for four months of silent seclusion, and many bhikṣus discarded their lay-person’s robes to wear rag-robes (pāṃśukūla), which are artificial garments."

The fourth rule concerning taking a robe from a nun who is not a relative: this is a unique precept (an-āveṇika-śikṣāpada) for which bhikṣuṇīs do not incur an offense, while śrāmaṇeras commit a *duṣkṛta*.

The reason this precept was established for the bhikṣus is precisely because it is inappropriate for men and women to associate with one another and become mutually habituated; such association leads to various unwholesome conditions, and therefore it was prohibited.
If it is a relative, there is no cause for suspicion nor is it contrary to the Dharma; therefore, it is permitted.
Regarding the taking of robes: this refers to robes of the proper measure.

If they are the robes of a layperson or robes of an improper color, one must not take them; because they must be dyed to conform to the Dharma, to take them [otherwise] constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If many bhikṣus take a single robe, all are guilty of an offense.
If one bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī, it is calculated as an offense for the bhikṣuṇī.
Regarding the five kinds of robes, three types may not be taken: those burnt by fire, those gnawed by oxen, and those chewed by rats; to take these constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Taking two types of robes constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Taking a bowl of proper measure constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one takes any clothing, vessels, or implements that are not of proper measure, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one takes a robe from a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it constitutes an offense identical to that for a bhikṣuṇī.
This excludes cases of exchange, because [exchange] allows those practicing the Path to attain peace and happiness, and ensures that disciples do not suffer distress.

If a bhikṣu obtains clothing suitable for a bhikṣuṇī, or a bhikṣuṇī obtains clothing suitable for a bhikṣu, and they do not exchange them, then because of those robes, they will engage in various pursuits that obstruct and waste their practice of the Path, resulting in all manner of afflictions and harms; therefore, I permit [such exchanges].

5. Causing a nun who is not a relative to wash old clothes; causing a nun who is not a relative to wash old clothes is the fifth [offense]. This is a unique precept (asādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada): if a śrāmaṇera causes a nun who is not a relative to wash old clothes, it is a duṣkṛta.

Regarding the offense herein: if one personally takes a robe and gives it to a nun who is not a relative, and then performs any one of the three acts—washing, dyeing, or beating—it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one performs these three acts simultaneously, one incurs one *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If the washing is not thoroughly clean, the dyeing does not achieve the proper color, or the beating does not make it supple, all constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one causes [another] to send a letter, a written message, or a seal, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes a robe subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) to be washed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If two people share one robe, or even many people share a robe, and one causes it to be beaten or dyed, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes an impure robe, or a robe woven from a mixture of camel hair, cow hair, or black sheep’s wool, to be washed, dyed, or beaten, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one causes a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) under training to wash, dye, or beat such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense in cases such as those involving those who have broken the precepts or those who dwell as thieves.
If one causes a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī to wash, dye, or beat old robes, it constitutes an offense identical to that of a bhikṣuṇī.
If a bhikṣuṇī has another bhikṣuṇī wash her old clothes, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Regarding this precept, it constitutes an offense whether the robes are of measured size or not of measured size.
6. Begging for Robes from a Householder Who Is Not a Relative. Regarding the sixth section on begging for robes from a householder who is not a relative, where Upavāna preaches various teachings:
some say that he first speaks of giving, in the middle he speaks of observing the precepts, and at the end he speaks of the meritorious rewards of rebirth in heaven.
Some say: The teachings on giving and its karmic rewards spoken previously were intended for all;

however, the establishment of precepts for the bhikṣus serves four purposes: first, to cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish; second, to cease disputes and litigation; third, to extinguish the unwholesome minds of those who have previously committed offenses; and fourth, to inspire faith and joy in the True Dharma among sentient beings.
This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense;
for śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu asks for clothing from one who is not a relative and obtains the clothing, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he causes it to be given by means of a messenger, a letter, or a seal, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If two people together beg for a single robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one begs on behalf of another, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one obtains a robe of the proper measure, it is an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If one obtains clothing that is not of the proper measure, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if one requests it from a relative;
if the relative has abundant wealth and many treasures, there is no offense in requesting from them.
If one requests from a relative who is impoverished, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a relative gives a small amount and one requests more, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one requests on behalf of another, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one acts for the sake of the Dharma and a relative gives it of their own accord, there is no fault.
If one has previously been invited, and a non-relative first invites one to accept a robe, there is no offense in requesting it from them.
Even if one has previously requested and received robes, if the donor later becomes impoverished and asks for them back, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one receives a small amount and then requests more, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one solicits on behalf of another, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If the person is not a relative and gives of their own accord without being solicited, there is no offense.
The Seventh Precept. At that time, the bhikṣu named Pārā was so called because this was the name of his native land; the bhikṣu was named after that place.

In the past, when the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was at the abode of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he spread his hair upon the ground for the Buddha to step over; by virtue of this cause, his hair attained its deep blue-black color, and at that very moment, he shaved his head and left the household life.

At that time, countless people obtained the Bodhisattva’s hair and honored it with offerings. By this cause and condition, many sentient beings encountered the Buddhas of the past, whereby they all attained the exhaustion of outflows and entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; the remaining forty people attained deliverance under the present Buddha.
Among these forty Bhiksus from Pāra, this person was the very last to be ordained.
He was one who walked about naked.
Someone asked him:

"Traveling afar is perilous and fraught with difficulties, such as the dangers of bandits, venomous insects, water, fire, hunger, and cold; why then does the Buddha command the bhikṣus to travel far on pilgrimage?"
He replied:
"The dispositions and natures of sentient beings' faculties differ; for this reason, the Great Sage established his teachings accordingly.
There are some sentient beings who give rise to roots of goodness through movement and wandering; therefore, the Tathāgata praises wandering, moving about at will without any attachment."

If there are sentient beings who increase their roots of goodness solely through silence, for this reason the Tathāgata praises dwelling in seclusion, maintaining silence, and self-restraint; as long as it is beneficial according to the circumstances, there is no fault.
The reason they go naked is twofold: first, because they do not dare to beg for robes due to the Buddha’s established precepts;
second, because they wish to create the conditions for the Buddha to provide an opening for future bhikṣus who may encounter many such hardships and difficulties.
Regarding "taking away the bhikṣu’s robe": these six group bhikṣus possessed profound wisdom and were skillful in means;
they first said to Pāla, "Your robes are complete."
"The elder gave it to me.
Because he permitted it as such, there is no offense.

Regarding the precept established for the bhikṣus: this is a shared precept; both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs incur a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, while for the three other assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu loses one robe, and his saṃghāṭī can be made by taking cloth from another garment, he should not beg for it.
If he begs for it and obtains it, it is an offense of expiation with forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya);
if he begs for it but does not obtain it, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one has sufficient remaining wealth to make a robe oneself, one should not beg for one; if one begs for one, it is an offense equivalent to that of the *saṃghāṭī*.
If two robes are lost, and there is a *saṃghāṭī* that can be torn down to make one robe, one should beg for only one robe.
If one succeeds in obtaining two robes by begging for them, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture;
if one does not obtain them, it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
In this context, "robes" refers to robes of the prescribed dimensions.
Regarding other robes that are not of the proper measure: if they are too small or if one has none, one should request [a robe]; if they are too long and one requests them, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Eighth Precept: This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the three groups [of female practitioners], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, there was a householder who provided the funds for the robes of the Śākya son Upananda.

This householder frequently engaged in business dealings with Upananda as both guest and host; for Upananda possessed great wisdom, merit, wealth, and abundant goods, and he constantly lent his capital to this householder to earn interest on its circulation.
At that time, this householder wished to provide a robe for Upananda in order to cultivate a bond of friendship, desiring that his business profits be shared without regard for the amount.
Knowing his intention, Upananda went to him and encouraged him to make it well-crafted.

Regarding this precept: if a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative has first prepared the price for robes, and [the monk] goes to their place and instructs them to add money to make them better—whether by making them more expensive, of finer color, or of greater measure—and if he obtains them as requested, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if he does not obtain them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one sends a messenger, a letter, or a seal, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

However, if one does not seek a garment of high price, fine color, or large quantity, but rather encourages its making according to what is appropriate—whether of equal price, equal color, and equal quantity, or of reduced price, reduced quantity, and reduced quality—there is no offense.
Regarding robes among these, they must be of the prescribed measurement, ranging from a minimum of four cubits to a maximum of eight cubits.

If one obtains a robe of the prescribed measurement, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; if one obtains a robe that is not of the prescribed measurement, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if one requests from a relative.
If the relative is wealthy and possesses abundant goods, there is no fault in requesting from them;
however, if the relative is poor, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one has been previously invited by a non-relative who has made an initial invitation, one may request whatever is needed.
If the donor who first invited you possesses abundant wealth, it is no fault to encourage them to prepare the meal well;
however, if they are impoverished, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one gives it oneself when not related by blood, there is no offense.
Ninth Precept: This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, while for the three groups of disciples, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is also a robe of proper measure; if one encourages [a donor] to obtain a robe that is not of proper measure, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Regarding the previous precept: a single layperson had already prepared the funds for a robe for a bhikṣu, and [the bhikṣu] encouraged him to increase the price and improve the quality of the color and measure.

Regarding this essence of the precept: two lay devotees each provided the funds for a robe and each made one robe to give to a bhikṣu; they then encouraged him to combine them, so that the price, color, and dimensions could be improved and made excellent.
The meaning is the same as for the preceding precept; the only difference is that it concerns two lay devotees (*gṛhapati*).
There is no offense if one requests from a relative, or if there was a prior invitation, or if they give of their own accord without being asked—all such cases are as explained previously.
If one sends a messenger, a letter, or a seal, it is all *duṣkṛta*.

The Tenth Precept: Formerly, when the Venerable Upananda was a householder, he was skilled in the art of archery and also knowledgeable in military strategy. The ministers and generals of the kingdom of Magadha sent five hundred men to learn from him; they mastered the art of archery and attained proficiency in military strategy, after which they returned to their own country.
The minister of Magadha immediately dispatched an envoy, carrying many precious goods, to repay his kindness.

At that time, Upananda had already donned the dyed robes of a renunciant and gone forth as a monk in Śrāvastī. When the Magadhan envoy arrived at Kapilavastu, he learned that [Upananda] had become a monk; searching from place to place, he reached the city of Śrāvastī. Upon meeting him at a marketplace, the envoy entrusted the treasures to him and returned to his own country.
This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, while for *ṣaḍ-dharmikā* bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the essence of this precept: if a donor sends a messenger to deliver precious objects to a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should say:
"According to my dharma, I ought not to accept precious objects."
"If you need robes and obtain pure robes, make them quickly and keep them.
If the messenger asks the bhikṣu, "Is there anyone pure?
[the bhikṣu should reply accordingly].
He should indicate where [the robe] is located.
He should have the price for the robe paid to a *kappiyakāraka* (a person authorized to handle allowable goods), instructing him to make a purified robe and give it to the bhikṣu.
The messenger should say to the bhikṣu:
"When you need robes, go and take them.
A bhikṣu should go to a person who is pure and request robes, saying:
"I need robes."
Thus he should request three times.
If he obtains the robe, it is well;
if he does not obtain it, he should stand silently before the *kappiya-kāraka* four times, five times, or six times.
If one stands in silence for up to six times and obtains the robe, it is well.
If one does not obtain the robe within those six times, but obtains it after the sixth time, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The essence of the precept lies precisely in the three requests and three silences; beyond these, there is no transgression.
If one obtains a robe for the seventh time, it constitutes an offense; it does not constitute a *duṣkṛta*.

The Eleventh Matter. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the first recitation, within the first thirty matters, this is the eleventh matter. When the Buddha was staying in the country of Kauśāmbī—this is the name of the land.
*Kauśeya* is the name for silk floss.
In this country they raise silkworms according to the methods of the people of the land of Qin; when the worms mature and the floss is obtained, it is called *kauśeya*.
In this country, garments are made from cotton wool, of which there are two types:
first, by carding the cotton wool and layering it like the method used for making felt;
second, by spinning the cotton into thread and weaving it into cloth.
To make these two types of robes is called making bedding (śayanāsana).
"Bedding" is a name for a robe.

The reason for establishing this precept for the bhikṣus is to prevent slander, to increase faith and respect, to ensure peace and happiness in the practice of the Path, and to avoid harming sentient beings.
This is an unshared precept; for a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense. Regarding the transgression herein:
if one begs for cocoons, begs for cotton, or begs for thread to make two kinds of robes, and the robe is completed, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
These two kinds of cloth may be accepted and maintained as part of the three robes.
If one begs for cocoons to make cotton oneself, there is no offense.
However, if one begs for cocoons to sell them, and they still contain living insects, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If there are no insects, there is no offense.
If one begs for and obtains cotton wool to store as clothing, there is no offense.
If one begs for and obtains cocoons or silk that has already been processed, there is no offense.
If *kauśeya* silk is damaged by insects, there is no offense in making it into bedding.
If one combines camel hair, sheep’s wool, or cow hair [with cotton] to make bedding, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one combines *kṣauma* cloth, flaxen cloth, cotton cloth, coarse woolen cloth, or *kambala* woolen cloth to make bedding, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one makes a robe even as small as four cubits, it is an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If one causes another to make it, it is likewise an offense of expiation with forfeiture, because *kauseya* silk is precious.
12. The Twelfth Matter: In this country, black sheep’s wool is expensive; therefore, its use is not permitted.
There are two methods for making robes from black sheep’s wool:
first, to select, process, and weave the black wool into cloth to make a fine felt; second, to spin it into thread and weave it into a robe.
These two kinds of robes are all termed *śayanāsana* (reclining gear).
*Śayanāsana* is a designation for robes.
This woolen robe may be used as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*) and may be maintained as such throughout the entire period.
This is an unshared precept; for the fourfold assembly, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding the transgression herein:

there are four kinds of wool—naturally black, dyed black with indigo, dyed black with mud, and dyed black with tree bark. If one takes any one of these four kinds of black wool, combs and weaves it to make a bedding mat, once it is finished, it is an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one obtains a worn-out black woolen rug to use as a bedding, there is no offense.
If one obtains a finished rug for a stūpa or for the Saṃgha, or if it is made by combining camel hair, ram’s wool, and cow hair, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one combines *śāṇa* cloth, *karpāsa* cloth, woolen cloth, or *kambala* cloth [to make a robe], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the robe made is as small as four cubits (*hasta*), it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one causes another to make it, there is likewise an offense of expiation (nissaggiya-pācittiya), because black wool is expensive.
The thirteenth matter: this precept differs from the previous ones precisely in that the bedding is made from mixed wool.
This is an uncommon precept; for the fourfold assembly, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding black sheep’s wool, it is as previously explained.
As for white sheep’s wool:

The hair from the back, the hair from the flanks, and the hair from the neck constitute the superior grade; the hair from the head, the hair from the belly, and the hair from the legs constitute the inferior grade.
To construct a bedding mat, one should use twenty *pātra* of black wool, ten *pātra* of white wool, and ten *pātra* of the inferior-grade wool, with each *pātra* weighing four *liang*.
If one makes bedding materials using black wool weighing twenty *pātra* or even exceeding one *liang*, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one takes white sheep’s wool weighing ten *pātra* or exceeding one *liang*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one takes even as little as one *liang* out of ten *bōluó* of inferior wool, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one makes a bedding of sixty *bōluó*, one uses thirty *bōluó* of black wool, fifteen *bōluó* of white wool, and fifteen *bōluó* of inferior wool.

If one makes a bedding cover of one hundred *pātra*, it shall consist of fifty *pātra* of black sheep’s wool, twenty-five *pātra* of white sheep’s wool, and twenty-five *pātra* of inferior sheep’s wool.
If one seeks wool oneself and makes a robe oneself, it is also a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Although mixing [materials) is permitted, because the labor involved is excessive, it causes interference and neglect; therefore, one incurs this offense.
If one hires another person to make it according to the Dharma, there is no offense.
Furthermore, even if it is as small as four cubits, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

The Fourteenth Matter: The substance of this precept is that if, within six years after having made the three robes, one begs from a donor for wool, thread, or various other materials for robes to make a robe of the prescribed measure, then as soon as it is woven and finished, it is a forfeiture offense (*naiḥsargika*), except by means of a formal monastic authorization (*saṃgha-karman*).
Once the *saṃgha-karman* has been performed, one may beg for clothing materials from a donor to make robes.
The essence of this precept is to sever excessive greed and excessive accumulation.
This is a unique precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*); for the fourfold assembly, its violation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one makes it from what was given to oneself, there is no offense.
If one makes it from clothing and materials belonging to oneself, there is no offense.
If one makes it from clothing and materials purchased, there is no offense.
15. The Fifteenth Matter: The Fifteenth Formal Settlement concerning the Circumstances of Making a New *niṣīdana*. [The Buddha] accepted the invitation in silence.
Question:
"Why did the Buddha accept the invitation in silence?"
He replied:
"The Buddha has completely exhausted the fetter of greed; regarding food, he is without craving and without defilement, and for this reason he remains silent.
Although the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have exhausted the fetter of greed, the residual stains of habituation still remain; therefore, they accept invitations and thus grant their consent."
It is further said:
It is for the sake of severing slander.
If the Buddha were to speak his approval regarding food, those of external paths and heterodox views would say:
"The śramaṇa Gautama claims to have transcended the three realms, yet he still has craving for food.
Furthermore, it was said:
"Because the Buddha manifests the marks of a Great Man, eating is a minor matter and is not worth mentioning."
For example, a king never acts precipitously over a minor matter; even when faced with a major matter, he deliberates thoroughly before acting.
The Buddha is likewise.
It is further said:
The Buddha enters the samādhi of emptiness on five occasions:

first, when receiving an invitation; second, when receiving food; third, when preaching the Dharma; fourth, when there is benefit and happiness to be brought about; and fifth, when facing slander and defamation.
When accepting an invitation, one should observe: who is it that invites me?
Who is it that accepts the invitation?
And when receiving food, who is it that gives the food?
"Who is it that receives food?
Likewise, who is it that reviles me?
Who is it that suffers the revilement?"
"It is because he has entered the samādhi of emptiness that he remains silent.
There are sūtras which state that the Buddha also sometimes accepts invitations by giving his consent through speech.
[The interlocutor] asked:
"Why does the Buddha at times grant permission and at times remain silent?
He replied, "This is inconceivable."
The Sūtra says:
"The Buddha is inconceivable, the nāgas are inconceivable, and the karmic retributions of the world are inconceivable.
This refers to the inconceivability of the Buddha.
If the Buddha wishes for sentient beings to know his mind—even those of inferior capacity and dull faculties—if he desires them to see him, they shall immediately behold him.
If he desires that they not see him, then even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who possess the divine eye would be unable to see him.

Furthermore, the Buddha emits a great radiance that extends downward to the Avīci Hell and upward to the Peak of Existence; those who are ready for deliverance are enabled to see it, while those who are not yet ready do not see it even before their eyes.
Therefore, the Buddha sometimes grants permission and sometimes remains silent; he is unfathomable.

Having prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him to the right, he departed. Those who held heterodox views and different opinions merely circumambulated him and left; those who had faith prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and then departed.

The Buddha’s body is pure like a bright mirror; within it appear all reflected images—the palaces of devas and nāgas, mountain forests, rivers, and seas. Those who behold this give rise to faith and reverence, and for this reason they prostrate themselves with their heads at his feet.
Regarding circumambulating to the right: it is done so as to accord with the Buddha-dharma; this is why one circumambulates to the right.
Furthermore, if there were anyone to circumambulate to the left, the Vajrapāṇi Mārṣa would shatter them with his vajra-pestle.

Furthermore, throughout all his lifetimes since time immemorial, the Buddha has always followed the Three Jewels, his parents, and his teachers; he has never contravened or opposed any of their instructions, and thus now he has attained this fruition as one who is free from opposition.

Furthermore, the Buddha’s body is pure; within it, sentient beings each see their own object of worship—whether a deva or a spirit—and there is none who does not behold it. Therefore, they depart after circumambulating him to the right with awe and reverence.
Question:
"Why do the heretics with their false views not prostrate at the Buddha's feet? Answer:
"Because they have practiced arrogance throughout successive lifetimes, and because they constantly harbor evil and heterodox views without a virtuous mind.
Furthermore, it is said:
'Each has their own particular business.'"
"Why did he circumambulate three times?
First, because by not disturbing the Buddha, he would not disturb himself; second, because it would create the causal conditions for liberation in the future.
Having returned, throughout the night he prepared various pure and delicious foods and drinks.
Question:
"Why do you prepare food specifically at night? Answer:
"It is very hot during the day, and food becomes foul and putrid; for this reason, one works at night.
Furthermore, it is said:
by working at night to prepare food, one obtains fresh food in the morning."
"If one prepares food beforehand, one would eat last night's meal; therefore, it is prepared at night.
He informed the Buddha that the time had arrived.
The Buddha asked:
"Since you have already invited the Buddha previously, why do you invite him again?
He replied,
"It is because I wish to generate superior merit."
Having previously made a request, I now request again so that merit may further increase.
Furthermore, it is because I wish to accomplish the three dharmas of firmness.
Moreover, the Buddha’s time has arrived, and he proceeds of his own accord.
By what means is this known?
A lay devotee was burning incense in a secluded place, making offerings from afar and inviting the Buddha; the fragrance came and circled the Buddha three times.
It is also said:
The Secret-Trace Malla (Guhyapada) announced, "The time has come.
He further said:
"Ānanda, when the time arrives, you must announce it."
It is further said:
"The Buddha knows the time himself and does not require external conditions.
As for the Buddha dwelling in his own room, it is because he does not practice that which would be of no benefit.
It is further said:
There are five causes and conditions for which the Buddha remains [in a particular place]:

first, to enter a quiet chamber; second, to preach the Dharma to the various devas; third, for the sake of a sick bhikṣu; fourth, for the purpose of establishing precepts; and fifth, to inspect the various rooms and bedding.
The reason for going from room to room was to inspire a sense of awe and reverence in the bhikṣus.

After the bhikṣus had departed, the Buddha personally inspected the various quarters; subsequently, the bhikṣus would naturally become solemn and cautious, not daring to allow any unrighteous things to exist within the rooms.
Furthermore, wishing to sever the improper discourse among the bhikṣus, the Buddha would personally enter their quarters; consequently, none would dare utter improper words.

Moreover, wishing to prevent people from committing theft and robbery, the Buddha would personally walk through the rooms; even if there were wicked persons, they would not give rise to thieving intentions.
Regarding the Elder who preaches the Dharma after the meal: the reason he preaches the Dharma to the donor after the meal is, first, to digest the offerings of faith;
second, to repay their kindness;
and third, to preach the Dharma so that they may rejoice and bring their pure roots of goodness to fulfillment.

This is because the four types of laypeople should practice the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), while those who have left the household life should practice the giving of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

At that time, a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal at his residence the following day. During the Buddha’s lifetime, offerings of food, clothing, and other requisites were always accepted from one person at a time.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one takes only one portion from among the three jewels.
A question is asked:
“When the Buddha was in the world, why did he take only the portion of a single person, yet after his parinirvāṇa, one takes one portion from the three jewels?”
He replied:
"When the Buddha was in the world, one made offerings to his physical body (rūpakāya); therefore, one took only a single portion.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one makes offerings to the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Because the merit of the Buddha’s Dharma-body surpasses that of the Sangha Jewel, one takes one portion from among the three portions."
If the Buddha is still in the world, when a donor says they are making an offering to the Buddha, his physical body (rūpakāya) receives and enjoys it.

If one says they are making an offering to the Buddha Jewel (buddharatna), the physical body does not receive and enjoy it; rather, it should be placed within a nail-stupa or hair-stupa, for the donor’s intention is to make an offering to the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), which exists eternally.
In performing any act of giving, one should ensure that both the mind and speech are focused; thus, the merit of the gift will be profound and easily distinguished.
If one gives to the Buddha, one should state with certainty: "I give this to the Buddha."
One who bestows the Dharma should distinguish clearly:

if one bestows the treasure of the Dharma, the mouth must be made stable; if one bestows scriptures, the mouth must likewise be made stable; and if one bestows those who preach the Dharma or recite the scriptures, their mouths must also be made stable.
If one makes offerings to the Sangha, there are likewise three types:
the *pravāraṇā* (Invitation) ceremony, the *svasti-vācanā* (Self-indulgence) ceremony, and the *mukha-dvāra* (Face-gate) ceremony; these three types should be properly distinguished.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of giving to the Saṃgha:
first, giving to the Jewel of the Saṃgha; second, giving simply to the Saṃgha.
If one gives to the Jewel of the Saṃgha, neither ordinary monks nor noble ones may take a share, because it has been given to the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
If one gives to the Sangha, both the noble Sangha and the ordinary Sangha may receive a portion, because there is no specific designation [of recipients].
If one says they give to the Three Jewels, it should be divided into three parts: one part is for the Buddha Jewel; [the second for the Dharma Jewel; and the third for the Sangha Jewel].
One portion is for the Dharma Jewel; it should be suspended within a stūpa and must not be made into scriptures, nor given to those who preach or recite the sutras.
One portion is for the Sangha Jewel; the assembly of monks must not take it.
This object should be returned to the donor; if there is no donor, it should be placed within a stūpa as an offering to the Saṃgha of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-saṃgha).
If it is explicitly stated that the gift is for the Dharma, it shall be divided into two portions:
one portion is given to the sūtras, and the other portion is given to those who recite the sūtras, but it is not given to the Dharma-treasure (dharma-ratna) itself.
The Vinaya Master said:

"If one does not bestow the Dharma-treasure, it is like the case in the land of Qin where goods were sent to be given to the monk Fa-feng; whether at the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony or in person, the distribution follows the spoken instructions."
If it is stated directly that the dharma-abundance is for the Saṃgha, it should be divided into three portions:

one portion is given to the *saṃghika* (the community), one portion is for the *pravāraṇā* robes, which is distributed at the time of the *pravāraṇā*, and one portion is for the *mukha-dvāra* (the mouth), from which food and drink may be taken as needed.
If there is an abundance of requisites but no monks present, down to the point where there is only a single śrāmaṇera, that śrāmaṇera should divide them into three portions:
for the Saṃgha, for the face-gate (the donor), and for the self-indulgence (prātimokṣa).
Regarding the *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence) *laba*, one should take it at the time of the *pravāraṇā*.
Regarding the *mukha-dvāra* (mouth-gate) *laba*, one may take it as needed for food.

When taking the *pravāraṇā* *laba* or eating the *mukha-dvāra* *laba*, one should strike the *gandī* (wooden gong). If there are bhikṣus who share the meal together, they should divide it; if there are none, one may eat it by taking it oneself, provided it is done according to the Dharma and with purity.
If there are no śrāmaṇeras, one should enter among the monks who observe the upavāsa precepts.
If there are no such monks, one should enter among the bhikṣuṇīs. The bhikṣuṇīs should deliberate carefully:
if the Dharma is flourishing and it is reasonable that the Sangha will eventually return, they should set it aside in one place; when the Sangha returns, they shall give it back to them.
If there is definitely no time for their return, they should be divided according to the previous method into three portions:
one portion is assigned to the *saṃghaprāyaścittika*, one portion to the *mukhadvārika*, and one portion to the *pravāraṇā*; these shall await the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
If items are sent from afar to be given to a bhikṣuṇī, the sequence is according to the Dharma as previously described for the bhikṣus; there is no difference.
If items are sent to be given to the *pāvāraṇā*, they shall be divided into three parts:

one part goes to the *pāvāraṇā* itself because there is no formal invitation (*pravāraṇā*) of the monks; one part goes to the *mukhadvāra* (the face-gate); and one part goes to the *pravāraṇā*, to be set aside until the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.

If it is a distant location where Buddhism flourishes, such as Kaśmīra, and one sends goods for the purpose of making offerings, these items should properly be given to both the Buddha and the Saṃgha; this is because the Saṃgha accords with the Buddha's teachings.
If one gives to the Buddha and the Sangha, this is equivalent to giving to the Dharma, because the Dharma is not separate from the Buddha and the Sangha.
One should divide it into two portions:
one portion for the Buddha and one portion for the Sangha.
If one sends goods as an offering to the Kasmira region, there are two schools of monks:
first, the Sarvāstivāda; second, the Mahīśāsaka. One may offer according to one's preference without fault.
If an object is offered to the *pañcavastuka* Sangha, and no members of the *pañcavastuka* Sangha are present, it shall go to the *pañcavastuka* Bhikṣuṇī Sangha.
If there is no Bhikṣuṇī Sangha, or if from the beginning there has never been anyone belonging to the *pañcavastuka*, these *pañcavastuka* objects should be divided into three portions:
for the *saṃghakāyika*, for the *pravāraṇā*, and for the *mukhadvārika*.
"The two types [of cloth] obtained for use by the Saṃgha may not be divided;
the face-cloth must be returned to its original place and may not be taken.
If a bhikṣu makes a sitting mat (niṣīdana), he should surround it with a border of one span (vitasti) of the Sugata’s measure from the old bedding material, in order to change its color.
A *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) is four spans of the Buddha’s cubit in length and three spans of the Buddha’s cubit in width.
Regarding "old bedding," this refers to all kinds of discarded clothing and bedding found within the *saṃghārāma*; all such items are termed "bedding."

When making a new *niṣīdana*, one should take the longest portion from an old sitting mat; from its width, one should cut off a span (*vitasti*) in length and divide it according to the breadth to form a border, which is then used to surround the new *niṣīdana*.
If there is no large-sized bedding among the existing items, one may use whatever is available;
if there is nothing large, even a small-sized one may be used;
if there is absolutely nothing at all, not using any is without fault.
If the Saṃgha of the four quarters possesses old robes that are not discarded items, they must not be taken and used.
If there is a place where they are not used, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

The sixteenth matter: When various bhikṣus brought wool from abroad, those who harbored jealousy in their hearts—namely, the merchants who wished to sell the wool—did not want the wool to enter the country in large quantities.
Second, seeing various śramaṇas carrying wool is contrary to the dharma of those who have left the household life; therefore, he censured them.
This is an exclusive precept (asaṃvāsa-śīla): for bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
Regarding the *yojana*: forty *li* make one *yojana*.
If a single bhikṣu obtains wool, he may carry it for up to three *yojanas*;
if two bhikṣus, they may go for up to six *yojanas*.
Thus, one does not calculate the number of people involved.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu carries wool himself for a distance exceeding three yojanas, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Question:
"Is this a temporary relinquishment or a fundamental relinquishment? Answer:
"Speaking in terms of the offense, this constitutes a fundamental relinquishment; speaking in terms of the Dharma, it is a temporary relinquishment.
If one causes the five groups [of monks] to carry it away beyond three yojanas, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
One must not transport [the items] by carriage or carry them on one's back; if one causes a *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person) to carry them for a distance exceeding three *yojanas*, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense within three *yojanas*.
If it is placed on the ear, or inside the ear, or down the throat; or if it is made into a felt mat, or placed inside a needle case and carried away, there is no offense.
"If one carries it away with another for three *yojanas*, there is no offense;
however, because it is contrary to the dharma of a bhikṣu, it also brings harm upon oneself. 17.
The Seventeenth Matter: He prostrated himself at his feet, stood to one side, and said:
Question:
"Why do the bhikṣuṇīs of the Gautamī community not sit? Answer:
"Women have many feelings of reverence and difficulty; for this reason, they do not sit.
Furthermore, it is said:
when the Buddha preached the Dharma to the assembly of nuns, even if he did preach to them, he did not preach extensively."
Furthermore, the Buddha never sat together with the community of nuns at any time, in order to prevent slander.
If he were to sit and listen to the Dharma, non-Buddhists would say:
"When the Śramaṇa Gautama was in the royal palace, he shared a single location with various court ladies; now that he has left the household life, he is no different from before."
"Because he wishes to extinguish such slander and defamation, he does not sit.
Furthermore, women are vulgar and often provoke derision and suspicion; for this reason, he does not sit."
The reason for establishing the precepts for the bhikṣus is to promote the superior Dharma (*adhipateyadharma*).
If the community of nuns were to engage in manual labor such as washing and dyeing, neglecting their primary spiritual practice, they would lack majestic virtue and destroy the superior Dharma.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of stopping the sequential causes and conditions of unwholesome dharmas, and also so that each of the two assemblies may maintain purity.
This is an exclusive precept; for the fourfold assembly, its violation constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and says,
"Wash, dye, or card wool for me," and the bhikṣuṇī performs any one of these acts—
whether washing, dyeing, or carding— he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for each act performed.
If a bhikṣuṇī further instructs another to wash, dye, or beat [the cloth], it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If she instructs a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī to wash, dye, or beat it, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense. If she sends a messenger, a letter, or a sealed message to have it washed, dyed, or beaten, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one causes wool that has been forfeited but not yet purified to be washed, dyed, or carded, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one causes wool that has been purified by *pariṇāmanā* (formal relinquishment) to be washed, dyed, or carded, the person who performed the *pariṇāmanā* incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense in the case of a *śrāmaṇerī* who is a relative, nor in the case of a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*.
The eighteenth matter: The reason for establishing this precept for the bhikṣus is to stop slander, to extinguish strife and contention, and to perfect the noble lineage.
This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs are not permitted to possess such items; if they do possess them, they incur a *duṣkṛta*, but there is no offense in merely holding them.
This essence of the precept is precisely established by the prohibition against possessing precious objects.
As stated in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra: "If a bhikṣu takes a precious object with his own hand, or causes another to take it—both these forms of taking constitute a full offense."
There are five ways of taking what one has kept for oneself:

taking from hand to hand; or taking from another's garment using one's own garment; or taking from another's vessel using one's own vessel; or saying, "Place it in this"; or saying, "Give this to the *kappiya-kāraka* (the person who makes things allowable)."
Because these are all for the sake of livestock, if one takes them using these five methods, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
One does not commit an offense if one does not take them with one's own hand, or if they have been formally purified (*śuddha*) according to the Dharma.
"Jewels" refers to precious treasures: gold, silver, mani-gems, pearls, coral, musaragalva, and agate.
These various jewels may be fashioned or unfashioned, and may be joined together or not joined.
"Created" refers to various vessels and implements made from jewels.
"Uncreated" refers to that which is merely a jewel and has not been fashioned into a vessel or implement.
"Characteristics" refers to jewels that have not been made into vessels, or those that bear the marks of letters or the marks of seals.
Regarding "non-characteristics": one does not fashion them into vessels or treasures, nor does one fashion them into letter-signs or seal-signs.
If one accepts and keeps such treasures, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

If a bhikṣu takes with his own hand iron coins, copper coins, tin coins, lead coins, resin coins, leather coins, or wooden coins—these various coins are also taken by five ways: taking with the hand from the hand; taking from clothing by means of clothing; taking from a vessel by means of a vessel; saying, "Place them in this"; or saying, "Give these to this *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites). For the purpose of keeping them, at the time of taking them by these five ways, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
"One shall not take it with one's own hand; if it was declared pure (*śuddha*) according to the Dharma at the time of taking it, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu has fallen into the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* regarding precious objects, if they are few, they should be discarded;
if they are many, even if a trustworthy layperson (*kappiyakāraka*) is found, he should be told:"
"I do not take it because it is impure;
you should take it.
After the attendant had taken it, he said to the bhikṣu:
"Give this object to the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu said:
"This is an impure object; if it were pure, I would accept it."
This constitutes the declaration of purity (*pārisuddhi*).
Having declared purity, one may then enter the assembly to confess the offense.
It is not for the purpose of keeping [the object]; whether one has taken another’s treasure or one’s own treasure that has been declared pure, merely by taking it, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding all coins, whether copper coins or even wooden coins, whether they belong to others or have been formally purified (*viśuddha*), merely taking hold of them constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; this is not the substance of this particular precept, but rather belongs to the ninety matters concerning the precept against handling precious objects.

If there are various coins resembling jewels—such as glass, amber, crystal, and various counterfeit pearls, or alloys such as brass, copper, iron, white tin, lead, and pewter—these are called coins resembling jewels and things resembling jewels.

If one keeps them, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; such money or treasures should be relinquished to a lay attendant (*śrāmaṇera*) of like mind who is pure, and they must not enter the property of the Saṃgha of the Four Directions.
If they are precious jewels and no like-minded pure attendant is available, they shall enter the property of the Saṃgha of the Four Directions.
If an object made of precious materials resembles a vessel and is included among the "one hundred and one items," it does not require the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification).
If it is not included among the "one hundred and one items," then all vessels, whether they are functional containers or otherwise, must undergo the ritual of *pariśuddhi*.
One may possess one of each of the one hundred and one items; anything beyond these one hundred and one is considered surplus property.

The Nineteenth Matter: At that time, the group of six bhikṣus first abandoned precious objects that were subject to forfeiture and used them for various purposes. These bhikṣus, having performed the ritual purification (*śuddhi*) of those precious objects according to the Dharma, subsequently exchanged them for various other goods.

This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, while for śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Regarding the essence of this precept:
