if one lends precious goods to another person to seek interest, at the moment they are to be returned, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If, for the sake of profit, one exchanges heavy valuables with another and obtains those valuables, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If, for the sake of profit, one uses heavy valuables to purchase other goods and obtains those goods, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Regarding trading by means of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): it is like trading what is produced for what is produced, trading what is produced for what is unproduced, and trading what is produced for both what is produced and what is unproduced.
There are also three cases regarding the unproduced:
trading a characteristic for a characteristic, trading a characteristic for what is not a characteristic, and trading a characteristic for both a characteristic and what is not a characteristic.
There are also three phrases regarding the non-corresponding:
this is called "exchanging jewels for jewels.
There are five kinds of utility:
First, taking; second, bringing; third, carrying away; fourth, selling; fifth, buying. Regarding "taking":
it refers to saying, "take this object," "take from within this," "take such an amount," or "take from this person."
The four types regarding taking and bringing back are likewise as described; the four types regarding selling and buying are likewise as described.
If a bhikṣu uses iron coins or even wooden coins to give to others in exchange for interest or profit, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, for the sake of profit, one buys goods with money, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it concerns other items resembling jewels, such as fine silk or plain cloth, if a bhikṣu lends them out or buys them for the sake of profit, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding this precept-body, one should properly say "various uses of precious objects" rather than "buying and selling.
This precept constitutes an offense immediately upon its commission; it is not like the precept against trading.
Regarding the precept against buying and selling: if one buys for the sake of profit and then resells, it constitutes an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If the money or precious goods are few, they should be discarded; if they are many, one should obtain a pure attendant (*śucipuruṣa*) of like mind, as previously described.

Regarding various items made of precious materials and the objects of the precept concerning trade, they must be relinquished by a layperson (*avadātavasana*) who is a pure attendant (*śucika-puruṣa*) acting with a shared intention; a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) is not permitted [to relinquish them].
A novice may also relinquish [them].
The precept regarding the hoarding of precious objects is likewise.

If one uses various forms of currency or counterfeit gems, one should relinquish them to a pure person of like mind; they must not enter the possession of the Sangha of the four directions, and one should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
"Posting a wooden notice for punishment" means writing the person's crimes and transgressions upon a board to show them to all who see it.
The Twentieth Matter: At that time, there was a brahmin who was a disciple of the six heretical teachers.

Regarding the six teachers: one teacher gave fifteen types of instruction to his disciples; as these teachings were each different, the disciples who received and practiced them each formed distinct views. In this way, one teacher produced fifteen kinds of divergent views.

Each teacher has a distinct doctrine that differs from those of his disciples; including both teachers and disciples, there are sixteen types for each, and thus these six teachers comprise ninety-six schools in total.

The methods employed by a teacher, when he is about to pass away, must necessarily be transmitted to one disciple; in this manner, they are passed down from teacher to teacher, and there are always six teachers.

He established the precepts for the bhikṣus for the sake of the flourishing of the Buddha-dharma, for the cessation of strife and contention, for the fulfillment of the noble lineage, and for the increase of faith and reverence.
This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, while for the three other assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Among all *pāyattikas*, this offense of buying and selling is the most serious; one would rather be a butcher than engage in such trade.

Why is this? When a butcher is in the act of slaughtering livestock, he deceives and harms all those who purchase his goods; regardless of whether they are monastics or laypeople, noble or foolish, observant of the precepts or violators of them, there is no one to whom he does not resort to deception.
Furthermore, they constantly harbor evil intentions; even if they deal in grain, their minds perpetually hope for the world to suffer from famine, frost, hail, and pestilence.
If they deal in salt or store up other goods, their thoughts always aspire to the rebellion of distant regions and the obstruction of the royal highways.
Indeed, those who engage in such trade possess these evils.
If the goods of such a trader are used to prepare food for the Sangha, the Sangha should not eat it.
If they are used to construct a monastery for the Sangha of the four quarters, one must not dwell within it.
If one constructs a stūpa or an image, one should not perform prostrations toward it.
Furthermore, it is said:
"One should simply pay homage with the mental intention that it is the Buddha."
Any bhikṣu who maintains the precepts should not make use of these items.
If this bhikṣu dies, the Saṃgha should perform a formal act (karmavācanā) to divide these items.
Question:
"If he did not enjoy these items while alive, why perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) upon his death?
He replied:

"The transgression of this trade is extremely grave. If the Sangha had consumed these items while he was still living, although they would have committed an offense by violating the precepts, they would nevertheless have been permitted to use them because he was a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for the Sangha."

Because it would lead to continuous and uninterrupted enjoyment, the Sangha’s field of merit does not permit such enjoyment; one would gain no merit in this life and incur grave sin in the next. For these reasons, I dare not do so again.
Since the bhikṣu has already died, there is no further cause for buying or selling; therefore, it is permitted to take the items through formal ritual action (karmavācanā).
In some cases, there may be an offense regarding the means employed, while there is no offense regarding the final result.

For example, if one buys grain or stores salt for the sake of profit, but later develops a virtuous mind and gives them to the Sangha to cultivate merit, this is called "attaining a *duṣkṛta* through skillful means" (*upāya*), while there is no fault in the final result.

Alternatively, there may be no fault in the preliminary means (*upāya*) but a fault in the final result (*phala*). For example, one might purchase rice for the sake of merit and not sell it; however, later, seeing a profit, one sells it for personal gain. This is called "no fault in the means but a fault in the result," and one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"All cases such as these can be understood by analogy.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu purchases for the sake of profit and, having purchased it, does not sell it, he commits a duṣkṛta (突吉羅).
If, for the sake of profit, one sells [an item] and does not buy it back, or buys it back, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
If, for the sake of profit, one buys [an item] and then sells it again, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one sells goods to make food for consumption, there is a *pāyattika* offense for every mouthful.
If one makes clothing, there is a *pāyattika* offense for every time it is worn.
If one makes a mat or bedding, there is a *pāyattika* offense for every time one turns over while lying upon it.
Regarding the rules for purchasing in the marketplace: one must not lower the price to seek other items; to do so constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.

If the price for the robes of the Saṃgha has not yet been increased after the three proclamations, it may be increased; once the three proclamations have been made, the price should not be increased, nor should the Saṃgha grant them, because the robes already belong to another.
If a bhikṣu has received a robe after three proclamations, he should not regret it; even if he regrets it, the Saṃgha must not return it.
If this is an item for sale and there is no trustworthy person (kappiyakāraka) of like mind, it should be made into bedding for the Saṃgha of the four directions in order to prevent slander.
If one were to enter as a Buddha, non-Buddhists would say:
"The śramaṇa Gautama, out of great greed for profit, causes his disciples to relinquish their property and take it for his own personal use."

Furthermore, setting aside the field of merit that is the Buddha, there is no field of merit superior to that of the Sangha of the four quarters; regardless of whether they have received the Dharma or not, whether they uphold the precepts or violate them, or whether their speech accords with the Dharma or not, there is no restriction whatsoever.
If a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts encounters another bhikṣu selling goods, clothing, or food, he should not consume them.
This twenty-first matter, for which the precept was established for the bhikṣus, is for the sake of fulfilling the noble lineages and increasing right livelihood.
This is a unique precept: for a bhikṣu, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense after ten days; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense after one night;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one keeps an extra white iron bowl, an unbaked clay bowl, or any bowl that is not of the proper measure, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is asked:
"If a layperson’s robe or a robe of improper color is kept beyond eleven days, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense because it has been dyed into an improper color."
"If it is a white iron bowl or an unbaked clay bowl, why does one not incur the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* after ten days have passed?
He replied, "The rules for robes and bowls are not the same."
When robes are dyed, they achieve the desired color without further increase or decrease.
However, as for alms bowls, whether they are fired or smoked, they may suffer damage or deterioration; therefore, they are not the same.
If an iron bowl or a ceramic bowl has not been smoked or oiled, it may be used for eating, but it does not constitute formal acceptance and possession (*pratigraha*).
As for the bowl, there are three types:
superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior bowl receives three *pātra* measures of rice, one *pātra* measure of soup, and half a *pātra* measure of other edible foods; this is called the superior bowl.
The lowest grade receives one *pātra* of rice, half a *pātra* of soup, and the remainder of edible food equal to half a *pātra* of soup; this is called the "lower bowl.
That which lies between the upper and lower grades is called the "middle bowl."
If it is larger than a large bowl or smaller than a small bowl, it is not called a *pātra*.

Regarding the *pātra*, the Vinaya masters say that although various teachers have diverse explanations, one meaning is taken as correct: that one *pātra* receives fifteen *liang* of rice, which in the Qin measure is thirty *liang* of rice.
This was a potful of cooked non-glutinous rice from India.
At that time, people all deliberated together, saying that the upper bowl should receive three *pātra* of rice, one *pātra* of soup, and the remainder of edible food should be half a *pātra* of soup.
Three *bhaṭas* of rice equal two *sheng* by the standard of the Qin;
one *bhaṭa* of soup and the remaining food that can be eaten amount to half a *bhaṭa*, which is one *sheng* by the standard of the Qin;
the large bowl (*upapātra*) has a capacity of three *sheng* by the standard of the Qin.
The Vinaya Master said:

"If there is no other food remaining, one should state plainly: 'I accept three *bhojanapātra* of rice and one *bhojanapātra* of soup. One should leave space at the top of the bowl so that the finger does not touch the food;
for the middle and lower bowls as well, one should remove any remaining edible food and leave space at the top so that the finger does not touch the food."

Regarding "lowering the bowl": one receives one *bōtā* of rice, half a *bōtā* of soup, and the remainder of edible food equal to half a *bōtā* of soup—this is one *shēng* according to the Qin measure;
one *shēng* of edible food and half a *bōtā* of soup would amount to one and a half *shēng*.
Thus, lowering the bowl means receiving one *shēng* or one and a half *shēng* according to the Qin measure.
Question:
"If a robe is either too long or too short, it can still be properly accepted and maintained;
yet if an alms bowl is either too large or too small, it cannot be properly accepted and maintained? Why is this so?"
He replied:
"If a robe is too long, it can be shortened or extended.
But as for an alms bowl, whether it is large or small, it cannot be increased or diminished; therefore, there is a difference."

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on a certain day, and on that very same day his mind becomes deranged, disordered by illness, or impaired, and he is neither suspended for not seeing [an offense] nor suspended for not relinquishing evil views, then even until the end of his life there is no offense;
however, if he later regains his senses or is released from suspension, he incurs an offense according to the number of days elapsed since then.

If one obtains a bowl and five days have passed, or if one is insane, mentally deranged, or has a diseased mind; or if one has not been formally expelled, or has been expelled for not abandoning evil and heterodox views—then for as long as these conditions persist, there is no offense.
Later, if one regains one's senses or is released from the expulsion, one must count back the previous five days; if one takes possession of it after that point, the offense is established.
If one obtains a bowl on a day when it is permitted, and goes to the heavens or to Uttarakuru, there is no offense for as long as one remains there;
later, if one returns to one's original location, the sequence is as previously explained.
22. The Twenty-second Matter. Regarding the twenty-second matter: [The Vinaya Master] saw on a shop stall a fine earthen bowl, perfectly round and lovely.
The Vinaya Master said:
"When the Buddha first appeared in the world, the community of monks had no bowls."
The Buddha commanded Śakra-devānām-indra to have celestial artisans fashion one hundred thousand bowls.
Those bowls found in the marketplaces of the world are those divine bowls; they were not made by human hands.
This is a shared precept: if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī requests a new almsbowl, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for both; for the three other assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one requests a bowl made of white iron or unbaked clay, or if one requests it on behalf of another, or by means of a messenger, a letter, or a seal, or if two people together request a single bowl, or if one purchases it, or if one gives it to oneself, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To possess any bowl that is not of the prescribed measure is also a *dukkaṭa*.
If one begs for and obtains a bowl made of white iron or an unbaked clay bowl, and then burns or fires it oneself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu’s bowl has four mends remaining and it is not yet five mends, yet he begs for a new bowl, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If the bowl is such that it ought to have five mends, whether it has been mended or not, begging for a bowl is not an offense.

If a bowl has four or five patches or fewer, after eating one should undo the patches; wash it thoroughly until clean, wipe it with the hands until dry, and place it in a clean location. On the following day, before eating, one should re-attach it with new cord and then use it for a meal.
If a bowl has fewer than five repairs and one seeks a new bowl, this should be handled according to the Vinaya text by circulating it sequentially among the Sangha.
If no one accepts it, it shall be returned to that bhikṣu, who must keep it for the rest of his life.
The alms bowl previously received and maintained should be maintained according to the Dharma; the later bowl is not to be accepted.
One should simply always keep these two bowls, and when it is time to eat, one should carry both bowls.
One should remain thus for the rest of one's life, in order to demonstrate the faults of excessive desire and to sever the causal conditions for future unwholesome states.
This bowl must always be cherished and protected as prescribed in the Vinaya texts; if it is allowed to break through a lack of care, one incurs an offense.

23. The Twenty-third Matter. Regarding the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣus as the twenty-third matter: it is for the purpose of eliminating unwholesome dharmas, for the purpose of stopping slander, and for the purpose of establishing the noble lineage.
This is a common precept: for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika; for śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu begs for thread himself, it is a duṣkṛta.
If he causes a weaver who is not a relative to weave it, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
If one sends a messenger, a letter, or a seal, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Because the weaver relies on the powerful influence of such authority, they will fear the consequences and the matter will certainly be accomplished; therefore, it constitutes an offense.
Regarding this precept, one incurs an offense once the robe has been obtained; however, there is no offense in requesting thread from a relative.
If one weaves it oneself, or causes a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, or śikṣamāṇā to weave it, in all such cases it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, for the sake of obtaining clothing, one begs thread from a person who is not a relative with the intention of making a robe, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one already possesses a small amount of clothing, one should properly beg for a robe; one should not beg for thread to make a robe.
If one sews garments with thread and makes them into belts, there is no offense.

If one does not rely on the influence of a person of high status but seeks [the materials] oneself from the local community, the weaver and the one who causes the weaving to be done are without offense.
In all cases where one personally seeks out others to weave silk or cotton cloth for oneself, there is no offense.
Regarding this precept, whether the garment is of appropriate size or not, one incurs an offense in every instance.
There is no offense if one has a relative weave for them.
If it is not a relative, there is no offense if one has them weave a garment of one cubit (hasta) in length, up to a meditation belt (dhyānabandhana).
24. The Twenty-fourth Matter. This is a shared precept; for a bhikṣuṇī, it constitutes a niḥsargika-pāyattika, while for the three other assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.

Regarding this essence of the precept: if a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative of a bhikṣu commissions a weaver to weave a robe for that bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu goes there in person to urge them to weave it as desired—well-made, broad, fine, and clean—and offers to provide food, utensils, or the value of food, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense if he obtains a fine robe; if he does not obtain a fine robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding this robe, whether it is of the proper measure or not, one incurs an offense in all cases.

If, for the sake of a weaver, one instructs them to weave well but does not provide food, utensils, or the price for the food, and thus obtains a fine robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one sends a messenger, a letter, or a seal, or agrees to provide food, utensils, or the value for food, and subsequently obtains fine robes, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense if one has thread of one's own and has a weaver weave [robes] from it.
25. The Twenty-fifth Matter. This is a shared precept; if a bhikṣuṇī violates it, she commits a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense, while for the three other assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu takes away the robe of another bhikṣu, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he takes away the robe of a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one takes back from a śrāmaṇera who has forfeited his precepts, one who is undergoing *parivāsa* or *mānatva*, one who is blind, deaf, or mute, one who has not been seen [to repent], or one who has not been expelled for holding evil and false views, it is entirely a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one seizes the robes of those whose minds are deranged, whose minds are disturbed by illness, or whose minds are impaired; or of those who have committed the four pārājika offenses, shed the blood of a Buddha, or are among the five types of persons who destroy the wheel of the Saṃgha—all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If a bhikṣuṇī seizes the robe of another bhikṣuṇī, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
To take the robe of a bhikṣu is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one takes the robe of a śrāmaṇerī who has received the precepts, or the robe of a bhikṣuṇī who is undergoing parivāsa, or one who is blind, deaf, or mute, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If one does not perform the formal act of suspension for one who is obstinate or holds wrong views, it is likewise a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The rest is as previously explained.

Regarding the essence of this precept: if a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another and subsequently, out of a desire to cause annoyance, temporarily takes it back by force, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one returns a robe to another after having relinquished it, it is a *pāyattika* offense requiring confession.
If one first gave a robe to another as a primary gift and later took it back as a primary act, one should calculate the value of the money to determine the gravity of the offense.
If one first temporarily gives a robe to another and later takes it back, there is no offense.
If a preceptor, for the purpose of subduing a disciple and causing them to abandon unwholesome dharmas, temporarily takes back the robe, there is no offense.
If, after the robes have been taken away, both individuals go beyond the boundary, they do not lose their robes.
However, if the monk who had his robes taken away carries them out of the boundary, while the monk whose robes were lost stays overnight outside the boundary himself, then he loses his robes.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this refers to the value of the robe being relinquished and returned to another, which does not need to be done within the Saṃgha.
The Vinaya Master says:
in the Hu (Chinese) version, there is no rule for relinquishing within the Saṃgha; the *pāyattika* offense is expiated through confession before another person.
The Vinaya Master said:

"Since the time of the Buddha’s appearance in the world until the present, there has been no śrāmaṇerī who has received the full precepts; how much less could there be one who, having committed an offense, does not conceal it for even a single thought-moment? To such a person, the training rules (śikṣamāṇā) should also be granted."
It is further said:
During the Buddha’s lifetime, there was once a person who studied the Dharma with him.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a śrāmaṇera who had received the precepts in Kaśmīra.
In all cases, there were two individuals who both attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
It is further said:

among the community of śrāmaṇeras who had received the precepts, none committed evil, nor did they give rise to heterodox views to enter the teachings of external paths; nor did they delight in worldly life to return home after renouncing the precepts. There was not one who passed away without having seen the Noble Truths.

If a bhikṣu originally did not intend to give a robe to another, but out of anger and resentment desires to cause that person distress, and forcibly seizes that person's robe by means of physical power for a brief moment, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
26. The Twenty-sixth Matter. This is an *asādhāraṇa-śīla* (unshared precept); none of the other four assemblies possess this precept.
At that time, there was the Elder Vīha—“Vīha” meaning “severance” in the Qin language; because he had already severed all afflictions (*kleśa*) of birth and death, he was called “Severance.”
Although all arhats have attained the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya), their original designations were established for various reasons; therefore, they are not the same.
For instance, the bhikṣu Vīha possessed an excellent saṃghāṭī robe worth one hundred thousand coins.

At that time, there was a band of thieves who wished to plunder his robes. Upon arriving before the bhikṣu’s room, they pointed at the door with their fingers, and he immediately asked, "Who is there?
The thieves replied:
“Bhikṣu! We wish to obtain your saṃghāṭī.
The bhikṣu placed the saṃghāṭī inside his undergarment and entered the fourth dhyāna, sustaining it with the power of that concentration so that they could not take it.
The thieves, unable to obtain the robe despite their various stratagems, said to one another:
"Since we cannot get it now, we should wait together until he goes out to beg for food; then we will surely succeed as we wish."
He then acted according to that plan; when [the other monk] did not return later, he took the robe and departed. By this cause and condition, he lost his *saṃghāṭī*.
When the three months of the summer retreat have passed and there is an intercalary month such that eight months are not yet complete, the prior *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) has already concluded.
Regarding the presence of an intercalary month, the Vinaya Master says:
one should not say that there is an intercalary month.
Regarding those who have not completed eight months, it is called the "later retreat" (paścima-varṣā).

From the sixteenth day of the seventh month until the end of the eighth month has not yet arrived—specifically during the successive six nights beginning from the sixteenth day of the seventh month—it is permitted for a bhikṣu observing the *āranyaka* rains retreat to stay overnight separated from his robe.
The reason it was permitted was that foreign bandits occasionally strike, and these six nights constitute the period during which such bandits set out; therefore, it was permitted.
This robe should be entrusted to the boundary of the Sangha or to the house of a layperson in a place free from the danger of bandits; by the sixth night, one must go back to retrieve the robe.

If one goes to the place where the robe is, or receives another robe, or does not take it back, or does not reach the place where the robe is and does not receive another robe, by the time the seventh day ends, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding the term *āraṇyaka* (a forest hermitage): a place located five hundred *dhanus* (bow-lengths) away from a village is called an *āraṇyaka*.
Four hundred *hu-bu* (Chinese steps) constitute one *dhanus*.
As for a *hu-bu*, one span (*vitasti*) is reckoned as one step.
In this manner, four hundred steps make one *dhanus* (bow-length), four hundred *dhanus* make one *krośa*, and four *krośas* make one *yojana*.
As for what is called one *krośa*: it consists of four hundred *dhanus*; in the kingdom of Magadha, one *krośa* is [reckoned], whereas in the north, it is half a *krośa*.
China is level with the ground, and for this reason it is near;
the north has high and low mountain ranges, and for this reason it is distant.
It further says:
In China there is much wind; at a distance, the sound of drums cannot be heard, but when near, it is heard—therefore, [the drum] is near.
In the north there is little wind; the sound of drums can be heard from afar—therefore, [the drum] is far.
The reason why there are differences in distance between the north and south is that the sound of the drum is heard at varying distances.
What is called a *krośa* is a designation for sound;
generally speaking, the area reached by the sound of a drum constitutes one *krośa*.
The Vinaya Master says:
This is the definition.
Regarding the twenty-seventh matter: this is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*; for śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
"Ten days remaining before the *pravāraṇā*" means that ten days still remain until the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.

Regarding "obtaining an urgent gift of robes": it refers to when a king, a queen, a prince, or a high-ranking military official, possessing a heart of faith and devotion, gives material goods as a gift to the Saṃgha.

Because it is difficult for noble persons to give with a virtuous mind and difficult to encounter them frequently, and because there may be other urgent circumstances, this is called "urgent robe-giving.
If one does not accept it, the donor's merit will not be fulfilled and the Sangha will be deprived of the robes; therefore, its acceptance is permitted.
If a woman, when about to marry, gives property to the Sangha out of a desire for independence— since she would otherwise lack autonomy upon going to her husband’s home—
and if a sick person gives property to the Sangha out of a virtuous mind, it will bring benefit both to the living and to the deceased.
All such instances as these are termed "urgent robes.
Once the Sangha has received the robes, they shall be distributed immediately according to seniority.

Regarding the period during which robes may be stored: from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month—if there is no *kaṭhina* robe—this interval is defined as the "robe season."

This month is called the "garment season" because, at the conclusion of the summer retreat, donors provide abundant food, drink, clothing, and other offerings to the community of monks, while the bhikṣus themselves engage in various tasks such as washing and dyeing their robes.
For these reasons, because there is relinquishment [of robes] during this one-month period, it is called the "robe season" (*cīvarakāla*).
If there is a *kaṭhina* robe, the period from the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month is also called the "robe season."

Regarding the offense herein: if there is no *guṇa-cīvara* (extra robe), by the fifteenth day of the eighth month, this robe must be relinquished, either by performing the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*) or by formally accepting it as one's own.

If one does not relinquish it, purify it, or take formal possession of it, by the eighteenth day of the eighth month at the conclusion of the rainy season retreat, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If there is a *guṇa-cīvara* (extra robe), by the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, that robe must be relinquished, or else purified, or taken into formal possession.

If one does not relinquish it, does not purify it, and does not take formal possession of it, by the sixteenth day of the twelfth month when the earth is cleared, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

With the exception of the ten-day emergency gift-clothing, all robes for the rainy season retreat must await the time of the *pravāraṇā*; if they are divided during the retreat, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā, Scroll Five;
The Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā, Scroll Six.
Translator’s name lost; now appended to the Qin Records.
28. The Twenty-eighth Matter. This is a unique precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*):

a bhikṣu is permitted to possess a rain-cloak, whereas a bhikṣuṇī may possess a bathing robe but is not permitted to possess a rain-cloak. Because bhikṣuṇīs are physically weak and it would be difficult for them to carry [the cloak], they are therefore not allowed to possess either a rain-cloak or a bathing robe.
There are generally two purposes for keeping a rain-bath robe (*varṣāśāṭī*):
first, when it rains, one uses it to shield the four sides while bathing therein; second, during the heat of the day, one likewise uses it to shield oneself while bathing therein;
and furthermore, as there is much rain during the summer months, one constantly wraps the three robes (*tricīvara*) in it to carry them while traveling.
Śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās are not permitted to keep [extra robes].

During the final month of spring, one should seek the rain-cloak; during the half-month, one should possess it. The final month of spring refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the third month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month. From the sixteenth day of the third month until the end of the third month, one should seek and prepare it; if the robe is completed, it should be possessed from the first day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day.
Regarding the rules for keeping [robes]: one may use them for bathing, carrying, and traveling.
If the robes have not yet been finished, one is permitted to seek [more material] or to continue making them until the fifteenth day of the fourth month.
Even if one seeks robe-material on the sixteenth day of the third month, should the robes be completed by the eighteenth or nineteenth day, the Vinaya masters say:
It may also be kept and used.

Examining the intent behind the regulation, within this one-month period one may seek to obtain it and keep it; however, according to the major regulation, one should seek it for half a month and keep it for the other half.
If one enters the preceding *anvārambhaṇa* (early) retreat, one should properly accept and maintain [the robes] until the fifteenth day of the fourth month.

Upon reaching the fifteenth day of the seventh month, they should be kept in a single location; they must not be stored for later use. If one stores them for later use, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Nor is it necessary to discard them; when the time for the next year’s rains retreat arrives, they may be used as before without needing to be formally received again.
If it is the later rains retreat, from the first day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month, they may be kept for forty-five days.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, one should collect [the robes] in one place; they should not be kept or used [individually]. The sequence is as in the previous rules for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat).

If there is an intercalary third month, a bhikṣu should not seek to have a rain-cloak made during the first three months; he should instead seek to have it made on the sixteenth day of the latter three months.

If a bhikṣu was previously unaware that an intercalary month existed and has already completed the request for and acquisition of a rain-bath robe on the sixteenth day of the first three months, he must not store or use it during the intervening extra month; rather, it should be kept in one place.
This is one item among the one hundred and one articles; it need not be given away to others, nor need it be purified (*pariśuddha*).

If there is an intercalary fourth month, one should enter the rains retreat on the sixteenth day of the preceding fourth month and, on that very day, should accept and maintain the rain-clothing (*varṣā-śāṭī*).

By the fifteenth day of the seventh month, one may have kept [the rain-cloak] for a period of one hundred and twenty days during that interval, because the summer months contain an intercalary month and are characterized by heavy rains and heat.
Regarding the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* for keeping it beyond half a month, the Vinaya masters state:

"The various treatise masters maintain that the intercalary month is the third month; one should seek to make the rain-cloak on the sixteenth day of the first three months, complete the making of the garment by the end of those three months, and then use it during the subsequent three months."
If, after the end of the third month, one receives [the robe] from [a donor], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one seeks it out or causes it to be brought, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called "keeping [the robe] for more than half a month"; this robe must be relinquished.

After having confessed and repented for the *pāyattika* offense, one may keep and use [the robe] from the first day of the fourth month until the fifteenth day of the fourth month; there is no fault provided it is not kept beyond the sixteenth day of the fourth month. The procedure for receiving and maintaining it follows the method as previously described.
If one seeks to have a robe made from cloth kept for more than half a month, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one keeps it during an intercalary month, it is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Even if the robe has not yet been relinquished and the offense has not yet been confessed, no further offense is incurred from the first day of the fourth month until the fifteenth day of the seventh month.

If a bhikṣu who was in a place without an intercalary month seeks a rain-bath robe and goes to a place with an intercalary month to observe the rains retreat, that person commits a *duṣkṛta* offense for coming from the place where he sought the robe and for coming with the robe made; if he comes having accepted and kept the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

In a year with an intercalary month, the intercalary month is the third month; in a year without an intercalary month, monks seek the rain-bathing robe from the sixteenth day of the third month. For those in a year with an intercalary month, this constitutes the first three months; once monks have obtained the rain-bathing robe in a year without an intercalary month, they reach the latter three months only upon arriving in a year with an intercalary month. During that interval, there is an extra month, before the time for seeking robes has yet arrived.
Because it was not the time for seeking robes, the offense of *dukkaṭa* (transgression) arises from the act of seeking them;
because he kept them for more than half a month, the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (forfeiture and confession) arises from the act of keeping them.
Because he previously possessed the intention [to keep it], a bhikṣu incurs no offense for not keeping a rain-bathing robe.
Regarding the rain robe, until the sixteenth day of the fourth month, it is permissible to accept one, and there is no fault in not accepting one.
29. The twenty-ninth matter. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, while for the three other groups of followers, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding this essence of the precept: if the object is directed toward the Saṃgha, one must inform the person [to whom it was originally intended] so that the object may enter the Saṃgha of its own accord; [if one fails to do so,] there is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, and the object shall be returned to the Saṃgha.
If the object is directed toward three, two, or one bhikṣu, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs, yet seeks it for himself, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
if he seeks it for three, two, or one [bhikṣuṇī], he commits a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu knows that a donor intends to give an object to the saṃgha but redirects it toward a specific stūpa, the object then belongs to that stūpa and need not be reclaimed; because the merit is the same, the bhikṣu should perform a confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu knows that a donor has given an object to this specific saṃgha, yet he redirects it to another saṃgha, and the object enters that other saṃgha, he need not retrieve it; because the saṃghas are equal, the bhikṣu should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.

If a bhikṣu knows that a donor has offered *pravāraṇā* robes to this specific community of monks, yet redirects them to other monks, those *pravāraṇā* items should be returned to this community because the intended recipients are different; the bhikṣu must perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
If one does not return this to the Sangha, a monetary offense is incurred.
The same applies to the *mukha-lava* (the portion for the face).

If a bhikṣu knows that an object was intended for one person but diverts it to another, he should take it back; since this object has already returned to its original owner, he must perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
If one does not return that object, it constitutes an offense according to its monetary value.
30. The Thirtieth Matter: This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

A disciple of Pīṅgalavatsa had leftover impure ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar; he ate these after they had been kept overnight, and he handled them improperly, failed to receive them with the proper ritual, and stored them indoors overnight.
The Buddha had previously only prohibited the five kinds of formal food and similar foods, but had not yet prohibited the seven-day medicines.
All instances of not receiving [food] or keeping it overnight were already violations of what had been established earlier.

Regarding this essence of the precepts: if a sick bhikṣu requires seven-day medicine and has no attendant of his own, making it difficult to find one through solicitation, he should receive it directly from the hand of a pure person (śucipuruṣa).
Having received it from the mouth of a bhikṣu, one may take and eat it oneself at any location for up to seven days.
If one is so severely ill that one cannot receive it by mouth, one may still consume it.
If a monk who is nursing a patient receives [the medicine] with his hands or by verbal consent, it also constitutes a valid act of receiving.
Once it has been received, if a lay attendant (kappiya-kāraka) touches it, it must be received again.
If it was received on that very day, or if medicine not previously received falls into it, one should receive it once more.
If one has already received medicine for two or three days and further medicine is added to it, one must receive it anew; starting again from the first day, one proceeds through to the seventh day.
If there are many medicines and one does not know which are to be accepted and which are not,
one should receive them again by hand and by word before consuming them.
If a bhikṣu who has been ill for six or seven days cannot receive medicine again for a period of seven days, he must not do so.
When this medicine reaches the seventh day, it must be purified, given to another, or consumed.
If it is not purified, not given to another, and not consumed, then at the end of the eighth day, upon the conclusion of the ground-time (bhūmi), it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If it is medicine for seven days that is not for the sick, once it has been purified by means of a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person), one may receive and eat it together with others at any time.
If one receives it oneself and eats it after it has been kept overnight, one commits the offense of eating stored food (*atiritta-bhojana*), and must perform the *pāyattika* confession.
Regarding these four kinds of medicines, there is no fault in consuming them at any time after midday.

If one uses occasional medicine (*kālika-bhaiṣajya*) or lifetime medicine (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*) to supplement a seven-day medicine (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*), making it into a seven-day medicine for consumption, there is no fault; this is because the potency of the seven-day medicine is predominant, and it has been supplemented by the seven-day medicine.
Just as when meat is boiled in ghee, this ghee and meat broth may be taken as a seven-day medicine;
or as when rock honey, whether it be a "time-medicine" (kālika) or a "lifetime-medicine" (yāvajjīvika), has already been processed into rock honey, it may be taken as a seven-day medicine.

In this way, one may use either *kālābhojana* (medicines taken at the proper time) or *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* (seven-day medicines) to prepare *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* (lifelong medicines); there is no fault in taking them as lifelong medicines.

Or, one may use either *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* or *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* to prepare *kālābhojana*; there is no fault in taking them as medicines for the proper time, because they are used according to their predominant potency and because they assist one another in their formation.
If the portions and potencies are equal, they are determined according to their names.
For example, although sugar-candy pills may be equal in potency, they are designated by name as "seven-day medicine" for the purpose of administration.
Just as with the five medicinal powders, which are named according to their constituent minerals and taken as a lifelong medicine,
so too, if one has great power, the name is assigned according to that power;
if the powers are equal, the medicine is fixed according to the name.
The thirty matters are concluded.

6. The Ninety Matters. First Precept. Regarding the first of the ninety matters: this is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it constitutes a pāyattika offense, while for the three groups of followers it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
There may be cases where false speech constitutes a *pārājika* offense, because one falsely claims to possess superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) when such qualities do not actually exist.
There may also be cases where false speech constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, because one slanders another bhikṣu with groundless charges.

There may be cases where false speech constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*, such as when one claims to possess superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) that are not fully established, or when one slanders another with groundless charges that do not amount to a full offense.
There may also be cases where false speech constitutes a *pāyattika*, such as when one slanders another with groundless charges of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Among these ninety matters, various kinds of false speech are termed *pāyattika* offenses for lying;
however, there are instances where false speech constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense, such as the false speech of the three groups [of novices].

There may be instances where lying is without fault, such as when one has previously made [a vow], or when a layperson lacks a teacher or preceptor, or when one who originally broke the precepts returns to become a bhikṣu.
There are seven factors that constitute a lie:

first, the prior intention to lie; second, the utterance of the lie; third, having spoken the lie, acknowledging it as such; fourth, a different view; fifth, a different desire; sixth, a different tolerance; and seventh, a different knowledge.
Furthermore, there are four factors that constitute false speech:
first, holding a different view; the latter three factors are as previously described.
Alternatively, there may be three factors that constitute false speech:
First, one forms the intention to speak falsely; second, one utters the false speech; third, having spoken the falsehood, one declares it to be such.
If a bhikṣu says he has seen something when he has not seen it, it is a pāyattika offense.

If one sees but says they did not see; if one sees but tells another that they did not see while claiming to have seen; if one does not see but says they saw while telling another that they did not see; if one has seen but, being doubtful whether they saw or did not see, tells another that they did not see; or if one has not seen but, being doubtful whether they saw or did not see, tells another that they saw—because of such mental states, all constitute a *pāyattika* offense.
Hearing, perceiving, and cognizing are also like this.
All such expressions are spoken according to the conceptual mind and involve no offense.

Regarding seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing: one sees with the eye, hears with the ear, perceives with the nose, tongue, and body, and cognizes with the mental faculty (*manas*). These three faculties are distinguished by name because their natures are sharp and their functional capacities are predominant.
The three faculties have dull natures and limited functional capacity; therefore, they are collectively termed "cognition" (*buddhi*).
Furthermore, the three faculties can apprehend objects from a distance, and thus each is designated separately;
the three faculties apprehend objects from close proximity, and thus they are combined into one designation.
Whether it be speaking falsely or writing a false letter, all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one has no prior intention to speak falsely, yet speaks falsely through error or confusion, all such instances likewise constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Whether discussing the meaning of the Dharma, transmitting the words of others, or speaking of any matter of right and wrong, do not harbor self-conceit by claiming it as your own; always ensure that your arguments are grounded in a source, and then you will be free from fault.
If one’s mind is deranged, disordered by illness, or impaired by disease, there is no offense.

Furthermore, there may be cases where speech is false but not divisive; for example, if a whirlwind, a spirit of dust, or a ghost comes to me and says, "I maintain the precepts purely and no lust arises," or if one claims superhuman attainments (*uttarimanussadhamma*) as if they were true, yet the person before them neither hears nor accepts it, it constitutes a heavy *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

If one wishes to slander another with groundless charges, one should first speak to those who are sympathetic, saying: "A certain bhikṣu has committed such-and-such an offense; help me, for this is a grave sthūlātyaya."
As with causing a schism in the Saṃgha, assisting [in such an act] constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if the period is not yet complete, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The second matter: This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *pāyattika*, while for the three groups of followers, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the teaching of the Jātaka causes and conditions: first, it is to prove the fault of disparagement;
second, it is to quell slander. For if the Jātakas were not taught, non-Buddhists would say:
"The śramaṇa Gautama lacks the supernormal power of recollecting past lives."
"Thirdly, it is because they constitute the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
This is the Jātaka; the Buddha knows the past by means of his vow-knowledge (praṇidhijñāna). Question:
"What is the difference between the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) and the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*)?
He replied:
"The knowledge of past lives knows the past; the knowledge of aspiration knows the three periods of time."

The knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) knows that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*); the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) knows both [the conditioned and the unconditioned].
The knowledge of past lives knows one's own past; the knowledge resulting from prayer knows both one's own and others'.

"Through the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), one knows one body and two bodies in succession; through the knowledge of aspirations (*praṇidhijñāna*), one knows a hundred kalpas in a single thought-moment.

As for why animals were able to speak in ancient times but cannot speak now, it is said that at the beginning of the kalpa there were first humans and devas, but the three evil realms did not yet exist.
In the beginning, those in the three evil realms all came from among humans and devas.
Because their past habits were close at hand, they were able to speak.
At present, most animals come from within the three evil paths; therefore, they do not speak.
Regarding the offenses within this context, there are eight types:
namely, first, lineage; second, craft; third, occupation; fourth, transgression; fifth, illness; sixth, perception; seventh, affliction; and eighth, abuse.

Regarding these eight ways of disparaging a bhikṣu: if one uses the three types of arts to disparage and insult any of three kinds of people—a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, or the son of a merchant—it is a duṣkṛta;
if one uses these three matters to disparage and insult others, it is entirely a pāyattika.
If one reviles a kṣatriya or anyone down to a caṇḍāla by means of the other five matters, it is a pāyattika.
If one reviles them in their presence by means of the eight matters, it is a pāyattika;
if one reviles them in private, it is a dukkaṭa.
If one disparages a bhikṣuṇī on account of these eight matters, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
To disparage any of the three assemblies [of śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās] on account of these eight matters is a *duṣkṛta*.

To disparage those with deranged minds, distracted minds, or diseased minds; householders who have no teacher; those who have transcended the saṃgha; all laypeople; or deaf persons—on account of these eight matters—is entirely a *duṣkṛta*. It is also a *duṣkṛta* for the six types of offenders.
If the person before one possesses these eight matters, and one treats them with contempt or disparagement, it is a *pāyattika*.
If they do not possess the eight matters, but one treats them with contempt or disparagement merely for the sake of causing annoyance, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one sends a messenger or writes a letter [with such intent], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one disparages them with the eight matters, saying:
"You possess these eight matters; none of them are in accordance with the Dharma for those who have gone forth," [it is likewise].
Because one speaks thus, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one disparages [another] directly by means of these eight matters, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Apart from these eight matters, if one disparages [another] by other means, even if one says:
"You eat too much, sleep too much, and talk too much; what is the use of leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?
This constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the substance of this precept: if one hears [these words], it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one does not hear [the announcement], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Generally, if there is one who has previously gone forth and later contracted leprosy, he may participate in all monastic affairs; however, at the time of eating, do not allow him to sit among the assembly.

3. The Third Matter: The Third of the Ninety Matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense, while for the three groups [of trainees], it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Regarding the offenses herein, there are eight types:
first, kind; second, performance; third, action; fourth, transgression; fifth, illness; sixth, perception; seventh, affliction; eighth, abuse.
These eight matters all involve five factors:
such a name, such a clan, such a lineage, such an occupation, and such physical characteristics.

Regarding these eight matters, if one transmits [false claims concerning] three of them—lineage, craft, or occupation—to a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa, a merchant’s son, or a bhikṣu, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one transmits these three matters to other bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika.
If one transmits these five matters to a single bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
If one transmits these eight matters to the fourfold assembly, it is a duṣkṛta.

To transmit [the precepts] to a layperson, to one who has no teacher, to one who sends a messenger or a letter, to one with a deranged mind, a distracted mind, or a diseased mind, to one who is deaf, to one who has crossed over [to the other side], to those who have committed the six grave offenses, or to any layperson whatsoever—[if one does so], it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
Regarding the five matters: if a bhikṣu transmits the words of this bhikṣu to that bhikṣu, even saying:
"He says you are a person who reviles others; what is the use of leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?"
He immediately asked,
"Who is he? and [the other] replied:
“[He is] of such-and-such a surname.
“Who is this person of such-and-such a surname? He replied:
"Something. "What is this 'something'?
He replied:
"Someone made it. "Who is this 'someone'?
He replied:
"Such-and-such a mark.
If the listener hears it, it is a *pāyattika*;
if they do not hear it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The reason for the sequential order of these five types is that because there are many instances where names and surnames are identical, it is appropriate to establish them in sequence.

There may be cases of divisive speech (*paiśunya*) that are neither false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) nor harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). For example, when a bhikṣu transmits the words of one bhikṣu to another; because he speaks what is true, it is not false speech; because he speaks with gentle words, it is not harsh speech; yet, because his intention is to cause separation, it is called divisive speech.

There may be instances where there is double-tongued speech (paiśunya) that is false speech (mṛṣāvāda) but not harsh speech (pāruṣya). For example, when a bhikṣu transmits the words of one bhikṣu to another bhikṣu with the intention of causing a separation, it is double-tongued speech because it aims at division; it is false speech because the statement is untrue; and it is not harsh speech because it is spoken in gentle words.

Or, there may be double-tongued speech that is harsh speech but not false speech; for example, when a bhikṣu transmits the words of this bhikṣu to that bhikṣu with the intent to cause separation, it is double-tongued speech because of the mind of division, and it is harsh speech because of the coarse nature of the utterance, yet it is not false speech because he speaks what is true.

There may be instances where double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*), false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), and harsh speech (*pāruṣya*) coincide; for example, as when a certain bhikṣu transmits the words of one bhikṣu to another bhikṣu. Because it is intended to cause separation, it is double-tongued speech; because it is spoken falsely, it is false speech; and because it is spoken with malicious intent, it is harsh speech.
The fourfold formulation regarding false speech and harsh speech is also like this.
Having explained it thus, it is further stated: [the offense of] *pāyattika* and *dukkaṭa*. Regarding "having explained":
one should say, "having heard it, he explains it again. If he has heard it, it is a *pāyattika*; if he has not heard it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There are two kinds of verbal abuse that constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Verbal abuse directed at a layperson consists of speaking of various kinds of impurity within secular life.
Verbal abuse directed at a renunciant consists of directly speaking of unwholesome matters regarding the life of a renunciant.
Regarding "further using other matters besides these eight," it says:
"You are a person who sleeps too much and eats too much, a person given to frivolous laughter; what is the use of leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?"
An *dukkaṭa*. If one says:
"You deceive many people; you are full of guile toward others."
Regarding one who thus transmits [the message] to a bhikṣu: if they hear it, it is a duṣkṛta; if they do not hear it, it is also a duṣkṛta.
If one does not transmit the words from one side to the other, but merely speaks to both parties to cause a schism, it is a duṣkṛta.
The fourth matter, the fourth of the ninety matters: This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a pāyattika, and for the three groups [of novices] it is a duṣkṛta.
There are five kinds of persons:
first, the resident; second, the visitor; third, the person who experiences desire; fourth, the person who recites the *karmavācanā*; and fifth, the person who witnesses the *karmavācanā*.

Regarding the offense herein: if a senior bhikṣu, regarding a dispute over points of discipline, perceives it as such; and after it has been settled according to the Dharma, perceives it as thus settled; yet he initiates it again, it is a pāyattika.

In a dispute arising from mutual recrimination, if one perceives it as a dispute arising from mutual recrimination, and after it has been settled according to the Dharma, one perceives it as having been settled according to the Dharma, yet initiates it again, it is a *pāyattika*.
The same applies to perceiving it as a dispute arising from an offense (*āpatti-vivāda*) or a dispute arising from habitual conduct (*ācāra-vivāda*).

Regarding disputes concerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vivāda*), there are four cases; likewise, disputes concerning assistance (*sahāya-vivāda*), disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*), and disputes concerning habitual conduct (*ācāra-vivāda*) each have four cases. Thus, there are sixteen cases in total, and for each of these cases, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

Just as an established bhikṣu may formulate sixteen propositions regarding the four types of disputes, so too may a guest, one who has received consent (*chanda*), one who recites the *karmavācanā*, and one who observes the *karmavācanā* each formulate sixteen propositions regarding the four types of disputes. Thus, for these five persons, there are eighty propositions in total; for each and every proposition, one incurs a *pāyattika*.

If an elder bhikṣu, regarding a dispute concerning points of discipline that has been settled according to the Dharma and with the perception that it was settled according to the Dharma, should initiate it again, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If, regarding a settlement that was made according to the Dharma, he has the perception that it was not settled according to the Dharma, and should initiate it again, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If one harbors doubt regarding a legal settlement that has been reached according to the Dharma and causes it to be reopened, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding verbal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), there are three phrases; for each phrase, one incurs a *pāyattika*.

The disputes concerning assistance (*anuvāda*), the disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti*), and the disputes concerning habitual conduct (*ācāra*) each likewise have three phrases, totaling twelve phrases.

As with the resident monks (*sthavira-bhikṣu*), so too for the visiting monks (*āgantuka-bhikṣu*), the monk who has received consent (*chanda-grāhaka-bhikṣu*), the monk who recites the *karmavācanā* (*karmabhāṣaka-bhikṣu*), and the monk who witnesses the *karmavācanā* (*karmajña-bhikṣu*), there are twelve phrases for each, making sixty phrases in total; in each and every one of these phrases, it constitutes a *pāyattika*.

If an elder bhikṣu, regarding a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) that has been settled according to the Dharma, conceives the notion that it was not settled according to the Dharma and initiates it again, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If, regarding a dispute that has been settled according to the Dharma, he gives rise to doubt and initiates it again, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Regarding verbal disputes (*vāda-vivāda*), there are two phrases; each of the remaining three types of disputes likewise has two phrases, totaling eight phrases. Each of the other four persons also has eight phrases, totaling forty phrases; for each and every one of these phrases, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If an elder bhikṣu, regarding a legal dispute that has been settled according to the Dharma, perceives it as not having been settled according to the Dharma, and re-initiates it, he does not commit an offense.
As with the phrase "legal dispute" (adhikaraṇa) being treated as a single unit, each of the remaining three types of disputes likewise constitutes a single unit.

Just as the senior bhikṣu formulated four propositions regarding each of the four types of disputes, so too did each of the other four bhikṣus formulate four propositions; thus there were twenty propositions in total, and in each and every one of them, he was not at fault.

Regarding this offense of the nature of a precept (śīla-skandha): regardless of whether the formal ritual (karma) has been performed or not, once the Saṃgha has acted in accordance with the Dharma through harmonious consensus, if one subsequently re-initiates [the offense], it constitutes a *pāyattika* (pāyattika) offense in its entirety, whether in the midst of the assembly or in private.
If it is a monastic regulation that does not enter into the Buddha-dharma, yet one initiates it again, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is neither Buddha-dharma nor monastic law, and after the community has acted in concord, one initiates it again with a mind of illegality, there is no offense.
Excluding five types of persons, all other incoming bhikṣus who grant their consent (*chanda*) are treated identically.

5. The Fifth Matter: This is the fifth of the ninety matters; it is a unique precept (*asādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada*). If a bhikṣuṇī teaches the Dharma to a man for more than five or six sentences, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If there are two men present, there is no offense.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is likewise a duṣkṛta.
If a śrāmaṇera preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, it is also a duṣkṛta.
A "woman" refers to one capable of receiving sexual desire; if she is a barren woman or a young girl not yet capable of engaging in sexual desire, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Regarding "five or six words": these refer to five types of speech—namely, that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is impermanent, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā, saṃjñā, saṃskāra, vijñāna*) are impermanent. There is no offense regarding these five types of speech.
If one exceeds five words, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The six-word formula is: "The eye is impermanent; the ear, nose, body, and mind are impermanent. This is called the five-and-six-word formula.
If one exceeds five or six words, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
A "wise man" refers to one who understands human sentiments and the intent behind speech.
One who may serve as a witness must be someone with whom there is mutual understanding of the language; those whose dialects or linguistic categories differ are in all cases prohibited.
The man must be a layperson (*avadātavasana*); it is not permitted for any ordained person (*pravrajita*), as the circumstances are identical.
Even if the community of monks (*saṃgha*) has assembled, if there is a woman—whether many or few—and no wise man is present, one must not preach to her.
It is permissible to preach the Dharma to a nun; because it is a teaching and admonition for the entire community of nuns, there is no offense.
However, if a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, it is a pāyattika offense.

At that very spot where he had previously sat, as there was no man of wisdom present, another woman came and he preached the Dharma to her once more; the first woman also sat among them, and both heard the Dharma.
Having finished preaching the Dharma, he rises from his seat and departs; on the way, he preaches the Dharma for another woman, and the first woman also hears the Dharma together with her.

If, after preaching five or six sentences to a woman, he enters another place and preaches the Dharma for another woman, and the first woman listens while standing by a wall or in some secluded spot, both hear the Dharma.
In these three instances of preaching the Dharma, the offense was incurred in relation to the first woman.

Even though the first woman had already departed after five or six words, if one subsequently preaches the Dharma to other women who likewise hear it, it is the same because of the prior causal connection.
If one speaks at the first instance, there is a *pāyattika* offense for every word spoken.
If one does not know that a woman was previously inside, there is no offense.
According to the Sūtra, there is a *pāyattika* offense for each individual act.
If one recites verses, for each verse there is a *pāyattika* offense.
A "verse" consists of thirty-two syllables, or thirty syllables, or twenty syllables.
If one recites a sūtra, there is likewise a *pāyattika* offense for every instance.

There is no offense if one speaks of the blessings and rewards of giving along with incantations and prayers; or if one answers a question; or if one receives the five precepts or the eight precepts; or if one recites hymns (*bhāṣya*).
If one speaks of mundane, worldly matters, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
6. The Sixth Matter: The Sixth of the Ninety Matters. This is a shared precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a pāyattika, and for the three groups of followers it is a duṣkṛta.

The reason for establishing the precepts for the bhikṣus is to distinguish them from non-Buddhists, to differentiate between teacher and disciple, to clarify the meaning of speech so that it may be understood, and to rely on the true meaning rather than valuing mere sounds.
Regarding "persons who have not received full ordination":
this refers to all persons other than bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
As for the substance of this precept, one incurs an offense by teaching the wording of the dharma to such persons who have not received full ordination.
There are two types of phrasing:
first, complete phrasing; second, incomplete phrasing.
Regarding complete phrasing, the Vinaya Master says:
"Same phrasing.
If the teacher recites a long phrase and the disciple also recites a long phrase, this is called "same phrasing.

Regarding the offense herein: if the teacher recites a long phrase to instruct the disciple by following the rise and fall of the voice, and the disciple recites the long phrase in unison with the teacher, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one recites short phrases while chanting in unison with others, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the teacher recites long phrases while the disciple recites short phrases, yet they chant in unison, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If the teacher recites a short phrase while the disciple recites a long phrase, or if they recite in unison, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There is no offense if the teacher has finished reciting and the disciple recites afterwards so that their voices do not coincide; in such cases, it does not matter whether the phrases are identical or different—there is no offense in any of these instances.
The essential meaning is that if one utters the words simultaneously with the same person, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; if the words are not uttered simultaneously, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
However, provided there is a sequence in the utterance of the words, there is no offense in any case.
If two people both possess mastery of the text, they may recite it together without offense, though they must not chant in unison (*saṃgīti*).

If a bhikṣu has no one from whom to receive the transmission for recitation, he may even receive the dharma from a śrāmaṇerikā; however, he should simply seek out a person of excellent precept-keeping and great virtue to serve as a companion and witness.

One may also receive the Dharma from a layperson (avadātavasana), but one must not address them as an ācārya; in this manner, the Dharma may be received through successive transmission, provided that one takes care to ensure that the dignified deportment (īryāpatha) is not lost.
The same applies to having sufficient flavor versus insufficient flavor, and having sufficient syllables versus insufficient syllables.
If one teaches a person who possesses the precepts using a verse with identical phrasing, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the teacher recites a long verse and the disciple mistakenly receives it as a short verse, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

7. The Seventh Matter, the Seventh of the Ninety Matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense, while for the three groups [of novices], it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one speaks to a person of full precepts for the sake of gain and offerings, it is also a *pāyattika*.
The reason the precept was established for bhikṣus is because it is the way of great men; to proclaim one's virtuous conduct while concealing one's faults and transgressions is the way of small men.
For the sake of the Dharma of equality, if one claims noble virtues for oneself, then the wise and the foolish become distinct, and that person lacks a mind of equanimity toward the Saṃgha.
"Is there any case where one speaks of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) to a person who has not yet received full ordination (upasampadā) without committing an offense?"
He replied: "There is.
If one speaks to a close friend with whom one shares the same mind and has no ulterior motives, and does so not for the sake of fame or profit, there is no offense."
If one encounters the danger of bandits, fearing the loss of one's life, one may say:
"If you kill me, you will incur a most grave sin.
Or, if one is ill and has no one to look after them, one may speak to another person as follows:
"If one looks upon me, they shall obtain great merit.
Such explanations given for these kinds of reasons are without fault; because a human body is difficult to obtain, there is thus no transgression.
"Those who have not received the full ordination" refers to all persons other than bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
"Truly existing" means that there truly exists a state beyond the human (uttarimanussadhamma).
If a bhikṣu, having truly attained the four paths and four fruits, speaks of them to one who has not yet received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.

If he has truly attained the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal powers, the contemplation of impurity, or mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), and speaks of these to another, it is a pāyattika.
Question:
"The contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) are minor, mundane dharmas.
Why are they called 'dharmas that transcend the human'?"
He replied:

"This is the initial gateway to the Deathless (amṛta); there are no noble ones (ārya) who do not pass through it. For this reason, it is called a 'dharma transcending the human' (uttaramanuṣyadharma).
... [down to] ... if, for the sake of fame or profit, one says, "I am pure and maintain the precepts," it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one says that devas, nāgas, or spirits have come to one's presence for the sake of fame or profit, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one says that whirlwinds or earth-spirits have come to one's presence for the sake of fame or profit, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one truly recites the Tripiṭaka but speaks of it to others for the sake of fame and profit, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

To whatever extent one recites the sūtras, understands their meaning, or is able to engage in question and answer, if one speaks of these to others for the sake of fame and profit, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

8. The Eighth Matter, the eighth of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense, while the three other groups do not commit an offense.
The reason the precept was established for the bhikṣus is for the great protection of the Buddha-dharma.

If one were to speak of a bhikṣu’s transgressions and evils to a layperson (avadātavasana), that person would lose their faith and reverence for the Buddha-dharma; it would be better to destroy a stūpa or damage an image than to speak of a bhikṣu’s faults to one who has not received full ordination, for to speak of such transgressions is to destroy the Dharma-body.

Regarding "except by formal monastic procedure (*saṃgha-karman*)," there are generally two types of formal procedures as explained in the Vinaya texts. If one speaks of a bhikṣu’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) to a person who has not yet received full ordination, it constitutes a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
To speak of the names of offenses belonging to the two categories [the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*] to a person who has not yet received full ordination constitutes a *pāyattika*.
To speak of the actual facts of such an offense constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
If one speaks of the names of offenses belonging to the three lower categories, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To speak of such matters of offenses is also a *duṣkṛta*.

Regardless of whether the preceding bhikṣu has committed an offense or not, to speak of his grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) to one who has not yet received full ordination constitutes a *pāyattika* for all such instances.
If one speaks of the offenses of the fourfold assembly, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one sends a messenger, a letter, or a sealed document [to report them], it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
If one speaks of shedding the blood of a Buddha or causing a schism in the Saṃgha, it is a *sthūlātyaya* when confessed face-to-face (*pratyekamukha*).
If one speaks of the limits of the four matters or the limits of the thirteen matters, it is all a sthūlātyaya or a duṣkṛta.
If one speaks of the grave offenses of the fourfold assembly, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense, or sees a bhikṣu speak of superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) to a woman, he regards it as a pārājika.
What is it that is called a *pārājika* yet referred to as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?

It refers to a bhikṣu of wrong views who speaks of superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) to a woman; that is, he utters improper speech to a woman. This is what is meant by calling a *pārājika* a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
What is meant by *pāyattika*?
It refers to seeing a bhikṣu speaking of superhuman dharmas (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) to a woman, that is, speaking more than five or six words to a woman.
What is meant by *pratideśanīya*?
Seeing a bhikṣu speaking of superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*) to a woman, it is said that he received food and drink from within the woman’s dwelling.
Why is this called a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing)?
Seeing a bhikṣu speaking of superhuman qualities to a woman, it is said that he addressed the woman, saying, "You are blind; you are sightless."
If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu speaking harsh words to a woman, this is called a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
What is meant by regarding a saṃghāvaśeṣa as a pāyattika?
Seeing a bhikṣu speaking harsh words to a woman, yet believing he has exceeded five or six words—this is what is meant by regarding a saṃghāvaśeṣa as a pāyattika.
What is meant by *pāṭidesanīya*?
It refers to seeing a bhikṣu engage in improper speech with a woman, namely, receiving food or drink from within a woman’s dwelling.
What is meant by *duṣkṛta*? It refers to seeing a bhikṣu speak harsh words to a woman, such as saying to her, "You are blind," or "You are sightless.
What is meant by *pārājika*?
If one sees a bhikṣu speaking harsh words to a woman, namely by claiming to have attained superhuman states (uttaramanuṣyadharma);
if a bhikṣu sees a bhikṣu speak more than five or six words to a woman, this is called a pāyattika offense.
