What is meant by *pāṭidesanīya*?
It refers to when one sees a bhikṣu engaging in more than five or six words with a woman, namely receiving food or drink from within a woman’s dwelling.
What is meant by *duṣkṛta*?
If a bhikṣu speaks more than five or six words with a woman— such as saying to a woman, "This is black" or "This is white"—
what is meant by *pārājika*?
If one speaks more than five or six words with a woman, it refers to speaking of superhuman attainments (*uttari-manussa-dhamma*).
What is meant by *saṃghādisesa*?
If one sees a bhikṣu speaking more than five or six words with a woman, it refers to speaking wicked words to a woman.
If one sees a bhikṣu receiving food or drink from within a woman’s dwelling, this is called a *pāyattika* (Pāṭideśanīya).
What is meant by a *duṣkṛta*?
Seeing a bhikṣu receiving food and drink from within a woman’s dwelling, he says to the woman, "This one is blind; this one is sightless.
Why is this called a pārājika?
Seeing a bhikṣu receiving food and drink from within a woman’s dwelling, he says that he has realized the superhuman states (uttarimanussa-dhamma).
What is meant by *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?
It refers to seeing a bhikṣu receiving food or drink from within a woman’s dwelling, and then accusing him of engaging in improper speech with that woman.
What is meant by *pāyattika*?
If one sees a bhikṣu receiving food or drink from within a woman’s dwelling, it is considered speaking more than five or six words with a woman.
If one sees a bhikṣu saying to a woman, "this is white" or "this is black," this is called a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
What is meant by *pārājika*?
It refers to a bhikṣu speaking to a woman, saying "this one is blind" or "this one is sightless," which is called claiming superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*).
What is meant by *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?
If one sees a bhikṣu speaking to a woman, saying "this one is blind" or "this one is sightless," it means he is engaging in improper speech with the woman.
Why is this called a *pāyattika*?
It is because one sees a bhikṣu speaking to a woman, saying "this one is blind" or "this one is sightless," exceeding five or six words in his address to the woman.
What is meant by *pāṭidesanīya*?
It refers to a monk who, having seen a woman, says to her, "This one is blind," or "This one is sightless," while receiving food or drink from within that woman's dwelling.

If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense and gives rise to doubt— wondering whether it is a pārājika or not a pārājika— such as seeing a bhikṣu engage in sexual intercourse with a woman,

thinking [the other] was intentionally emitting semen or that she was a stone-woman (barren), and subsequently his doubt is severed, he then definitively forms the perception of a pārājika regarding that pārājika offense.
Question: "By what means is doubt severed? Answer:
“By encountering a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one cuts off doubt.
By encountering a spiritual friend, one is able to sever unwholesome dharmas, extinguish false dharmas, and cut off indeterminate dharmas.”
If one sees a bhikṣu commit a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and a doubt arises—seeing him embracing a woman naked, one wonders whether he is naked or clothed;
whether she is a stone-woman (barren woman) or not a stone-woman.
If a bhikṣu has committed an offense by speaking more than five or six words to a woman, he may wonder: "Did I speak more than five or six words, or did I not?
Was she a barren woman, or was she not?"
If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu taking food from a family under training, he may wonder whether a formal act (karmavācanā) has been performed against him or not.
If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu say to a woman, "This one is blind," or "This one is squint-eyed," he may harbor doubt as to whether these words were actually spoken.
Is it for the sake of explaining other matters?

Regarding the ninth matter, the ninth of the ninety matters: when the Buddha established the precepts for the bhikṣus, it was for the purpose of extinguishing strife and contention, for the purpose of extinguishing suffering and affliction, and for the purpose of attaining peace and happiness while practicing the Path.
This is a shared precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense, while for the three other assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

Regarding the essence of this precept: if the Saṃgha has performed a formal act (karmavācanā) in unison to bestow property upon those who manage affairs or perform laborious service—whether it be items dedicated by the Saṃgha or items from the *pravāraṇā* distribution—and having thus bestowed them, one later reproaches them, saying, "You gave these out of favoritism," it is a pāyattika offense.

In any assembly of the Saṃgha, whether it be those who perform laborious service for the Saṃgha, those of great virtue, or those who are impoverished, if the Saṃgha grants them anything through a formal act of harmony, they shall all receive it.
If one has granted consent and subsequently revokes it after the assembly has reached a consensus, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one revokes it from outside the assembly, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding this precept, it does not necessarily require that the consent was given out of intimacy; it is a violation in all cases where it is said that one "should not grant [consent]."
10. The Tenth Matter. This is the tenth of the ninety matters; it is a common precept, which the three assemblies do not violate.
Channa was the half-brother of the Buddha, the son of King Udayana’s sister.
The kingdom of Kauśāmbī is the birthplace of Channa; it was where King Śuddhodana resided in his palace.
In the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, there was also a separate palace where Channa’s mother constantly resided.
There was also a beautiful woman who married into this country; for these reasons, Channa resided in this country frequently.
Furthermore, because there were many opportunities here to benefit sentient beings, he resided in this country often.
The reason for establishing the precepts with the bhikṣus is to show respect for the Prātimokṣa, to nurture the ethical discipline, and to extinguish unwholesome dharmas.
Twelve years ago, when the Buddha was constantly reciting a single verse, he now speaks of five sections which are called the "Minor Rules" (kṣudrānukṣudra).

Regarding those who violate these: if one objects to the four *pārājika* rules, or if one objects to a single precept by saying, "What is the use of preaching this rule against sexual misconduct? [one incurs an offense].
One incurs one *pāyattika* offense.
If one censures the matter itself, there are four *pāyattikas*.
If one censures in all four ways, there is one *pāyattika*.
If one utters a rebuke while the preface of the *Prātimokṣa* is being recited, one incurs one *pāyattika*.
A question is asked:
"The preface of the *Prātimokṣa* is not the actual precepts; why does one incur an offense?"
He replied:

"The introduction to the precepts explains the meaning of the two hundred and fifty precepts; if one reviles the introduction to the precepts, one is reviling all the precepts, and for this reason, one incurs an offense."

"In this manner, there are thirteen matters, two undetermined matters, thirty matters, ninety matters, four matters requiring confession, and the rules of training; these comprise one hundred and eight matters. If each one is censured, there are one hundred and eight *pāyattika* offenses."
If one rebukes [the assembly] collectively, it is one *pāyattika*.
The same applies to the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
If one rebukes by citing a Sūtra that conforms to the Vinaya, it is likewise a *pāyattika*.
If, during the recitation of any Sūtra other than those that follow the Vinaya, one utters a reproach, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, with the exception of Sūtras that follow the Vinaya.
If, during the recitation of any other Sūtra, one utters a reproach—whether much or little—it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Question: Why is it said that the offenses against the *Vinaya*, the *Sūtras*, and so forth are grave, while the offenses in other sūtras are light? Answer:
“Precepts are the level ground of the Buddha-dharma; from them all virtues arise.
Furthermore, all disciples of the Buddha rely upon and dwell within the precepts; those without precepts have no basis for reliance, and all sentient beings exist by virtue of the precepts.”
Furthermore, the precepts are the initial gateway to the Buddha-dharma; without the precepts, there is no means by which one may enter the city of Nirvana.
Moreover, the precepts are the jeweled ornaments of the Buddha-dharma, serving to adorn it; for this reason, their violation is a grave offense.

11. The Eleventh Matter. This eleventh of the ninety matters combines two conditions to form a single precept: the first condition concerns pulling grass from within a monastery; the second condition concerns cutting down large *bībarā* trees and destroying a village of spirits.
Later in the night, this tree deity went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
He asked,
“Why have you spirits come to the Buddha’s dwelling at night?”
He replied:
"When the Buddha was in the world, he frequently preached the Dharma to devas, nāgas, and spirits at night, and frequently preached the Dharma to humans during the day.
The reason for this was that if humans were to see such spirits, they would give rise to fear; therefore, his activities differed by day and night."

Regarding those who stand to one side: because the various deities possess a profound sense of love and respect for the Buddha, and because they have requests to make, most conditioned deities delight in purity, whereas the ground was not pure.
For these various reasons, he did not sit.
During the eight nights of winter, the cold wind splits the bamboo; in India, the end of winter and the beginning of spring—during these eight nights—are the peak of the severe winter season.
The reason for this is that when the power of cold is about to end, it must first reach its peak before it begins to decline.
Furthermore, it is said that because the sun descends closer to the earth, the intensity of heat diminishes; therefore, the cold becomes extreme.
The reason for speaking specifically of "breaking bamboo" is that since bamboo is the hardest of all things yet can still be broken, how much more so other types of wood?
It is also said:
the nature of bamboo accords with heat; it remains evergreen through both winter and summer.
Since even this [wood] was split because of the extreme cold, how much more so would other woods be?
The reason for establishing these precepts for the bhikṣus is to avoid causing distress to sentient beings, to cease slander, and to provide great protection for the Buddha-dharma.
There are three precepts that bring great benefit to the Buddha-dharma, which are found in other recitations:
first, one must not carry [loads]; second, one must not kill plants or grasses; third, one must not dig the earth.
If these three precepts were not established, all kings would compel bhikṣus to perform various types of labor;
because these three precepts exist, all sovereigns and kings restrain their minds.
This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense. For the three groups [of novices], as they are attendants (paricāraka), there is no offense.
There are five kinds of seeds:
root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, spontaneously falling seeds, and fruit-seeds.
Root seeds refer to those produced from roots, such as carrots and turnips.
Stem seeds refer to those produced from stems, such as pomegranates, grapes, and willows.
Regarding seeds produced from joints: these include sugarcane, coarse bamboo, and fine bamboo—such as those that grow from their nodes.

Regarding seeds produced by spontaneous shedding: these refer to *mālatī* (blue flax), *rōrakē* (basil), *hūsai* (coriander), tangerines, and pears—such as those that grow from spontaneously fallen seeds.
Regarding "seed from a fruit": rice, hemp, wheat, large beans, small beans, millet, and the like are all seeds from fruit.

If a bhikṣu, among these five kinds of seeds, cuts them himself or instructs another to cut them; breaks them himself or instructs another to break them; burns them himself or instructs another to burn them—in each case, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding "instructing others": if one instructs a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, one incurs a pāyattika;
if one instructs the three other assemblies [of the saṃgha], it is a duṣkṛta.
If one burns five types of seeds at the same time, it constitutes a single pāyattika.
If one burns them one by one, for each instance, whether many or few, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one plucks tree leaves, for each leaf plucked, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one cuts down a tree with a single stroke, it is a *pāyattika*.
Such cases may be understood by analogy.
Regarding all fruits grown from seeds or raw vegetables, if they are eaten together with their seeds, those belonging to the five types of seeds must all be purified by fire.

If one does not eat fruits with their seeds intact, provided that the fruits and vegetables do not contain the five types of seeds, they may all be eaten after being purified by means of a knife or fingernails.
A Vinaya master says:
"All fruits, if to be eaten with their seeds intact, must be purified by fire."
If one does not eat the seeds, one may eat them at all times; there is no need to purify them with knives or fingernails before eating.
The Buddha himself stated that for raw fruits and vegetables, regardless of whether they contain seeds or not, they must be purified before being eaten.
If one swallows impure fruit together with its seed, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one bites it open, it is a *pāyattika*.
This twelfth matter of the ninety matters is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a *pāyattika*, and for the three groups of followers it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding this precept: if one scolds or reviles those fourteen persons previously appointed by the Sangha, it is a *pāyattika*.
In general, whether the appointment of the fourteen persons has been performed through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) or not, there is no fault in either case.
If one reviles these fourteen persons while their formal act (*karmavācanā*) has not yet been rescinded, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one reviles these persons after their formal act has been rescinded, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Even if one directs anger and derision toward a person appointed as a food supervisor—whether they be in a separate room or performing the same duties—it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one directs anger and derision toward fourteen people from afar, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation) if they hear it, and a *duṣkṛta* if they do not hear it.
Regarding "reproaching from afar": this refers to speaking words of censure without being face-to-face; it is sufficient that the sound reaches the other party for the act to be complete.
If one sends a messenger or a letter to do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅).
This thirteenth matter of the ninety matters is a shared precept (*sādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada*).
This precept has two aspects: the formal act of *smṛti-vinaya* (reinstatement through recollection) and causing annoyance by not complying with questions and answers.
If one performs the formal act of *smṛti-vinaya* and subsequently causes annoyance by not complying with questions and answers, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one causes annoyance by not complying with questions and answers before the formal act has been performed, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

Second, intentionally annoying others by remaining silent while performing a *smṛtivinaya* (act of recollection), or after having performed the *smṛtivinaya*, annoying others by remaining silent: these are *pāyattika* offenses;
if one annoys others by remaining silent before the *karma* has been performed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Among the five categories of precepts, there are three precepts in which two offenses have been combined into one; for example, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct among the four matters:
first, the offense is defined by engaging in sexual intercourse with a human being, and second, the offense is defined by engaging in sexual intercourse with an animal.

Among these ninety matters, there are two precepts; two distinct formulations are combined into a single precept, as in the preceding case of the precept concerning anger and derision. This was initially formulated because of the anger and derision directed toward the *pāṭimokkha* assembly; thus, it constitutes a single formulation.
Later, when [the offense] was not manifest before one's face, one instead reviled from afar; thus another precept was established.
These constitute two establishments of the rule, yet despite these two prior and subsequent establishments, they remain a single precept concerning reviling with anger.

These two rules concerning not answering questions when asked are also two types of disciplinary offenses (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). First, because one did not answer questions when asked, the rule was established; this is the first offense.
Second, because one troubled others by remaining silent; this is the second offense.
Although these are two fetters, they constitute a single precept against causing distress through evasive answers.
Regarding the recollection and recognition of the Dharma, one should provide full recollection and recognition to all members of the five assemblies.
Question:
"Is this recollection and cognition present before one's eyes or not? Answer:
"The monks and nuns must be present, while the three other assemblies need not be present.
This requirement applies specifically within the boundary (sīmā); as with the formal act for a "family under discipline" (śikṣādattaka-karman), it likewise takes place within the boundary.
The *pātra-nyāsa* (turning-over-of-the-bowl) *karmavācanā* is performed in the absence [of the person]; the same applies to the three assemblies, which are also performed in their absence.

Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed: if a *śrāmaṇera* renounces the precepts, the original *karmavācanā* remains; if he returns from the laity and subsequently becomes a *bhikṣu*, the original *karmavācanā* remains; if his gender changes and he becomes a *bhikṣuṇī*, the original *karmavācanā* remains; and the same applies if a *bhikṣuṇī* changes her gender.
One may likewise perform the *poṣadha* and the *pravāraṇā*; all one hundred and one *karmas* may be performed.
The *saṃghakṣamaṇā*, the *pravāraṇā*, and the face-to-face *kaṭhina* ceremony are in every respect identical.
He may receive the transmission of sūtras and dharmas from others, and he may also receive sūtras and dharmas from others; in all these matters, he is without obstruction.
However, he is not permitted to act as an upādhyāya, to serve as a preceptor for dependence, or to maintain śrāmaṇeras.
One may receive full ordination through the *karmavācanā* of non-renunciation.

Regarding the substance of the precepts, one must necessarily recite the *Prātimokṣa* together with the bhikṣus; if, out of malice, one does not comply with the questioning and answering, it constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If a nun of the three assemblies asks about matters concerning the precepts and one does not answer in accordance with the question, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If she asks about other matters concerning the sūtras or the Dharma and one does not answer in accordance with the question, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one confesses the offense committed, the *karmavācanā* of release may be obtained.
If a *ṣaḍdharmikā bhikṣuṇī* changes her faculties to become a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerikā* changes her faculties to become a *śrāmaṇera*.

14. The Fourteenth Matter. This is the fourteenth of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both monks (*bhikṣu*) and nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), it is a *pāyattika*; for the three groups [of novices], it is a *dukkaṭa*.

He established the precepts for the bhikṣus for the sake of practicing the Path in peace and happiness, for the sake of nurturing faith and reverence, and for the sake of bringing the roots of goodness of the donors to fulfillment.
"Monastic bedding" refers to coarse or fine rope beds, wooden beds, and various kinds of coverlets, quilts, and pillows.
"In the open air" means in a place without any covering or enclosure.
Regarding the offenses herein, there are generally two occasions:
When the first watch of the night has ended, or when the second watch has ended:

if a bhikṣu spreads out a monastic bedding on the open ground during the first part of the first watch of the night, and sits or lies upon it, and upon departing does not himself put it away nor instruct another to put it away, when the first watch of the night has ended, it is a pāyattika offense.

If, until the ground has been cleared, one spreads out bedding for the Saṃgha and neither picks it up oneself nor instructs another to pick it up, when the clearing of the ground is finished, it is a *pāyattika*.
If, at the time the ground is cleared, one spreads out bedding for the Saṃgha on an open space and sits or lies down upon it, then departs to enter a room to rest until sunset, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one spreads out the bedding of the Sangha on an open space at sunset and enters a room to rest, committing the act until sunset has passed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If, after spreading out the bedding of the Sangha on an open space, one leaves the monastery and travels more than forty-nine paces, such that the ground is clearly left behind, it is a *pāyattika*.
If, after spreading out the bedding of the Saṃgha on an open space, one wanders through the various rooms without entrusting it to someone else, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If it is one's own bedding, and one does not put it away at the proper time, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If one spreads [a rug or mat] on the open ground, the reason for picking it up at the proper time is threefold: first, fear of being dampened by rain; second, fear of being scorched by the sun; and third, fear of being blown away by the wind. For the sake of protection, one should pick it up and cover it in a suitable place.
If one spreads out monastic bedding on an open ground, whether or not one leaves the monastery, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense when the time for the ground to dry has arrived.
Even if there is some covering or shelter, if the rain reaches the bedding, it is in all cases a *pāyattika* offense.

If one has spread out bedding belonging to the Saṃgha and goes outside the monastery—regardless of the distance—and the ground has not yet been cleared and the sun has not yet set, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Fifteenth Matter, the Fifteenth of the Ninety Matters: This is a common precept; for both monks (*bhikṣu*) and nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), it is a *pāyattika* offense, while for the three groups [of trainees], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a visiting bhikṣu spreads out monastic bedding in a room and departs beyond the boundary, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a resident bhikṣu spreads out monastic bedding in a room and departs beyond the boundary with the thought that he will return immediately, yet due to urgent circumstances is unable to return immediately, then upon reaching the end of the day outside the boundary, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
"Bedding and requisites" refers to coarse or fine rope beds, wooden beds, blankets, quilts, and felt rugs.
"Spreading" refers to spreading out monastic bedding within a room.
Whether leaving the monastery for a short or long distance, one must entrust these items to others; if they cannot be entrusted, one should personally fold them up and carry them away.
The sequential methods for entrustment are all contained within the Vinaya texts.
A great śrāmaṇera who is well-versed in the precepts may also receive such entrustment.
If a visiting bhikṣu spreads bedding within a room and departs the boundary with the intention of returning, yet fails to do so by the time the ground is cleared, it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
If one does not intend to return, and having gone beyond the boundary, reaches the time when the ground-work is finished, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a resident bhikṣu has finished spreading out bedding and one goes beyond the boundary without intending to return, reaching the time when the ground-work is finished, it is a *pāyattika*.
16. The Sixteenth Matter of the Ninety Matters. This is a shared precept; for the three assemblies, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The reason the precepts were established for the bhikṣus is to avoid causing suffering to sentient beings and to extinguish strife and contention.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, personally drags someone from their bed to the ground, it is a pāyattika.
This applies even if he drags them from a raised earthen platform to the ground; it is likewise a pāyattika.
If one is able to pull [the robe] by force, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one is not able to do so, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one causes another to pull it—whether that other person is a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, or even a layperson who pulls the bhikṣu—it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu is able to pull [the object], both incur a pāyattika;
if he is unable, both incur a dukkaṭa.
If he instructs another who is able to pull it, he incurs a pāyattika.
If one is unable [to do so], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one drags a *bhikṣuṇī* or those of the three other assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one drags one who is deaf, blind, lame, or mute, or a *śrāmaṇera* who has received the precepts, or one undergoing *parivāsa* or *mānatva*, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one ordains those who live at home without a teacher-monk, former bhikṣus who have broken the precepts, those who have renounced the path, the six types of offenders, or those who follow the five-fold dharma, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"O layperson, there is no offense.
Regarding 'except for special circumstances': if the dwelling is collapsing or if one is pulled out of the room due to various dangers, one does not commit a *pārājika* offense.
However, if one first forms the intent to kill and forcibly pulls someone out, and that person dies, it is a *pārājika* offense."
If one does not die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one drags a bhikṣuṇī with a lustful mind and touches or seizes her, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one drags a bhikṣuṇī out of anger or resentment, if he succeeds, it is a *pāyattika*; if he does not succeed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a nun pulls a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu, while in a monk’s dwelling or a nun’s dwelling, pulls a nun, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a nun drags a bhikṣu into a private room belonging to the saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
If a nun drags a bhikṣu into her own room, it is a dukkaṭa.
This seventeenth matter, the seventeenth of the ninety matters, is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a pāyattika, and for the three groups of disciples it is a dukkaṭa.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu knows that bedding has already been spread in another bhikṣu’s room, yet later comes and spreads it himself or causes another to spread it in any one of the following places—before a sitting bench, before a sleeping bed, within the room, outside the room, in a walkway, on a high place, or in front of a raised earthen platform—he commits a *pāyattika* if he is able to spread it; if he is unable to spread it, he commits a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding this essence of the precept: one must not, under the guise of observing the precepts, forcibly contravene another person’s wishes to perform any action.

If, for the purpose of annoying others, one closes or opens a door, closes or opens a window, lights or extinguishes a fire, or lights or extinguishes a lamp; or if one performs recitations, incantations, vows, reading scriptures, preaching the Dharma, or engaging in debate—whichever actions the other finds unpleasant—one commits a *pāyattika* offense for each such act.
It constitutes an offense only because it is intended to distress the mind of another.
(18) The Eighteenth Matter: This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika, while for the three groups of disciples, it is a duṣkṛta.

Regarding the offenses herein: if one sits or lies down on a bed for sleeping or a meditation seat—whether it has one pointed leg and three non-pointed legs, two pointed legs and two non-pointed legs, three pointed legs and one non-pointed leg, or four pointed legs—and does so by applying force while on an upper story of a multi-storied building, each instance constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one uses any soft material to support the legs of a bed, there is no offense.
If one uses materials such as bricks, stones, or tiles that could cause injury to others to support the legs of a bed, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If the place where the bed is situated on an upper story of a multi-storied building is secure, thick, and without leaks, there is no offense.
If the legs of the bed are not pointed, there is no offense.
Even if they are pointed, provided one does not sit or lie down with force, there is no offense.
Regarding this precept: if one sits or lies down with force upon a multi-storied building, a bed with pointed legs, or a seat with a thin base, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

In all matters concerning the proper method for a bhikṣu to sit or lie down, one must be thorough and careful; if one is not careful, injury will inevitably result, and furthermore, one’s dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) will be impaired, constituting a *dukkaṭa* offense.

19. The Nineteenth Matter, the Nineteenth of the Ninety Matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense, while for the three groups [of novices], it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Generally, there are three types of killing living beings:
there is killing sentient beings out of greed for their fur, horns, hides, or flesh;
and there is killing sentient beings out of hatred, resentment, or malice.
To kill sentient beings while having neither greed for gain nor malice toward them is called killing sentient beings out of delusion.
For example, when Channa uses water containing insects, this is called killing sentient beings through delusion.
Regarding this precept against taking life, there are four such precepts in total; among these four, this one was established first.

Once it was established that one must not use water containing living beings to sprinkle on grass, soil, or mix with mud, [the rule] was immediately followed by the prohibition against drinking water containing living beings.
Since they were not permitted to use water containing living creatures, they intentionally deprived those animals of their lives.
Once it was prohibited to deprive animals of life, they then began to deprive human beings of their lives.
There are four precepts concerning the taking of life; because the circumstances differ, they are all designated as "previously committed" offenses.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu takes water containing living organisms and pours it over grass or mixes it with mud, for every instance of its use, regardless of the quantity, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

If one wishes to establish a place of residence, the rule is that one must first inspect the water. Using a fine cloth one cubit in length, one should fashion a water-strainer; having had it filtered by one who strictly observes the precepts and is thoroughly conscientious, one should place the water in a vessel and examine it carefully in the light of the sun.
If there are still insects present, one should make a water-strainer of double thickness, or a water-strainer of triple thickness.
If insects are still present, one should not remain in that place.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Six;
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Seven.
Translator’s name lost; now appended to the Qin Records.
20. The twentieth item of the ninety matters.
This is an *asaṃvara* (unshared) precept: for a nun it is a *duṣkṛta*, and for the other three groups of disciples it is a *duṣkṛta*.
When Channa constructed a hall, it collapsed on the very day it was finished.
Although he spent three hundred thousand coins and exerted great effort in building this large hall, the monks preached the Dharma for the sake of the donor;
thus, although the hall collapsed, the merit was fully accomplished.
Even before the room was destroyed, the Buddha had already arrived within this room; thus, it was already being utilized by him.
The Buddha is the unsurpassed field of merit; since the Buddha has utilized it, its merit is profound and vast, beyond measure.
It is further said:
When the room was first completed, there was a young bhikṣu who had recently received the precepts and whose virtue was pure; he entered this room and leaned a *yānjī* (tooth-stick) against the wall.
By means of this single bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, the donor’s merit from their act of faith is already fulfilled.

Even if one were to construct billions of various chambers and pavilions with all manner of adornments, reaching down to the adamantine foundation of the earth, lofty, vast, and magnificently decorated like Mount Sumeru; [the merit would still not equal that of supporting such a precept-holder].
If a bhikṣu of pure precepts makes temporary use [of these items], the donor’s grace is already fulfilled. Why is this?
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Buddha cultivated the bodhisattva practices; having now attained the Way of Buddhahood, he first realized the *prātimokṣa* and bestowed it upon sentient beings.
The Prātimokṣa is not a worldly dharma; it is that which turns away from the mundane and proceeds toward the gate of Nirvāṇa.
Ordinary dwellings, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal requisites are worldly dharmas; they are not the supramundane dharmas that are difficult to obtain.
Therefore, if a bhikṣu of pure precepts makes even a momentary use of such things, the donor’s grace is already fulfilled.
However, if one constructs new monastic dwellings or stupas and images, digs wells on desolate roads, or builds bridges, this person’s merit arises at all times, except under three conditions:
first, if the previous work is destroyed; second, if this person dies; or third, if they give rise to evil and heterodox views.
When these three causes and conditions are absent, merit constantly arises.
The Buddha previously entered this room and walked back and forth across its upper and lower levels, ensuring that the donor’s meritorious gift would not be in vain.
The Buddha, through his supernatural power, inspired his disciples and the donors to preach the Dharma to them in succession.
Regarding the method for constructing a dwelling, there are three grades:
superior, middling, and inferior.
The methods for roofing a room each have their own limits.
If one uses the method for roofing a middle or upper room to roof a lower room, it is because of the need for careful handling and because it can be completed all at once.
If one uses grass for the covering, for every blade of grass there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If the upper room is covered according to the method used for the middle room, it is likewise because of the principle of careful treatment.
If one uses grass for the covering, for every blade of grass there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one follows the method of covering [the wall] in superior, middling, or inferior degrees, because it is completed all at once, there is one *pāyattika* offense once the room is finished.
If the wall is not built up all at once, there is no offense.
21. The Twenty-first Matter. The Twenty-first of the Ninety Matters. Regarding the initial circumstances of the precept concerning the Sangha not appointing [a monk] to instruct bhikṣuṇīs:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "I am utterly exhausted from teaching and transforming the fourfold assembly."
Question: "The Buddha has attained the body of Nārāyaṇa, so his body knows no fatigue;
he has attained the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and great loving-kindness and great compassion, so his mind knows no fatigue."
"Why do you say he is exhausted?
He replied, "The Buddha is not exhausted; it is only because he conforms to worldly conventions."

It is like a father who knows his son is capable of managing the household affairs; although he himself possesses the strength, because his son is competent and he wishes to entrust the business to him, he says, "My vigor has declined and I am decrepit; you shall know all matters of the household."

The Buddha is likewise; although he does not experience exhaustion, he wishes to transmit the teachings to his disciples, and thus, in accordance with worldly conventions, he speaks of being exhausted.

There are four reasons why he instructs the disciples to admonish the bhikṣuṇīs: first, to demonstrate that he has no stinginess regarding the Dharma; second, so that the teacher and the disciples may share the same vision and knowledge; third, to manifest the merit and wisdom of the bhikṣu Paṇḍaka; and fourth, because each of the bhikṣus has specific karmic conditions with the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs through which they ought to receive instruction.
22. The Twenty-second Matter. Regarding the twenty-second of the ninety matters: as for "Nanda," this refers to another Nanda; it is not the Nanda who was the Buddha’s younger brother.
In the past, when the Buddha Vipaśyin appeared in the world, he preached the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
After that Buddha had passed into extinction, there was a king who erected a stupa of ox-head sandalwood, adorned with all manner of ornaments.
This king had five hundred consorts who made offerings to this stūpa, each making a vow, saying:
"May we, in the future, attain liberation from this king."
"The king at that time was none other than Nanda;
the five hundred ladies at that time were these five hundred nuns.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of this original vow, they shall attain liberation through Nanda."
In this context, because the person who instructs nuns has already relinquished the three precepts through the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), those three precepts are also relinquished.
Furthermore, if one continues to preach the Dharma to nuns until sunset, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense due to the violation of dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*).
If one scolds a person who teaches the Dharma to nuns, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense because it violates the rules of decorum.
Regarding the "Kumāra Verses," there was a hall named Kumāra; because the presiding master of that hall was named Kumāra, the hall itself was called Kumāra.
The Buddha was in the Kumāra Hall, where he spoke these verses for the sake of the Kumāra devas, enabling them to enter the vision of the Truths (dṛṣṭisatya).
For this reason, they were named Kumāras.

The Twenty-third of the Ninety Matters: Missing in all versions. The Twenty-fourth of the Ninety Matters: Missing in all versions. The Twenty-fourth Matter: If one happens to travel the same road with another without prior appointment, one should keep them at a distance such that their speech cannot be heard; if they can hear each other and then return [to being within hearing], it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

If a bhikṣuṇī makes an appointment with a bhikṣu and the bhikṣu does not consent, or if a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī and the bhikṣuṇī does not consent, yet they hear each other’s voices, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The same applies to waterways.
"Water" refers to traveling by way of water.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes an appointment with a bhikṣu to travel [by water], it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This precept is not shared [with other groups]; for the three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu makes a prior appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together by land from one village to another, it is a *pāyattika*;
if he turns back midway, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one goes toward an open space where there is no village, even for the distance of one *krośa* (five hundred *dhanus*), it is a *pāyattika*;
if one returns midway, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The same applies to traveling by waterway.
If one travels the road together with a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is the same as [travelling] with a *bhikṣuṇī*.
As for the reason the Great Assembly goes first: it is because the Buddha attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* among men, and because the *bhikṣu* is the foremost among the fourfold assembly.
For these reasons, it is called "the great assembly.

Regarding the exception to these conditions: if one has many companions, yet there is doubt or fear regarding the path to be traveled—where "many companions" refers to two or three laypeople—if one consults with such practitioners, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The same applies even if there are hundreds or thousands of companions.
If it is a layperson who does not deliberate, there is no offense.
It is the same regarding waterways.
Regarding this precept: if many *bhikṣuṇīs* travel together by prior appointment, it constitutes one *pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense if they do not travel by prior appointment.
Furthermore, there is no offense if they travel with the wife of a king.
If there is a lady and one makes an appointment with her, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
The Twenty-fifth Item of the Ninety Matters: This is a unique precept for bhikṣuṇīs. If a bhikṣuṇī consults with a bhikṣu regarding traveling on a boat, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for the three other assemblies [śrāmaṇerī, śikṣamāṇā, and śrāmaṇera], it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the offenses herein: if one bhikṣu makes an appointment with one bhikṣuṇī to ride in the same boat, it is a pāyattika.
If one bhikṣu, even down to being in the same boat with four bhikṣuṇīs, there are four pāyattikas.
According to the number of nuns, one incurs that many *pāyattika* offenses.
If four bhikṣus travel together with one nun on the same boat, each incurs one *pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, according to the number of *bhikṣuṇīs*, one incurs that many *pāyattika* offenses.
If one makes an appointment with a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī* to board a boat together, it is the same as [an offense] with a *bhikṣuṇī*.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to ride in the same boat, traveling upstream from one village to another, it is a pāyattika;
if they turn back midway, it is a duṣkṛta.
If there is no inhabited village or open space for even a *krośa*, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one returns midway, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The same applies to going downstream.
There is no offense if there was no prior agreement, or if one was simply crossing.

Or if, while intending to cross straight across, one is carried away by the current; or if, while crossing straight across, the bank collapses in front of one; or if one loses one's belongings; or if the boatman does not know how to handle the boat—wherein the bhikṣu originally intended to cross straight across but, due to these various difficulties, goes upstream or downstream: in such cases, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī and a bhikṣu are on separate boats and have made an appointment together, and there is no layperson as a companion, it is a pāyattika.
If they have not made an appointment, they must ensure that their voices cannot be heard by one another; if they can be heard, it is a duṣkṛta.
If there is fear while traveling by land but no fear while traveling by water, making an appointment [to meet] is without offense.
If there are many laypeople on board the boat, making an appointment is without offense.

26. The Twenty-sixth Matter: This is the twenty-sixth of the ninety matters; it is a unique precept (*asādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada*). If a bhikṣu measures the robes or bowl for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If a śrāmaṇera gives a robe to a nun who is not a relative, it is a duṣkṛta;
if a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇerikā gives a robe to a bhikṣu who is not a relative, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu gives [an item] to a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇerī, or a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
If he sends a messenger to give it, it is a duṣkṛta.
If he gives five kinds of paṃsukūla robes, three [of those instances] constitute a pāyattika.
Cloth chewed by oxen, cloth gnawed by rats, and cloth burned by fire;
two kinds of cloth constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense:
cloth defiled by the first sexual union of a man and woman, and cloth defiled by a woman’s place of childbirth.
If one gives a garment of appropriate measure to a white-robed layperson, it is a *pāyattika* offense, because it must be dyed according to the rule.
If one gives a garment of improper color, it is also a *pāyattika* offense, likewise because it must be dyed according to the rule.
If two bhikṣus together give a robe to one bhikṣuṇī, or if one gives a single robe to two bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If it concerns robes or bowls that are not of the proper measure, or any utensils such as needles, spoons, or ladles—even down to a single button on a robe, or a length of one chi and one cun, or a single thread; or even within a bowl of food, down to a single cake or a single fruit—all such cases constitute a *duṣkṛta*.
Except when striking the ghaṇṭā (wooden gong), if one distributes food in order among the assembly, there is no offense.
An offense occurs herein if one gives to a nun who is not a relative, thinking she is a relative.
Regarding those who are said to be "relatives": it is as when sisters have been separated for a long time, and later seeing another person, they claim them to be a relative;

or as when one marries again and has children by a different mother, or by a secret liaison, or gives birth to sons and daughters from a pregnancy conceived previously—due to such causes and conditions, they claim them to be relatives.
The same applies to these various bhikṣus by analogy.
If one gives clothing to [a nun who is] not a relative, it is a pāyattika.
If one gives to a bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, or śrāmaṇerī who is not a relative, while believing her to be a relative, it is a pāyattika.
If a nun who is not a relative gives rise to doubt as to whether she is a relative or not a relative,
or even as to whether she is an ordained nun or not an ordained nun,
and [the donor] gives her a robe, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu has a relative who is a bhikṣuṇī, yet conceives the notion that she is not a relative—for instance, if a sister has been separated from him for a long time and, upon meeting her later, he regards her as a non-relative.

For example, if a father has an extramarital affair and fathers sons or daughters; or if a woman with different mothers becomes pregnant and subsequently marries into another family, giving birth to sons or daughters; or if a father consorts with his own domestic slave and fathers sons or daughters—these are called "relatives" when one perceives them as "non-relatives."
If one gives a robe [to such a person], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a relative nun is addressed as a non-relative, or even addressed as one who has left the household life, or if one harbors doubt as to whether she is a relative or not?
...up to: whether she is a nun who has left the household life or one who has not;

whether she is a nun who is not a relative; whether it is said so or not said so; whether there is doubt or no doubt—if one gives her an impure robe, such as a camel-hair robe, a cow-hair robe, a goat-hair robe, or a robe woven from mixed fibers, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
27. The twenty-seventh matter of the ninety matters: If a bhikṣuṇī makes a robe for a bhikṣu who is not a relative, it is a duṣkṛta;
the same applies to the three assemblies [of novices], which is also a duṣkṛta.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, he commits a pāyattika for each individual act involved.
If he cuts or sews it, it is a duṣkṛta.
If it is stitched with needles, for every needle there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If it is sewn straight, for every needle there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If it is joined with cord, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If she trims the border, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If she makes one for a relative nun, there is no offense.
In this context, making robes refers exclusively to robes of the proper measure; if she makes a robe for a layperson or a robe of improper color, it is entirely a *pāyattika* offense.
If one makes five kinds of *paṃsukūla* robes, three types constitute a *pāyattika* offense as previously stated;
two types constitute a *dukkaṭa* offense, also as previously explained.
If a nun sends a messenger with cloth materials to have a robe made for her, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one causes another person to make [the robe], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If two people together make a single robe, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one makes a robe for a *śikṣamāṇā*, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one causes another to make any kind of improperly measured robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing).
If one washes it, for each individual act it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one dyes it, for each application of dye it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
If one makes a garment from camel hair, cow hair, or the wool of a black sheep, it is also a *pāyattika*. 28.
The twenty-eighth matter of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for a nun it is a *pāyattika*, and for the three groups [of novices] it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one sits in a secluded place with a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
"Secluded" means a place lacking shame and modesty, a place where sexual intercourse could be committed.
"To sit alone with a single nun" means there is no third person present.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu sits alone with a bhikṣuṇī in a secluded and concealed place, it is a *pāyattika*.
Having risen and then sitting back down again, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every instance of rising and then sitting back down, one incurs that many *pāyattikas*. 29.
The twenty-ninth item of the ninety items. This is a common precept; for a nun, it is a *pāyattika*, and for the three other groups of disciples, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one commits sexual intercourse with a barren woman or a young girl who is incapable of such acts, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
The preceding [set of rules] concerns offenses regarding secluded places; this [set] concerns offenses regarding exposed places.

The latter two concern offenses regarding eating in a house: namely, the offense of staying overnight for more than two nights in the same room as a person who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the offense of staying overnight in the same room as a woman.
Regarding these six precepts, while the matters of censure are similar, their meanings differ.
Among them, the four precepts concerning secluded places, exposed places, and eating at two families involve exactly two persons; no third person is required for the offense to be established.

Next are the offense of staying overnight again and the offense of staying in the same room as a woman; regarding these two precepts, one incurs the full offense even if there are many people present.
Furthermore, the first four precepts are offenses committed during the day, while the latter two are offenses committed at night.
These two precepts differ in this way:
regarding the offense therein, if a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in an exposed place, it is a pāyattika.
If one rises and then sits down again, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every instance of rising and sitting down again, one incurs that many *pāyattikas*.
If one sits at a distance of one *vyāma* from another, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one sits at a distance of one *vyāma* and a half, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one sits at a distance of two *vyāmas* or more than two *vyāmas*.
30. The Thirtieth Matter. This is the thirtieth of the ninety matters; it is a unique precept (asādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada), and for a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The essence of this precept is as follows: if a bhikṣuṇī, in order to obtain food, praises the merit and wisdom of a bhikṣu to a donor (dānapati) in a biased manner, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī prepares food for a specific cause, it is also a pāyattika offense.

There are five qualities by which one may be invited [to receive offerings], such as Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmoggallāna, and Anuruddha, and which enable one to serve as a field of merit for sentient beings in the present life:

first, entry into the path of seeing the truths; second, the great knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); third, the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); fourth, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); and fifth, the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇasamādhi*).
Emerging from the path of seeing the truths (satyadarśanamārga), one thereby enables the attainment of merit in the present life.

Having been afflicted by false views since beginningless time, one now realizes the vision of the truths; all five types of wrong views are exhausted without remainder, and the indestructible faith and vision are now first accomplished.
By these causes and conditions, people obtain blessings in the present life.

As for the arising of the great knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) causing people to obtain blessings in the present life: since beginningless time, sentient beings have been afflicted by delusion, craving, and pride; now that they have attained the knowledge of exhaustion, the three impurities are forever extinguished.
By these causes and conditions, it enables people to obtain merit in the present life.
Furthermore, when emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it likewise enables sentient beings to obtain merit in the present life.
It is also said:
Emerging from the attainment of cessation is exactly like returning from nirvana; for this reason, one obtains merit in the present life.
Furthermore, it is said:

if one enters the attainment of cessation, one must necessarily proceed through the stages in order, from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and only then enter the attainment of cessation.

When emerging from meditative absorption, one necessarily enters the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) in succession from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), proceeding down through the first dhyāna until entering a state of distracted mind.
Because the power of the mind’s pervasive cultivation throughout these various dhyānas is profound and weighty, it causes sentient beings to obtain merit in the present life.
Regarding the four immeasurables: by taking infinite sentient beings as objects with the mind to uproot their suffering and bestow happiness upon them, one benefits others profoundly and extensively.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, it enables sentient beings to attain merit in the present life.
The samādhi of non-contention (araṇā-samādhi) is a mundane (laukika) samādhi, not one that is untainted (anāsrava).
There are three kinds of contention:
first, the contention of afflictions (kleśa); second, the contention of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha); and third, the contention of strife (raṇa).
All Arhats have exhausted two kinds of conflict:
the conflict of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the conflict of strife (*raṇa*); these two conflicts are exhausted.

However, because the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) remain, they are not yet fully exhausted; it is these five aggregates that can give rise to human conflict, and only the *araṇā-samādhi* (the concentration of non-conflict) can extinguish this conflict.
Although all Arhats themselves are free from contention, they cannot prevent others from giving rise to contentious thoughts toward them.

An Arhat who dwells in the state of non-contention (*araṇā-vihārin*) can cause both self and other to be free from contention; because all [afflictions] are extinguished, he can cause sentient beings to obtain merit in the present life.
The bhikṣuṇī said to the householder’s wife,
“Please invite the bhikṣus.
[She asked,] “Whom do you wish to invite?”
She replied,
"I have invited such-and-such a bhikṣu.
The nun then said to the householder’s wife:
“If you prepare polished rice, ghee-bean soup, chicken, francolin,
and quail meat,” and a bhikṣu eats it, it is a pāyattika.
Even if he is instructed to put a small amount of ginger into the food, and the bhikṣu eats it, it is a duṣkṛta.

Regarding this precept, its essence is solely to praise its gravity: regardless of whether the recipient is an ordinary person or an arhat, if one eats [the food], it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī says:
"Please invite a bhikṣu."
The householder’s wife asked,
“Whom have you invited? He replied:
"Please [someone else].
The householder’s wife said,
"I have already invited him first."
Question:
"What food have you prepared?
Answer: [He] replied:
"Coarse food.
[If one says,] "Prepare rice, even up to the meat of the francolin partridge," and a bhikṣu eats it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one does not offer indirect praise for their virtues, but merely speaks of the merit of giving to a śramaṇa, that merit is exceedingly great.
Thus, when the merit of giving is spoken of in this manner, there is no fault for a bhikṣu who eats.
31. The Thirty-first Matter. This is the thirty-first of the ninety matters; it is an *asādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada* (an exclusive precept), which bhikṣuṇīs and the three other assemblies do not violate.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, during the autumn months, suffered from a severe condition of alternating cold and heat, such that he could neither eat nor drink.

On the eighth day of the final month of winter and the eighth day of the first month of spring—in these sixteen days—the force of the cold is extremely violent, and many cases of cold-related illness arise because the energies of winter and spring contend with one another.
Furthermore, when the sun travels in its lower course, the area illuminated by its light is small, and for this reason the cold is extreme.
On the eighth day of the final month of spring and the eighth day of the first month of summer—these sixteen days—the heat reaches its peak intensity, and many cases of feverish illness break out.
Because the sun is directly overhead, the area it illuminates is vast, and for this reason it is intensely hot.

On the eighth day of the final month of summer and the eighth day of the first month of winter—these sixteen days—it is neither cold nor hot, because the path the sun travels is neither too high nor too low. Since both cold and heat are present together, diseases of chills and fevers arise.
For the benefit of the bhikṣus, it is permitted to eat three kinds of complete meals, namely those possessing excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.
A sick bhikṣu may accept one invitation, but he should not accept two invitations.
If one cannot be satisfied by accepting a single invitation, it is permitted to accept a second invitation, but one should not accept a third.
If one cannot be satisfied by accepting a second invitation, it is permitted to accept a third invitation, but one should not accept a fourth.
If, after accepting a third invitation, one cannot be satisfied, one should eat gradually until midday after having accepted it.
If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly, it is a pāyattika offense.
The "exceptional times" refer to the time of illness.
If one is ill, and if the illness is alleviated by means of food, it will otherwise be aggravated; therefore, eating repeatedly is permitted.
Furthermore, the time when robes are offered is also called an exceptional time.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu has been invited for food and clothing, and the host arrives with food and clothing, it is not an offense to accept the invitation and eat.
If a bhikṣu has been invited for food and clothing, but the host arrives without food and clothing, it is not an offense to accept the invitation; however, to eat [the food] constitutes a pāyattika.
If there is an invitation for both clothing and food, and the person comes with clothing but without food, accepting the invitation is not an offense; however, eating constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If there is an invitation for neither clothing nor food, and the person comes without either clothing or food, accepting the invitation is a *duṣkṛta*; eating constitutes a *pāyattika*.

If there is an invitation without clothing or food, but that [person] comes having received an invitation with clothing and food, accepting the invitation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; for the one who eats, there is no offense.

If there is an invitation without clothing or food, but that [person] comes having received an invitation with clothing but without food, accepting the invitation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; for the one who eats, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there is an invitation for one who has robes but lacks food, and he comes having both robes and food, accepting the invitation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; if he eats, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there is an invitation for one who has robes but lacks food, and he comes having both robes and food, accepting the invitation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; if he eats, it is a violation.
If there is an invitation for clothing and food, but the person comes without clothing or food, accepting the invitation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;
eating [the food] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. There is no offense if one has received an invitation for many garments and food, and all [invited persons] come with clothing and food.
From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to eat repeatedly on festival days; having finished giving to others, they may receive their midday meal from them.
What is meant by "giving to others"?
It refers to eating together.
"Characteristics" refers to the characteristics of fortune and misfortune; therefore, one prepares food.
One who prepares food does so for the sake of a bhikṣu of great virtue.

On days of fasting, on the first and sixteenth days of the month, when the community of monks is in separate rooms, whether it be an invitation to the entire community or an individual invitation, one should in all cases give [the food] to others.
If one has been invited by the fivefold assembly, one should not give [the invitation] to another.
If there is an invitation for robes and food, and someone comes who has either robes or lacks robes and food, it is not an offense to accept the invitation.
If one goes outside and a donor invites one, saying:
"A bhikṣu has come for a meal; we shall give you a robe.
To accept such an invitation is not an offense, and to eat there is also not an offense.

Regarding invitations with both food and robes versus invitations with neither food nor robes: if it is an invitation with both food and robes, accepting the invitation is not an offense, and eating there is also not an offense.
If there is no invitation for food or clothing, to accept such an invitation constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense; to eat [the food] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Generally, where there are two [conditions], one must necessarily obtain one and lose the other; if it is a single phrase, it must necessarily correspond.
If there is an invitation for food and clothing, accepting the invitation is not an offense, nor is eating the food an offense.

If that person goes outside without food or clothing, and a donor says, "I will give you food," then accepting the invitation without clothing is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), while eating the food is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
The meaning may be understood through these analogies. 32.
The thirty-second matter: This precept is common [to all]; for a bhikṣuṇī it is a *pāyattika*, and for the three other assemblies it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu stays at a house of merit for more than one meal, he commits a pāyattika.
If he stays for more than one night without eating, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one stays elsewhere and eats a meal there, one commits an offense of falling (pācittiya).
If one who is not ill consumes food there more than once, one commits an offense of falling.
As for those who are ill, even coming from another village with a body wounded and broken, or even being injured by a bamboo leaf, all such cases are termed "illness."
There is no offense in the following cases: staying for one night and accepting one meal; being ill;

if the owner of the merit-dwelling (*puṇya-śālā*) is a relative; if previously invited; if waiting for companions before entering a dangerous path; if there are many merit-dwellings and one stays in succession among them; or if one knows that the person in charge of the merit-dwelling has invited one to stay. In all these instances, there is no offense.
Regarding the "House of Merit" (*puṇya-śālā*): its primary purpose is for all monastics who are disciples of the Buddha, in order to cause their merit to become profound and vast.
However, it is not permitted for any other renunciants, whether lay or ordained, nor for śramaṇas or brahmins.
Regarding the prohibition against eating when food has been set aside: this applies primarily to renunciants; for householders, it is not fixed, as they may either give or not give.

The thirty-third matter, the thirty-third of the ninety matters: Whenever sentient beings give rise to afflictions and become deranged, it is always because they have lost something they previously deeply cherished and loved. Therefore, the Buddha used his supernormal powers to manifest a transformation so that they might see it.
Because this elder had lost his daughter’s husband, he became insane with grief and rage.

The Buddha, by means of his supernatural powers, manifested a phantom husband and placed him in the same location; through these circumstances, the elder’s heart of anger was immediately extinguished.

Regarding the statement that "the Buddha's power of loving-kindness causes that anger to be extinguished": if there are sentient beings who are destined to receive benefit from the Buddha, even if they give rise to afflictions, the Buddha will first use the supernatural power of his mind of loving-kindness to cause those afflicted minds to be extinguished, and only then will he preach the Dharma.
There are thirteen such causal conditions of this kind:

first, the father of a squinting girl went to the Buddha’s dwelling harboring anger; because the Buddha employed the power of his compassionate mind and supernormal faculties, that anger was immediately eliminated, after which he preached the Dharma.

Second, there was an elder in the kingdom of Śrāvastī who had an only son whom he loved very dearly; the boy died young, and furthermore, his vast stores of grain, wheat, and other crops were utterly destroyed by hail and frost. Because of these events, he became deranged.
Through the Buddha’s supernatural power, his madness was immediately dispelled; he listened to the Dharma and realized the Truths.
Third, there was a Brahmin who had fathered six sons, all of whom were handsome and upright in appearance; when they all died at once, he wandered about in a state of frantic madness.

By the power of his compassionate mind, the Buddha manifested six sons who all appeared before him; immediately, [the man's] shame and joy were so intense they became disordered, but these were soon dispelled as the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, leading him to enter the Path of Seeing the Truths.

4. King Ajātaśatru, intoxicated with drink, intended to come and trample the Buddha with an elephant. The Buddha, through his compassionate mind and supernormal power, transformed the ground into a pit of fire and manifested his five fingers as a lion king. The elephant, struck with terror, knelt and paid homage to the Buddha; the Buddha stroked its head with his hand, and its life ended, it was reborn in heaven.

5. Upasena harbored anger toward the Buddha; the Buddha, through his compassionate mind and supernormal power, manifested a great venomous snake on both sides of the path, causing him to realize that because of his poisonous heart of hatred he would fall among such snakes, and that through this sense of dread, his malice was immediately extinguished.

Sixth: When King Virūḍhaka punished the Śākya kingdom, he had the Śākya sons buried waist-deep in the ground so that they could not move. The Buddha used his supernormal powers to manifest a garden with bathing pools to gladden their hearts.
King Virūḍhaka was sporting with the Śākya women in the hall, enjoying the five sensual pleasures.
The women asked the king, "Why are you so joyful and engaged in such various diversions?
The king replied to the women:
"It is simply because he has overcome his enemies.
The woman said, "It is because all the Śākyas are noble sages who do not contend with others over material things; therefore, the King has achieved victory."
"If it were not so, we would merely have one man fight with the king, and the king could not defeat him.
Vairāṭa then became enraged; he cut off the man's hands and feet and threw him into a ditch.
By the power of his compassionate mind, the Buddha enabled them to hear the Dharma and realize the Truth with their own hands and ears.
Seventh, while the Buddha was beneath a tree, the Māra King arrived with countless hosts of soldiers, intending to harm him.
By means of his supernatural powers, the Buddha subdued the demonic adversaries, transforming himself into various forms according to their species to subdue them:
he manifested as a lion to subdue the tigers, and as a garuḍa to subdue the dragons; for the yakṣas, he appeared as King Vaiśravaṇa, and so forth.

8. Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, unable to bear witnessing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, entered parinirvāṇa first; because they entered parinirvāṇa first, seventy thousand arhats entered parinirvāṇa simultaneously with them.
At that time, among the fourfold assembly of disciples, there was none who was not in a state of agitation and confusion.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested two great disciples standing to the left and right of the Buddha. For this reason, sentient beings were filled with joy and their distress was immediately dispelled; the Buddha then preached the Dharma for them, and each attained benefit.
9. There was a householder whom the Buddha had prophesied would end his life and enter hell in seven days.
Ānanda went to inform him, and it was exactly as the Buddha had said, without any discrepancy.
Yet, with his mind stained by worldly pleasures, he paid no heed to this and continued to enjoy himself with music.

As the day was drawing to a close, Ānanda, who possessed great strength, forcibly led him to the Buddha's presence. The Buddha stroked him with his hand, ordained him, and taught him the Dharma according to his needs, whereby he attained the path of Arhatship.

10. There was once an elder who had an only son whom he loved dearly. When the elephant trampled and killed him, the father immediately fell into a state of wild confusion and wandered aimlessly from east to west.

The Buddha, by means of his supernatural powers, manifested a transformation of the son so that the father might see him; the father’s frantic mind was instantly dispelled. The Buddha then preached the Dharma for him, whereby he gave rise to the causal conditions for becoming a *pratyekabuddha*.

11. There was a nāga girl who went to where the Buddha was; her husband was filled with anger, but the Buddha moved him so that his anger was extinguished, and he immediately received the Dharma teaching and took the three refuges.
12. A dove entered the Buddha’s shadow and did not move away.
13. For a sick bhikṣu, the Buddha personally bathed him and then preached the Dharma, whereby he attained arhatship.
Thus, through these thirteen causes and conditions, one eliminates evil thoughts by the power of a compassionate mind and subsequently bestows the benefit of the Dharma.

According to the customs of foreign lands, when householders rise at dawn to prepare food, they regularly set aside a portion for bhikṣus seeking alms; this is placed in a designated spot to be given to those who arrive.

According to the monastic rules of foreign lands, when begging for alms, they each designate separate locations, such that a certain bhikṣu goes to one place and another bhikṣu goes to another, so that each may receive their respective share of gain and benefit.
If a donor first divides out one *śoṇa*, one should take one *śoṇa* and must not demand more.
If one demands more and receives an additional small bowl, it is a *pāyattika*; if one does not receive it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the host first prepares one large bowl and gives it entirely to a bhikṣu, he may not ask for more; if he asks for more and receives it, it is a pāyattika offense.
Once he has received the food, there is no rule permitting him to go outside to give it to a bhikṣu.
If this food can be consumed entirely by oneself, then one should stop; if it cannot be finished, one may distribute it as desired.
If one wishes to act according to the Dharma, the host should first give three bowls to the bhikṣu; it is best if one takes only what is sufficient for one's own stomach.
Regarding other elders who see a bhikṣu begging for alms: they should indicate the place [where the food is kept];

if they do not indicate the place, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. As for the measure of the bowls: one large bowl (*mahā-pātra*) is equal to two medium bowls (*madhyama-pātra*), and three small bowls (*hīna-pātra*). Two medium bowls are equal to three small bowls.

If a donor’s household has previously set aside one superior bowl to give entirely to a bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu further requests another, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if he obtains a small bowl, it is a *pāyattika*.

If the host first leaves one small bowl and gives it entirely to the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu asks for more, it is a duṣkṛta offense; even if he asks repeatedly until he obtains two more small bowls, it is likewise a duṣkṛta offense.
Because the original formulation of the precept restricts [the number] to three small bowls, if one further requests and obtains three small bowls, it is a *pāyattika*.

If the host first sets aside two medium bowls and gives them entirely to the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu further requests [more], it is a *duṣkṛta*; if he further requests and obtains one small bowl, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the host has not previously invited one to eat, it is no fault to accept as much as the donor provides; however, to ask for more is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the host first gives one small bowl, and one asks for more until obtaining two small bowls, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; if one obtains three small bowls, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

In this manner, if one asks again after having already received a certain amount, whether large or small, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; if one receives three small bowls and then asks for one more, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
One may infer other cases by analogy, as they can all be understood in this way.
If a donor makes an invitation at their own discretion, it does not matter whether the number [of guests] is large or small.
This is a common precept; both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs fall into an offense, while for the three groups of followers, it is a duṣkṛta.
Among the five destinies, if one takes food from a human being beyond the limit, one falls into an offense; in the other four destinies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu takes food with his alms bowl, he should take only one bowl and must not exceed this; if he takes two bowls, he falls into an offense.
If one takes with a medium-sized bowl, one may take at most two bowls; if one takes three bowls, it is an offense of falling (pācittiya).
If one takes with a small-sized bowl, one may take at most three bowls; if one takes four bowls, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
34. The Thirty-fourth Matter. This precept is not shared; the three other assemblies do not incur an offense. Regarding the offense herein:
if a bhikṣu, having finished eating and risen from his seat, departs without receiving the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the method for consuming leftovers), and then eats a root-food, it is a *pāyattika*.

Among these fifteen kinds of food, if one eats any of them after having risen from one's seat and departed, and does not receive the *vighasa-dharma* (the practice of consuming leftovers), one falls into an offense for eating any of those fifteen kinds of food.
If one eats fifteen kinds of food at one time in a single combination, it is one *pāyattika*.
If one eats each kind separately at different times, there are fifteen *pāyattikas*.
Regarding the practice of receiving leftover food (*vighasa-dharma*), one should place as much as can be eaten into the bowl.
Knowing that the monks had not yet finished their single meal, he rose from his seat, approached those men, bared one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, held up his bowl, and said:
"Venerable sirs, please remember!"
"I have received the *vighasa* (leftover food) rule.
If the preceding bhikṣu did not take a small amount [of food], it is not called receiving the *vighasa* rule.
If one places the bowl-food on the ground or upon one's knees, it is not called receiving the *vighasa* rule; if one considers this to be receiving the *vighasa* rule, one falls [into an offense].
If the distance between them is such that their hands cannot reach one another, it is not called "receiving.
If one receives impure food or impure meat, it is not called the "method of receiving leftover food" (vighasa-bhakṣaṇa-vidhi).
Impure food refers to leftover food from the previous night, food improperly handled, and food that has been kept overnight.
Impure meat refers to dog meat, the meat of wicked birds, and the like.
If one wishes to eat five kinds of *khādaniya* (hard foods) while receiving five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods), it does not constitute a valid reception.
In this manner, if one successively intends to eat this while receiving that, none of them constitute a valid reception.
All those who eat without having formally received [the food] commit a *pāyattika* offense.
The method for receiving *vighasa* (leftover food) may be obtained from a fully ordained *bhikṣu*, but it may not be obtained from the four assemblies.
If one is in the presence of a senior elder (sthavira), one should bared the right shoulder, kneel with the right knee on the ground, and perform every action according to the Dharma.
If one is in the presence of a junior, one should omit only the kneeling; all other procedures are the same.
Upāli asked the Buddha:
"In how many postures does a bhikṣu perform the *pravāraṇā* while walking, how many while standing, how many while sitting, and how many while lying down?
The reason for asking was that if one does not inquire about the meaning with the Buddha, the characteristics of that meaning will not be revealed.
