Having asked these questions, the principles and characteristics became clear, and the practitioner was without obstruction.
After Upāli questioned the Buddha and received his seal of approval, all the disciples reverently upheld and practiced them.
Just as one who has received a royal fief can travel through the four border gates without anyone daring to obstruct him,
so it is with this. Furthermore,
just as the Buddha is sovereign over the three thousandfold world-system within the Dharma, such that none can surpass him;
Within Jambudvīpa, Upāli was peerless in his mastery of the Vinaya;
it is further said that within the trichiliocosm, no one could equal him. When this person questioned the Buddha, the Buddha answered for himself, leaving no principle unexplained.
The Buddha told Upāli:
"There are five circumstances under which a bhikṣu may act according to his own will while walking, and five while standing, sitting, or lying down.

Regarding the five while walking: knowing [the path], knowing [how to] receive offerings, knowing [when it is] appropriate to eat, knowing various kinds of food, and violating the dignified deportment."
It is the same when standing, sitting, or lying down.
If, while a bhikṣu is walking or rinsing his mouth, a donor offers him the five kinds of food, the bhikṣu should eat it.

One should perform the ritual for receiving leftover food (vighasa-vidhi); one should not remain standing, sitting, or lying down. If one remains standing, sitting, or lying down, it should be known that the deportment is violated and it is not called "receiving.
If one considers this to be the reception of food, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.

There is no offense if the bhikṣu says, "Wait a moment," or if it is still early in the day, or if he is sipping gruel, or if he entrusts [the meal] to something that may be eaten at all times; in these cases, there is no offense.
All five groups of monastics and all those who have mastered the Dharma may receive instructions from a layperson.
However, if one person accepts the *kṛtānna* (leftover food) rule, others may not eat it.
When distributing food, one should give instructions at the time of distribution; however, the procedure for receiving leftover food (vighasa-dharma) need not be performed.
"Knowing the time of distribution" means knowing that it is the time to distribute.
"Knowing the recipient" means knowing that the person before one is being given food.
"Knowing what is appropriate" means knowing what should be accepted and what should not be accepted.
"Knowing various kinds of food" means knowing how to distinguish between types of food.
"Deteriorating one's deportment" means knowing when, during the time of eating, one's deportment is thus deteriorated and when it is thus not deteriorated.

35. The Thirty-Fifth Matter. This is the thirty-fifth of the ninety matters; it is a unique precept (*asādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada*) not violated by the three other assemblies. Regarding the essence of this precept:

if a bhikṣu, without having been invited to eat and without the food being considered "leftover" (*atiritta*), out of a mind of anger and wishing to cause annoyance, forcibly urges another to eat, then if the other eats, it is a *pāyattika* offense; if they do not eat, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu who has finished eating and has not offered the remainder of his food, yet he himself freely requests and eats any of the fifteen kinds of food, for whichever food he eats, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
All grains such as wheat, millet, rice, hemp, and beans, so long as they have not been made into flour, cooked rice, or gruel, are entirely termed "similar food" (pratikṛtibhakta).
Once they have been transformed into flour, cooked rice, or gruel, they are entirely termed "proper food" (bhakta).
Eating in a Group Apart from the Assembly.
(36) The Thirty-sixth Matter, the Thirty-sixth of the Ninety Matters. This precept applies equally to nuns; the other three assemblies do not incur an offense.
When partaking of food offered by the Saṃgha, one should employ four types of gestures:
First, strike the *gandī*; second, blow the conch; third, beat the drum; fourth, proclaim the announcement so that it is heard and known within the boundary.

These four types of signs must necessarily have fixed limits; one must not at times strike the *gandī*, at other times beat the drum, or at yet other times blow the conch, causing the sequence of affairs to become disordered and lacking definite rules, whereby the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*) will not be established.
If one consumes *saṃghika* food without performing the four formalities, it is impure and is termed "stealing *saṃghika* food.

Regardless of whether there are monks within the boundary or not, whether they are many or few, whether they are barred or not barred, and whether one knows there are monks or knows there are none—such acts are all termed "improper consumption" and are also termed "stealing *saṃghika* food"; they are not termed the offense of eating separately from the community (*pṛthag-varga-doṣa*).

If one prepares food for the Sangha by means of the four characteristics, then regardless of whether there are bhikṣus or no bhikṣus within the boundary, whether they are many or few, or whether one knows whether bhikṣus are present or not, or whether they will come or not—as long as it does not obstruct [the distribution], there is no fault whatsoever.
If there were an obstruction, even if the *gandī* were struck, the meal would be impure, and this is termed "stealing from the Sangha's offerings.

If within a single great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) there are two or three locations where the Sangha has a common beginning and end for their offerings and performs the same *poṣadha*, then at the time of the meal, one need only strike the *gandī* at each location; in all such cases, there is no obstruction, it is pure, and there is no fault.
If there is a donor who provides a long-term meal for one month or ninety days, it would be a most excellent and great merit if it were entirely unrestricted.
If it cannot be unrestricted, on the first day the meal is prepared, one should strike the *gandī* and announce:
"Those with sixty years of seniority may enter."
"If there are those with sixty years of seniority, whether many or few, let just one enter, and that shall suffice for purity.
If there are none with sixty years of seniority, next call out for those with fifty-nine years of seniority."
If there are none, one should call out in succession down to the śrāmaṇeras;
even if only a single śrāmaṇera enters, it is pure.
If there are none at all, it is likewise called pure.
If it is not proclaimed on the first day, it should be proclaimed every day according to the procedure for the first day.
If it is proclaimed on the first day, then until the end of the long session, whether there is an obstruction or no obstruction, there is no fault whatsoever.
If it is not announced on the first day, it should be announced every day until one person has entered; whether others are then barred or not barred, there is no fault.

If these two methods are not performed, and at the time of eating there is a prohibition such that even a single bhikṣu within the boundary is unable to eat because of that prohibition, then the entire Saṃgha therein incurs the offense of eating separately from the assembly.
If there is a prohibition because there are no bhikṣus within the boundary, the food is not pure.

However, if one prepares a long-term meal for ninety days, having performed the formal proclamation according to the Dharma on the first day, then upon the completion of the ninety days, if a donor continues to provide food for another month or half-month, the previous proclamation remains valid and pure; it is not necessary to proclaim it again.

Regarding the bedding and furniture of the saṃgha’s quarters, at the conclusion of the ninety-day period, one must announce [the distribution] every day; if one does not announce it daily, it is not pure.

If a donor invites four or more persons to eat within the boundary of the saṃgha’s poṣadha, one must invite one monk from the saṃgha to the place of the poṣadha or send a portion of the food; if one does not invite one person nor send a portion of the food, it is a pāyattika.
If there are two or three locations, it should be treated in the same way.

If each location sends one person to the assembly at the *poṣadha* site or sends a portion of food, then they are pure in their respective places; there is no need for them to send people back and forth or exchange food.
In whatever place one does not invite a single monk from the Saṃgha or does not provide a portion of food, it is a pāyattika.

Even if one has invited a single person and provided a portion of food, if another bhikṣu arrives from outside and one obstructs him, even to the point of not giving food to that one person, it is a pāyattika.

If, within the boundaries of a village, there is no monastic boundary (sīmā), yet two donors invite four or more monks to eat at two separate locations, one should strike the *gandī* bell; furthermore, one person from each location should mutually invite [the other] or a portion of food should be sent.

If there are other bhikṣus present, they should enter [the meal] according to the Dharma; even down to a single person, if one does not mutually invite them or send a portion of food, the one who eats it commits an offense.
If one prevents another from being given food, that too is a pāyattika.
If there were no community of monks previously within the boundaries of a village, and a donor invites four or more [monks], one should strike the *gandī* (wooden gong).

If the *gandī* is not struck, even if one knows that there is at least one bhikṣu who has not come to eat, one incurs the offense of eating separately from the assembly (*pṛthag-bhaktika* / *bhedabhakta*).
If one eats while suspecting that there may be a bhikṣu present, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If there is no suspicion at all, or if the ghaṇṭā has been struck, there is no offense whatsoever regardless of whether a bhikṣu is present or not.

Regarding the method for distributing food from the *saṃgha-kṣetra* (monastic fields): wherever there are people, whether few or many, one should establish a regular limit for the food. One should calculate the food from the *saṃgha-kṣetra* to provide for one day’s meal for each person, determining how much is required to sustain them for an entire year.

If one consumes one *hu* [of food] per day for the duration of a year, one should always take one *hu* as the limit; if one reduces it by less than one *hu*, it is called stealing from the Sangha’s provisions, and if one exceeds it by more than one *hu*, it is likewise called stealing from the Sangha’s provisions.
If one reduces the food by one *hu*, the Sangha will lose that food which they ought to receive;
if one increases it by one *hu*, it will cause the Sangha’s alms-seeking to be interrupted and not continue.
Since there is a fixed limit, it may be shared by all without restriction, regardless of the number of people.
If the Sangha is large, they may eat together; if the Sangha is small, they likewise eat together.
If there is any remainder, it should be set aside until tomorrow to be performed in sequence; such a method is entirely without fault.
However, setting it aside until tomorrow is not permitted.

If, while traveling on a journey, four or more bhikṣus are invited by a donor to eat, and if even one bhikṣu among the group eats separately, these bhikṣus incur the offense of eating in a separate assembly (gaṇabhojana).
When traveling on a journey, within the area extending one krośa in length and breadth wherever one stays, one must not eat separately nor perform the poṣadha separately within that boundary.
Although this is not within the boundary of a robe, if individuals each bring their own food, there is no fault even if four people eat together in one place.
If it is the meal provided by a donor (*dānapati*), there is likewise no fault if three or fewer people eat in separate locations.
If all eat together in one place, it is very good.

However, when eating *saṃgha*-food or food provided by a donor (*dānapati*), if there is a separate donor who gives food specifically to four bhikṣus, and those four bhikṣus sit in sequence alongside the rest of the *saṃgha* to receive and eat this food, they incur the offense of eating separately from the assembly (*pṛthag-bhaktaka-āpatti*).
If four people first take their turn from the communal meal provided by the Sangha, and later receive additional portions, they are without offense.

If, during the time of the communal meal, the *karmadāna* (steward) uses the property dedicated to the Sangha to separately prepare rich and excellent food for the four of them to eat together, although these four are in one place, there is no offense of eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇabhojana*), yet it is an impure meal.

If a bhikṣu, whether eating food from the Saṃgha or food provided by a donor, takes his portion of the meal and eats it in a separate location with three or more others, he does not commit the offense of eating separately from the group (pārivāsika).

If there are four or more persons, even though they are within the same boundary, if each has their own food and they eat together, it does not constitute the offense of eating separately from the group.
If four persons each beg for alms and eat together in one place, there is likewise no offense.
If among four persons, one person has food while three have no food, and they eat together in one place, it is a *pāyattika*.
If they are in separate rooms and a donor provides small meals separately to each, there is no offense, as four or more persons do not constitute a full meal.

If one subsequently provides a meal, one should invite a single person from among the Sangha or send a portion of food; if they eat separately, it does not constitute a communal meal, and there is no offense.
If one does not do so, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the Sangha has finished eating and guest bhikṣus arrive, and the donor provides food for four or more people, there is no offense.
If a visiting bhikṣu, while traveling, enters an area where a Saṃgha resides and accepts food from a donor, and four or more persons eat together in one place, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one has previously brought their own provisions, and they happen to be from a donor who gives them food to eat together, there is no offense.
However, if among four traveling companions, one person possesses food and eats it in a single location within the boundaries of the *saṃgha* together with the other three, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one is in a remote place where no *sīmā* (monastic boundary) exists for the Saṃgha, and there are several bhikṣus traveling together as companions, if one bhikṣu separately invites three other bhikṣus to eat at the same location, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, because a natural *krośa* boundary exists according to the location where they reside.
If there is travel-provision food, there is no fault in eating together in one place.

If many guest bhikṣus enter a village boundary together with companions, even if it is not within a formal monastic boundary (*sīmā*), if a bhikṣu or a layperson acts as a donor and separately invites four or more [bhikṣus] to eat in one place, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

If four or more companions within the boundary of a village accept a meal from a single donor, even if there was no Saṃgha present beforehand, yet they know that at least one bhikṣu is among them and do not invite him to eat together, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one harbors doubts and does not inquire whether food is available or not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one wishes to act in accordance with the Dharma, one should properly ascertain whether there are monks or no monks in the village; if one eats without harboring such doubts, there is no fault.
If it is not so, one should strike the *gandī* (wooden gong).
If they are too far away to hear it, or if they hear it but do not come, then [the meal] is pure and in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, whether within the boundary of the Sangha, the natural boundary, or the boundary of a village, if there is food provided by a donor (*dānapati*) and guest bhikṣus arrive after the Sangha has finished eating, and the donor gives them food, there is no offense provided there are four or more people [present].
If the Bhikṣu Saṃgha has no fault of eating separately from the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, then all such separate meals are considered food provided by a donor (*dānapati*).

If it is food offered by the Saṃgha (*saṃghabhakta*), there is no offense of eating separately in any case; however, if one eats the Saṃgha’s offered food in an improper manner, the meal is impure, and one incurs the offense of stealing from the Saṃgha’s offerings.
If there is a donor within the monastic boundary who provides separate food, one should invite a single person from among the Sangha or send a portion of the food to them.
If this is not done, there is no fault in three or fewer monks eating separately in different locations.

If there is a meal provided by a donor within the monastic boundary, and one has previously intended to invite a member of the Sangha but forgot to do so, and that person arrives before the meal is served, one should set aside a portion of the food at the head of the senior monk (upādhyāya) and present it to the assembly of monks.
If the Sangha is far away, one should take this food and distribute it in order.
Regarding the general rule for the donor's meal, one must first invite a bhikṣu.
If the donor is within the boundary of the Sangha, one should tell the donor to invite one person from among the monks within this boundary.
If one invites monks from another realm, the offense is not avoided.

If these monks have established a *krośa* boundary (ten *krośas*) and are far from the path of the [host] monks, and if they were not invited beforehand but are invited on that very day, one should also set aside a portion of food and place it at the head of the *upādhyāya*.
If one is able to send it to the Saṃgha, that is good.
If one is unable to send it to the Saṃgha, one should distribute it in successive order.
If there are three bhikṣus and one bhikṣuṇī, there is no offense.
If there are three bhikṣuṇīs and one bhikṣu, there is no offense.
This applies even up to the case of three bhikṣus and one śrāmaṇerī; there is no offense.
If three bhikṣus are outside the boundary and one bhikṣu is inside the boundary, there is no offense.
If three bhikṣus are within the boundary and one bhikṣu is outside the boundary, there is no offense.
If three bhikṣus are on the ground and one bhikṣu is in the air, there is no offense.
If three bhikṣus are in the air and one bhikṣu is on the ground, there is no offense.
This excludes the time of illness and the time of making robes.
Regarding the making of robes, it does not matter whether the robes are of the proper measure or not; all such cases are permitted.
If food is difficult to obtain while making robes, eating in a separate group is permitted.
If food is easily obtained, eating in a separate group is not permitted.
Regarding the exception for those on a journey, this extends up to half a yojana, whether traveling there or returning.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu arrives yesterday and eats today, he commits a *pāyattika* offense; if he travels tomorrow and eats today, he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
However, if he eats on the very day he travels while on the road, or if he eats upon arriving at his destination, there is no offense.
The same applies to the ship.
Regarding the time when the great assembly gathers: it may be for a Dharma matter or for some other reason that the Saṃgha assembles.
When there are at least four resident bhikṣus and four visiting bhikṣus, this is termed a "great assembly."
"Even though a large assembly has gathered and food is not difficult to obtain, one is not permitted to eat separately from the group; whoever does so commits a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding 'when śramaṇas invite one to eat': these are non-Buddhist śramaṇas; with the exception of the Buddha’s fivefold assembly, all those who have left the household life among non-Buddhists are termed śramaṇas."

Regarding the offense herein: if a śramaṇa has been invited, and after being invited he returns to secular life as a layman (avadātavasana) and gives food to a bhikṣu, if that bhikṣu eats it, it is a pāyattika.
There is no offense if one accepts an invitation.

However, if a layperson invites a bhikṣu, and after the invitation has been made, that person leaves the household life to become an ascetic (śramaṇa) under a non-Buddhist teacher and offers food from their own hand to the bhikṣu, if the bhikṣu eats it, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a śramaṇa invites a bhikṣu, and the śramaṇa brings food to give to the bhikṣu, accepting the invitation and eating the food does not constitute an offense.

If there is a donor who prepares a long-term meal—whether for one month or ninety days—they first invite people according to their preference and have them each designated. On the first day of the meal preparation, everyone is ordered to assemble. At dawn, the *gandī* is struck; once the Saṃgha has gathered, the presiding monk who exhorts the donors should stand in one place and call out loudly:
"Those with sixty years of seniority, enter!"

"First, those among the invited assembly of monks who have each taken their seats in their respective places, if there is one among those not yet invited who has sixty years of seniority (ṣaṣṭi-varṣa), he should enter.
If there is no such person, then next one with fifty-nine years of seniority should be called to enter."
If there is no one in the proper sequence, one should announce, "The śrāmaṇera enters.
If there is no śrāmaṇera, it is still considered pure.
If a donor prepares food within the boundary of the saṃgha but the hall cannot accommodate them, and they go out to another place in the proper sequence to eat, there is no fault.

When the Sangha is eating—whether it be food provided by the Sangha or food provided by a donor—if each person takes their portion of food outside and the four eat together in one place, there is no offense.

If a donor’s household invites four or more monks for a meal, even if the *gandī* has been struck, if the donor prohibits it and knows that one monk will be unable to eat, all [the monks] incur a *pāyattika*.

If there are two monastic assemblies within a single great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), and on one day both locations have offerings from donors, there is no fault regarding the place where the *poṣadha* is held.

However, at the location where the *poṣadha* is not being held, if not even a single person is invited from the place where the *poṣadha* is being held, or if not even a portion of food is sent there, all the monks at that location incur a *pāyattika* offense.
If one who is insane, mentally deranged, or whose mind is impaired is expelled;
or if there are three bhikṣus and one who is insane, or one bhikṣu and three who are insane;
even if there are four bhikṣus within the boundary and all four are insane, and each is given food by a donor, there is no fault in any of these cases.
The same applies to those with distracted minds, those with minds impaired by illness, and those who have been expelled.
In all cases, eating separately from the community must take place within a boundary (*sīmā*).

There are various types of boundaries established for the Saṃgha: village boundaries, household boundaries, and natural wilderness boundaries of one *krośa*. Within these boundaries, one may not eat separately nor perform the Uposatha separately; however, this does not apply to the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*). Thus, a bhikṣu who is within such a boundary may not eat separately.
Furthermore, it must be a donor [who provides the meal], and four or more [monks] must be together in one place.
If there are members of the Saṃgha within the boundary who eat in a manner contrary to the Dharma, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If one knows that even a single person has eaten food contrary to the Dharma, it is a *pāyattika*. 37.
The thirty-seventh matter. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *pāyattika*, while for the three groups of followers, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.
If he eats the five kinds of *khādaniya*, the five kinds of *bhojaniya*, or the five kinds of similar foods—if he eats fifteen kinds all at once, it is one pāyattika;
if he eats them one by one, it is one pāyattika for each.
If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time while perceiving it as an improper time, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If he eats at an improper time while perceiving it as a proper time, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If he eats at an improper time while being in doubt, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If one eats at the proper time while perceiving it as the improper time, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one eats at the proper time while doubting [the timing], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one eats at the proper time while perceiving it as the proper time, there is no offense.
If one eats at an improper time, for every swallow there is a *pāyattika* offense.
"Improper time" refers to the period from midday until the final watch of the night; this is called improper time.
From dawn until midday is called the proper time.
Why is this? Because from the sun’s initial rising until midday, the light gradually increases until it reaches its fullness; therefore, this is called "the proper time" (*kāla*).
From midday until the end of the night, the light gradually diminishes and disappears; therefore, this is called "not the proper time" (*akāla*).
Furthermore, from dawn until midday, when worldly people engage in their affairs and prepare food and drink, it is therefore called "the proper time.

From midday until the latter part of the night, which is the time for social gatherings, amusements, and personal recreation, if a bhikṣu wanders about during this period and causes disturbance or offense, it is therefore called "the improper time."
Furthermore, from dawn until midday, when the various worldly affairs of laypeople have not yet given rise to sexual desire or affliction, it is called "the proper time.

From midday until the latter part of the night, when worldly affairs have ceased and there is sexual play, idle talk, and laughter—if a bhikṣu enters or exits, wanders about, or at times is slandered and subjected to various harms—it is called "the improper time."
Furthermore, from dawn until midday is the time for begging food; one should enter the village and travel about during this period, and thus it is called "the proper time.

From midday until the latter part of the night, one should remain silent, composed, sitting upright, reciting the sūtras, or practicing meditation according to one's respective practice; this is not the time for traveling or entering the village, and is therefore called "the improper time."
38. The Thirty-Eighth Matter. This precept applies equally to both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; it is not an offense for the three other assemblies.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu eats food that has been set aside as leftovers or kept overnight, it is a pāyattika.
If one eats fifteen kinds of food at once, it constitutes one *pāyattika*;
if one eats them one by one, there is a *pāyattika* for each.
Regarding the essence of this precept, there is a *pāyattika* for every swallow.
There are three cases regarding eating food that has been stored overnight:

if, after receiving the food, one regards it as one's own, then whether the food was kept overnight or not, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) for the night, and a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation) for eating it.

If one takes food with one's own hand, it is called "improper taking. At the moment of taking it, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense; if one forms the thought that it belongs to oneself and keeps it overnight, there is also a *duṣkṛta* offense; the same applies to eating it.

If one eats food that has not been formally received (*pratigraha*) nor taken by hand, yet forms the thought that it belongs to oneself and keeps it overnight, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense; eating it also constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Whether one has stayed overnight with them or not, if one merely perceives the food as one's own, it is called "storing internally" (*antar-śaya*).
If another bhikṣu eats food that has been stored overnight, there is no fault.
Once a layperson has handled or taken hold of food, if the layperson subsequently gathers it up themselves and gives it to a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu may eat it.
If one finds abundant food and drink in the wilderness, having eaten it, one should discard what remains; however, if there are no birds or beasts to consume it, one may take it and eat it.
If many people together touch millet or wheat with their hands, once each has divided their portion, it is pure.

If one eats food that is the Buddha’s *khādanīya*, the *mukha-vyañjana* (food for the mouth), or the *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence) offering, even if one first takes hold of it and later purchases it, one may eat it; because there is no notion of "one's own," there is no offense.
The Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā, Scroll Seven;

39. The Thirty-ninth Matter. This precept is common to both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; it is not common to the other three groups.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, without having received it, places food or drink into his mouth, it is a pāyattika.
For however much he places into his mouth, for every swallow, it is a pāyattika.
There are four types of persons from whom one may receive food:
men, women, eunuchs, and those with both sexual organs.
All non-humans and animals also constitute valid recipients for receiving food.
In all cases of receiving food, there are two purposes: first, to sever the causes and conditions for theft; second, to serve as a witness.
If one receives food from a non-human being, it constitutes the act of receiving food, but it does not constitute a valid witness.
The reason for permitting the acceptance of food from non-human beings is that in desolate places where no humans are present to receive the food, it is therefore permitted.
However, if one is among humans, it is not permitted at all to accept food from non-humans, animals, or ignorant children.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of stopping slander, for the sake of having few desires and knowing contentment, and to give rise to faith and respect in others.
For example, in the past, there was a bhikṣu who traveled with some non-Buddhists; they stopped beneath a tree where there were fruits upon it.
The non-Buddhist said to the bhikṣu,
"Climb the tree and fetch some fruit.
The bhikṣu replied:
"It is the rule for us bhikṣus that one should not climb a tree higher than a man.
He then said:
"Shake the tree and take the fruit."
The bhikṣu said, "In our Dharma,
it is not permitted to shake a tree to make its fruit fall.
The non-Buddhist ascetic climbed the tree, gathered some fruit, threw it to the ground, and gave it to him, saying:
"Take some fruit and eat it.
The bhikṣu said,
"In my dharma, one must not eat without having received [the gift]."

The non-Buddhists conceived a heart of faith and reverence, realizing that the Buddha’s Dharma was pure; they immediately followed the bhikṣu to go forth within the Buddha’s Dharma and soon attained the exhaustion of outflows.
If one receives food, using large leaves as a vessel to receive the meal—
provided it is not a large platter, but rather a small platter, a round dish, or a table— there is no fault in a single person receiving it.
If one receives food with hands that are not clean, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.

(40) This is the fortieth of the ninety matters. This precept is not common: for a bhikṣu it is a *pāyattika*; for a bhikṣuṇī it is a fourfold *deśanā-garhaṇīya*; for the three other assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
That which is called "fine food" is so named because its price is high, because it is difficult to obtain, and because it cures illness.
There may be fine foods that are not fine medicines, such as milk, curd, and clarified butter.
There may be excellent medicines that are not excellent foods, such as fresh butter (sarpis).
There may be things that are both excellent foods and excellent medicines, such as meat and dried fish.
Or there may be things that are neither excellent foods nor excellent medicines, such as harītakī and the like.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu who is not ill seeks for himself milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, fish, meat, or dried meat, he commits a pāyattika;
if he does not obtain them, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu who is not ill seeks for himself rice, soup, vegetables, or the like,
he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense upon obtaining them.
To fail to do so is also a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense in the following cases:
if one is ill; if it is a relative; if one has been invited beforehand; or if the person gives it of their own accord without being asked. In these cases, there is no offense.

When a bhikṣu goes on his almsround, he should snap his fingers or shake his staff upon reaching the door of a donor. If the donor asks him anything, he should speak according to what is required so that the donor understands his needs;
if he receives food, it is well. If he does not receive it, he must not insistently demand it; to do so constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
In this context, regarding the regulation on food: if one who is not ill requests ghee, oil, or other such items, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the regulation on medicine after the four months have passed: once the invitation for the four-month period has concluded, if one requests ghee or oil, it is a *pāyattika*.

41. The Forty-first Matter, Third Recitation; the Forty-first of the Ninety Matters. This is a common precept: for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense; for the three groups [of novices], it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The previous regulation permitted using water containing insects to sprinkle on grass, soil, or mix with mud; this regulation prohibits the use of such water altogether.
"Water containing insects" refers to that which is seen by the eye or caught by a water-strainer.

At one time, Śāriputra, with his purified divine eye, saw insects in the air as numerous as the sands along a riverbank or the grains in a vessel—boundless and immeasurable. Having seen this, he ceased eating for two or three days.

The Buddha commanded that they eat; as for the regulation regarding water containing insects, it applies only to what is visible to the naked eye and what can be caught by a water filter, not to what is seen with the divine eye.

Regarding the method for using water: one should take a high-quality, fine cotton cloth, one cubit in length and breadth, and make a water-strainer bag. One bhikṣu who maintains the precepts, is learned, has deep faith in the consequences of sin and merit, is composed and discerning, and possesses pure physical vision, should be made to examine the water. He shall strain the water according to the Dharma and place it in a vessel, sufficient for one day’s use.
Examine it again tomorrow; if there are insects, you should filter it even more thoroughly, placing clean water in a pure vessel and observing it carefully toward the light.
If there are still insects present, you should make a double-layered water-strainer.
If there are still insects after filtering twice, one should filter three times.
If there are still insects after that, one should not remain in that place, but should move away immediately.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu knowingly uses water containing insects, for every insect that dies as a result, he commits a *pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu uses water containing living insects for cooking rice, making soup or broth, washing or dyeing clothes, or for rinsing the mouth, body, hands, or feet—in all such uses—for every insect that dies as a result, he incurs a pāyattika offense for each one.
If there are insects in the water and one uses it with the perception that there are no insects, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there are insects in the water and one uses it with the perception that there are insects, or if there are insects in the water and one uses it while doubting their presence, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses water that is free of insects while perceiving it as containing insects, or if one uses it while doubting whether it contains insects, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one uses water that is free of insects while perceiving it as being free of insects, there is no offense.

42. The forty-second matter. This is the forty-second of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a pāyattika, and for the three groups of followers it is a duṣkṛta.
Regarding this precept, among the five destinies, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense within the human realm, while in the other realms it is a *dukkaṭa*, because the destinies differ.
"In a family" refers to a woman eating where men eat.
"House" refers to the dwelling of a layperson (*avadātavasana*).

Regarding this precept, if a layperson’s house is a place where sexual intercourse occurs and there is no other person present, and one sits down forcibly in that place, thereby preventing the husband and wife from acting according to their will, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu sits forcefully in a family home where a meal is being served, it is a pāyattika.
If he rises and then sits back down, or rises again and sits back down, he incurs as many pāyattikas as there were instances of rising and sitting.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is in the home of those who have severed sexual desire; or if one is in the home of those observing the fast; or if there is a person worthy of respect seated there, such as an upādhyāya, an ācārya, or one’s parents—these are what are called persons worthy of respect.
If this dwelling is a place where many people enter and exit, there is no offense.
This precept differs from the subsequent one [regarding] being in a place with a husband and wife in that it concerns being alone with a single woman.
43. The forty-third matter. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika, while for the three groups of disciples, it is a duṣkṛta.
Among the five destinies, if this occurs within the human realm, it constitutes a *pāyattika*; in the other realms, it is a *dukkaṭa*, because the destinies are distinct.
The meaning of "in a family home" is as explained previously.
Regarding this essence of the precept: if a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Alone" means being alone with one woman, with no third person present.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu sits alone with a single woman in a place where food is being served, three conditions give rise to one *pāyattika*:
first, it is a place where food is being served; second, he is alone with a single woman; third, they sit in a secluded place.
If one rises from one's seat and sits back down, for each such instance one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; furthermore, for every three actions [of rising], one incurs one *pāyattika*.
For each time one rises and subsequently sits back down, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each such instance.
If the door is closed facing outward and there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), it is a *pāyattika*.
If the door is open facing outward and there is a *kappiya-kāraka*, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If the door is open facing inward and there is a *kappiya-kāraka*, there is no offense.

Regarding these two preceding and succeeding precepts: if the person is a young girl, a barren woman, or a small girl incapable of engaging in sexual desire, or if her organ is impaired, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Regarding the precept against sitting with a woman in a secluded place, there are generally two types:
first, sitting together with a married couple; second, sitting alone with a woman.
Sitting with a woman in an open space constitutes only one type, wherein there is no third person present.
There is also the precept against sitting in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, as in the preceding precept.
Regarding the precept against sitting in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, there is likewise the precept against sitting in an exposed place with a bhikṣuṇī.
These ninety matters are not found within the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts; however, because there were circumstances involving the *bhikṣuṇīs*, these common precepts were established.
44. The forty-fourth matter. This forty-fourth of the ninety matters is a common precept; for the three assemblies, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
The country of Vaiśālī is named Vaiśālī because it is situated near the Snowy Mountains; it is a place where non-Buddhist śramaṇas find delight.
As for Ajātaśatru, he is named Ajātaśatru because he makes offerings to the sacrificial fire.
Question:
Is there perhaps a śramaṇa who serves as a teacher for the great assembly and is revered by many people?
[The Buddha] caused this thought to arise because he was about to receive the retribution of his past deeds.
"Uprightness" means being upright in body, upright in dress, upright in deportment, and upright in the Dharma.
"Tranquility of the faculties" means that the six sense-faculties are not distracted.

The body possesses a circular halo like a mass of pure gold; were one to place Jāmbūnada gold before the Buddha, as soon as the Buddha extends an arm, that gold would become like earth or stone, devoid of any further luster or color.
He immediately returned to his own country and prepared abundant and delicious food and drink for the Buddha and the Sangha for the four months of the summer retreat.

The reason he prepared [provisions] for four months was that the summer season consists of four months, and furthermore, because in that country the *anvaya* (rainy-season retreat) is always observed for four months.

He dismissed all outside visitors and ceased the musical entertainments for his own amusement; furthermore, no matters concerning external affairs, whether good or bad, were permitted to be reported to him.
Someone asked:
"The Buddha is of noble lineage, and moreover, as the Dharma King, he is venerated by the entire world."
"Why is it that he does not fear the loss of his reputation or the reports of those far and near?
He replied, "This Brahmin king has been blinded by the darkness of ignorance since beginningless time; he disregards what is good and what is evil, and for this reason, he acts thus."

Furthermore, this brahmin has long harbored evil and heterodox views; he is an enemy and a thief of the Dharma. Although he invited the Buddha, he lacked faith and reverence, and for this reason, [the Buddha] did not take it to heart.
Furthermore, it was simply because the Buddha wished to manifest the experience of past retribution that he acted in such a manner.
It is also said:
Ajātaśatru originally had no evil intent; he was merely misled by outsiders, which is why it happened thus.
During the night, the king dreamed that he saw himself falling to the ground, and the Buddha pulled him up.
Upon waking, he invited various Brahmin masters to interpret this dream.
Driven by jealousy, the Brahmins spoke deceitfully:
"This dream is a great ill omen.
Ajātaśatru asked,
"How can it be averted?"
The brahmin said,
"Your Majesty should prohibit outsiders and guests for four months and amuse yourself with female musicians;
thus you may put this matter to rest."
He then followed those words and practiced according to the Dharma.
As for the "Unsurpassed Way," there are generally three kinds of paths:
first, the ultimate path of the śrāvaka; second, the ultimate path of the pratyekabuddha; and third, the ultimate path of the Buddha.
These three paths ultimately lead to entry through the gate of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, they are called "paths.
Among these three paths, the Buddha’s ultimate path is the most unsurpassed.
Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the kāṣāya robe,
he asked:
"Does the Buddha always shave his hair?"
He replied: "No.
The Buddha’s hair always remains as it does one week after being shaved."
Question: "When the Buddha first attained the Way, did he wear the kāṣāya? Answer:
"No one in white robes can attain Buddhahood.

One must possess the thirty-two marks, leave the household life to don the dharma robes, be fully endowed with dignified deportment, abandon all afflictions, and have the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) enter within their being—just as in the parable of the princess."
Whether they be ordinary beings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas, the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) will ultimately never enter their bodies.
The Buddha practiced austerities for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas; the pratyekabuddha for one hundred kalpas; and the śrāvaka may attain it after two or three lifetimes.
The Buddha and the great assembly stayed in this forest for this reason:
to proclaim the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) according to their original essence, and also to subdue the prideful minds of future disciples.

If there are disciples who have attained various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and are moreover learned, having mastered the scriptural collections (*piṭaka*), one might say they ought to dwell constantly in monasteries, halls, and pavilions rather than in forests and thickets;
yet even the Dharma King of the triple world dwells in the wilderness, let alone others.
Furthermore, it was to establish a model for future disciples; once the Buddha had accepted dwelling in the mountains and marshes, his later disciples would willingly accept and practice this.

Moreover, it was because he wished to preach the Dharma to devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits; since most devas and nāgas delight in solitude and tranquility, the Tathāgata dwelt beneath the forest trees.
At that time, Śāriputra was staying alone on Mount Anaśanapatha, having accepted an invitation from the wife of Śakra, Lord of Devas, and an asura maiden for the four-month rainy season retreat.
He asked:
"How can a human being digest the food of the devas?"
He replied:
"The attainment of meditative concentration by such a person is inconceivable; there is no need for doubt.
Furthermore, while the gods consume much food, even if humans obtain food, they cannot digest it as the gods do; for the gods, by eating little, their food is digested."
In the past, during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin, the story of the high-practicing brahmin should be told here as the causal context.
An ordinary horse eats two *doṇas* of barley; one *doṇa* is given to the horse and one *doṇa* is given to the bhikṣu.
Among them was an excellent horse that consumed four *dō* of barley; two *dō* were given to the horse and two *dō* to the Buddha.
Someone asked:
"The Buddha’s Dharma is impartial; why is one portion large and the other small?"
He replied:
"Regarding the property of the Saṃgha, the Dharma dictates that it should be shared equally; however, this barley from the donor belongs to the donor's intention.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s body is large while the bhikṣu’s body is small; each shall eat according to the capacity of his own belly, and thus the principle of equality is not lost."

Ānanda took the Buddha’s portion of barley along with his own, entered the village, and before a certain woman praised the Buddha’s merits, extolling his physical body (*rūpakāya*), his Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and his Brahma-like voice.
When a bodhisattva practices, among the four types of vocal karma, they cultivate two preeminently:
first, by refraining from harsh speech, they attain the Brahma-voice;
second, by cultivating the avoidance of untimely speech, they attain such that all who hear their words believe and accept them.
If one prepares this rice, one shall become the Woman-Jewel of a Wheel-Turning Sage King during the time of Maitreya Buddha.
For one who prepares this rice themselves, the merit is immeasurable; by virtue of these causes and conditions, they will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
There are two ways in which one generates the bodhicitta:
first, generating it upon seeing the Buddha; second, generating it upon hearing the Dharma.
This woman has both seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma; she first heard Ānanda describe the virtues of the Buddha.
Later, when they went to harvest the wheat, because the merit of their hearts was so profound and weighty, all the forest obstructions were suddenly cleared away.
Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, Ānanda pointed him out, saying, "This is the Buddha."
When the woman saw the Buddha’s radiant marks were so extraordinary, her heart was filled with joy and courage, and she gave rise to the bodhicitta.
The Buddha said:
"With the exception of the fivefold assembly of my disciples, all other renunciants are termed 'outsiders' (tīrthika)."
Regarding "food," all fifteen kinds of food are termed "food.
Among these, as for the offense: if a bhikṣu gives the fifteen kinds of food to a non-Buddhist all at once, it is one *pāyattika*;
if he gives them one by one, there is a *pāyattika* for each.

There is no offense in the following cases: if it is given to an outsider or an outsider’s daughter who is ill; if it is given to a relative; or if it is given at the time one seeks to leave the household life.
Regarding "the time of leaving the household life": during the four-month period of testing, if the host of the transformation-food wishes for the person to eat until full, they shall become full;
if the host does not so wish, they shall not become full.
If one steals transformed matter (pariṇāmita-vastu), one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense that can be confessed before another person.
If one consumes transformed food, there is no offense of eating stored food (*śeṣabhakta*).
If the fivefold assembly encourages a donor to prepare food, there is no fault whatsoever.

If a bhikṣu eats food that has been specially recommended by three types of people, he commits a pāyattika offense; however, there is no offense if he eats food recommended by other bhikṣus or śrāmaṇeras.
If one gives food with one's own hand to any of the ninety-six kinds of followers of heterodox views—whether they be householders or renunciants, naked or clothed—it is entirely a pāyattika offense.
If one instructs another to give [food], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no fault in giving food to anyone who holds no [wrong] views.
Likewise, there is no transgression in the Sangha giving food to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), provided that one does not give with one's own hands.

45. The forty-fifth matter. This is the forty-fifth of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense, while for the three groups [of novices], it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.

The reason for establishing the precepts together with the bhikṣus is to show respect for the Buddha-dharma, to eliminate slander, and to cause unwholesome dharmas to cease and wholesome dharmas to increase.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu intentionally goes to see an army setting out for battle, he incurs a pāyattika if he sees it, and a duṣkṛta if he does not.
There are four types of military forces:
elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry.

Whether four types of troops constitute one army, or three, two, or one type of troop constitutes one army, if one intentionally goes to observe even a single troop of soldiers—whether from high to low or from low to high—and sees them, it is a *pāyattika*; if one does not see them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one does not go intentionally, but passes through the middle of the path due to the circumstances of coming and going, there is no offense.
If one stands still to look, it violates the rules of dignified conduct (*airyāpathika*) and constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one looks back to the left or right, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing), except when there is a specific cause.
A "cause" refers to instances where one is summoned by a king, a queen, a crown prince, a high minister, a great official, or various generals; going in such cases does not constitute an offense.
Ordinary people are likewise; because they harbor slander, if one calls them, they do not go.
One should say:
"When a bhikṣu has something he seeks, he comes of his own accord without being called; when he has nothing he seeks, even if called, he does not come."

For the sake of the fruits of the śrāmaṇya, if one goes to preach the Dharma, some may attain the stage of srotāpanna, some sakṛdāgāmin, and some anāgāmin; furthermore, because it increases the roots of faith, reverence, and goodness, and because the monastic and the lay must rely upon one another to nurture the Buddha-dharma, one is permitted to go.
Because of a joyful heart, one attains the fruits of the śramaṇa. 46.
The forty-sixth matter. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a pāyattika, and for the three groups of followers it is a duṣkṛta.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu goes into an army and stays for more than two nights, at the conclusion of the third night, it is a pāyattika.
There is no offense if he is ill within the army, or if his mind is deranged, confused, or impaired by disease.

47. The Forty-seventh Matter. This is the forty-seventh of the ninety matters. It is a shared precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a pāyattika, and for the three groups of followers it is a duṣkṛta.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu goes to view a military array or to view weapons, he incurs a *pāyattika* if he sees them, and a *duṣkṛta* if he does not see them.
If he goes from a lower place to a higher one, or from a higher place to a lower one, he incurs a *pāyattika* if he sees them, and a *duṣkṛta* if he does not see them.
The same applies to the four divisions of the army down to a single unit.
If one observes the ivory banners, standards, and streamers, or watches two armies engaged in combat, it is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense if one did not intentionally go there, or if one passed through the middle of the road due to a necessary reason.

Regarding this essence of the precept: if a bhikṣu, while staying in an army for two nights, intentionally goes to view military formations, weapons, toothed banners, standards, or the battle between two opposing armies, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one stays with an army for two nights or more, and intentionally goes to watch it—even if only to see the battle lines drawn for combat—it is a *pāyattika*.
If one sits down and does not see [the battle], yet intentionally stands up to watch, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Even down to seeing the banners and streamers of an army, it is a *pāyattika*. 48.
The forty-eighth matter. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *pāyattika*, and for the three groups [of novices], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, out of a mind of anger, strikes with his hand, or strikes with his elbow, knee, foot, or staff, it is all a pāyattika.
If he strikes any other part of the body, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
If he strikes for the sake of incantations, or strikes because of choking while eating, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu strikes a bhikṣuṇī, it is *duṣkṛta*.
If one strikes any of the three groups [of monastics], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one strikes a novice who has received the precepts, or one who is blind, deaf, mute, or a monk undergoing *parivāsa* or *mānatva*, it is all a *pāyattika*.
To strike another in jest or laughter constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

To strike any of the following—those who have committed the six types of offenses, those who hold the five views, those who have crossed over [to another sect], those who dwell as thieves, those who were originally of broken precepts, those who renounced the precepts and returned to lay life but have again become bhikṣus, householders, those who lack a teacher or a saṃgha, those who have defiled a bhikṣuṇī, those who have killed an arhat, impotent persons, those not expelled for not seeing an offense, those not expelled for not confessing an offense, or those not expelled for not relinquishing evil views—constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in each case.
If one strikes another, it may constitute a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *sthūlātyaya*, a *duṣkṛta*, or a *pāyattika*.
If one strikes another with the intent to kill and the other dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If one does not die [from the blow], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If, with a lustful mind, one strikes a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇerī, or a laywoman, it is in all cases a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one strikes a bhikṣu with a mind of anger, but without the intent to kill, it is a pāyattika.
Striking less than that, or striking anyone other than a bhikṣu, constitutes a duṣkṛta.
49. The forty-ninth item. This is the forty-ninth of the ninety items. This is a common precept; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika, and for the three other assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.
This differs from the preceding precept regarding striking and threatening; otherwise, all other meanings are identical to the preceding precept.
If one strikes, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one raises [the hand] with the intent to strike but stops, it is a *dukkaṭa*, because the striking was not completed.
The underlying intent of this precept is not to actually strike, but merely to brandish the palm to cause distress and fear; for such mere brandishing, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the original intent was to emit semen by means of a woman, and that intent is fulfilled, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if no semen is emitted and one stops after merely touching or grasping her, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one’s original intention was simply to seize or grasp, and the intent was for pleasure, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
These two precepts are treated in the same manner.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu raises his palm or the sole of his foot, raises his elbow or knee, or brandishes a staff toward another bhikṣu, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one intends [to strike] a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.

If one intends [to strike] a śrāmaṇera who has received the precepts, or those who have undergone the karmas of being blind, deaf, mute, undergoing parivāsa, undergoing mānatva, or being subjected to the karmas of harsh treatment or expulsion, it is in all cases a pāyattika.

The six types of offenders, the five types of persons who violate the Dharma, those who have crossed over [to another sect], those who dwell as thieves, those who were originally of broken precepts, those who renounced the precepts and returned to lay life but again become bhikṣus, those who live at home without a teacher or a Saṃgha, those who have defiled a bhikṣuṇī, those who have killed an arhat, those who are suspended for not seeing [their offense], those who are suspended for not making amends [for their offense], those who are suspended for not relinquishing evil views, and those who are impotent—all these commit *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
There may be cases where [the act] is directed toward another, resulting in a *pārājika*, a *sthūlātyaya*, a *pāyattika*, or a *duṣkṛta*.
If one directs the intent to kill toward another and that person dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If [the victim] does not die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one has no intent to kill, but merely strikes toward a bhikṣu with a mind of anger, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one strikes toward any other part of the body, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one intends to strike another person, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There is no offense if a bhikṣu raises his hand to ward off a vicious beast or to ward off a wicked person; such acts done for the purpose of protecting against danger or fear do not constitute an offense.
50. The fiftieth item of the ninety items. This is a common precept, with a small portion being uncommon.
For a nun, concealing seven *pārājika* offenses constitutes a *pāyattika*;
concealing an act of sexual intercourse constitutes a *pārājika*.
This is a unique offense (*asaṃvāra-śīla*); for the three assemblies, it is a *duṣk᾽ta*.
There are four types of groundless defamation of another:
to defame another with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one falsely accuses another of shedding the blood of a Buddha without basis, or of breaking the wheel of the Sangha without basis—regarding these four offenses—it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one falsely accuses another of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense without basis, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one falsely accuses another of a *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *duṣkṛta* offense without basis, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
These are called the four types.
To speak of another's grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) to a person who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*) is of three kinds:
regarding a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
Second, if one falsely accuses another of shedding the blood of a Buddha or causing a schism in the Saṃgha, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense that requires confession before another person;
third, if one falsely accuses another of a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta* offense, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are three types of concealing gross offenses:
concealing a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense incurs a *pāyattika*;
concealing the shedding of a Buddha’s blood or the causing of a schism in the Saṃgha incurs a *sthūlātyaya* requiring confession before another person.
For the [offenses] in the following three articles, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

51. The fifty-first matter. This is the fifty-first of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both monks (*bhikṣu*) and nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), it constitutes a *pāyattika*, while for the three groups [of novices], it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding this essence of the precept: if a bhikṣu, for the sake of causing annoyance, causes another to lose their food by leading them toward the house of a layperson and then annoying them so that they are made to return;
herein, one commits an offense if a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
"Come, let us go together to another's house."
If one causes [a person] to turn back before they have entered the city gate, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one causes them to turn back after they have entered the city gate, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one causes them to turn back before they have entered the outer gate, the middle gate, or the inner gate, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one causes someone to turn back while they have entered the inner gate but have not yet reached the place where they can hear [the instruction], it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one causes them to turn back once they have reached the place where they can hear it, it is a *pāyattika*.
For example, when Baddhālī told Dharma to turn back, the place where the donor could hear was defined as "the place where one can hear."
If a donor happens to go out and sees [the monk] returning and leaving, he should call him to stay.
If the monk hears this and does not stop, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he does not hear it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

52. The Fifty-second Matter. This is the fifty-second of the ninety matters. It is a shared precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika offense; for the three groups [of novices], it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Regarding this essence of the precept: if one is free from illness and lacks other causal conditions, it is an offense to light a fire in the open air and sit facing it.
If one suffers from cold, heat, wind, or any other ailment that requires the use of fire for relief, this is termed "illness."
There are five kinds of things that may be used for kindling fire:
first, grass; second, wood; third, cow dung; fourth, tree bark; and fifth, refuse.
If one lights these five kinds of things oneself or causes another to light them, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
It must be in an unobstructed place and directed toward an object.
Among the five items, if one simultaneously places all five kinds into the fire, it constitutes one *pāyattika*;
if one places them into the fire one by one, there is a *pāyattika* for each.
If another person has already lit a fire, and one subsequently places anything into that fire for any purpose, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each act.
If one provides fuel to another who has already lit a fire, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one carries fire from room to room with one's hand, there is no offense.
If one places even a single small piece of firewood or a handful of grass into the fire, it is a *pāyattika*.
If fire, ash, or charcoal from an open space is placed back into the fire, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill; if cooking rice, soup, porridge, meat, or broth; if boiling dye or fumigating a bowl; or if repairing a staff or a door-bolt. For such causes as these, there is no offense.
If one is traveling on a road during intense cold, there is no offense.

53. The fifty-third item. This is the fifty-third of the ninety items. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika, while the three groups [of novices] do not commit an offense.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* against Upananda, some say it was the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), some say it was the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence), some say it was the *adarśana-utksepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension for not seeing [one's offense]), and some say it was the *apratinihsarga-pāpaka-dṛṣṭi-utksepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension for not relinquishing evil and false views).

Regarding Ananda’s statement that "Anuruddha was one of the group of six bhikṣus," some say he was one person among the six themselves, while others say that the disciples of the group of six were very numerous and he was one among those disciples.

Regarding "monastic affairs": these include formal announcements (*jñapti*), the *jñapti-dvitīya* and *jñapti-caturtha* procedures, the *poṣadha* for the recitation of the precepts and the *pravāraṇā*, or the appointment of the fourteen types of persons.

As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu has already granted his consent (*chanda*) to a monastic affair conducted in accordance with the Dharma, yet later regrets it and says, "I should not have granted my consent."
A *pāyattika* offense.
For every instance of expressing regret according to one's own mind, there is a *pāyattika* offense, except in matters concerning the formal procedures (*saṃgha-kamma*) of the Saṃgha.
If, after the Saṃgha has collectively settled a matter through formal procedure, one later regrets it and reproaches it, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If the Saṃgha has performed all formal acts (karmas) in accordance with the Dharma, and one later rebukes them saying it is "not permissible," it is a pāyattika offense.

If the Saṃgha performs all formal acts in a manner not in accordance with the Dharma, and one remains silent without rebuking them at that time because one lacks the power to change or alter the proceedings, there is no offense in subsequently saying it is "not permissible."

Except for matters involving formal monastic procedures (*saṃghakamma*), regarding all other non-procedural matters that the Saṃgha has collectively settled through harmony, if one subsequently censures it—provided that the decision was in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya—it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If it is a royal regulation but does not conform to the Vinaya, it is a *duṣkṛta*. 54.
The fifty-fourth item of the ninety items. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *pāyattika*, while for the three groups [of novices], there is no offense.
Regarding "a peripheral small room": some say it is called "peripheral" because the various rooms and dwellings are located at the very outer edge.
Others say it is called "peripheral" because the room is lowly and dilapidated, lacking the necessary bedding and furnishings, and is thus the lowest among the three grades.
The reason for establishing this precept for the bhikṣus is to show respect for the Buddha-dharma and to put an end to slander.
To stay more than two nights in the same room with one who has not received the full ordination is a pāyattika offense.
The reason for permitting two nights is that if you were not permitted to stay at all, there might be circumstances leading to the loss of life;
furthermore, if staying for two nights were not permitted, there would inevitably be various causes and conditions for distress.
Out of compassion, one is permitted to stay together for two nights;
however, to protect the Buddha-dharma, staying for three nights is not allowed.
Regarding those who have not received the full precepts (*upasampadā*), this applies to all persons except for *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs*.
There are four kinds of dwellings:
first, those that are completely covered and completely enclosed;
second, those that are completely enclosed but not completely covered.
Third, all-enclosed with partial obstruction;
fourth, all-enclosed with slight obstruction.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu stays overnight for more than two nights within any of these four types of dwellings with a person who has not received the full ordination, it is a pāyattika.
If, having risen, one lies down again, one incurs that many *pāyattikas*.
If one remains seated throughout the night, there is no offense.
If, after staying together for more than two nights, one stays with another person on the third night, it is a *pāyattika*, because of the continuity with the previous person.
If, after spending two nights together, one moves to another location and then returns to stay together again after having spent one night elsewhere, there is no offense.
If it is merely covered but not enclosed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there is only an obstruction but no enclosure, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one enters within and closes the door, there is no offense.
If it is inside a large fence or wall, there is no transgression.
If one stays overnight with a eunuch or a person of dual sexual organs, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it exceeds two nights, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If all [four sides] are covered, but three sides are enclosed while one side is not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

55. The fifty-fifth matter. This is the fifty-fifth of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a pāyattika, and for the three groups [of novices] it is a duṣkṛta.
The bhikṣu Ariṣṭa was formerly a disciple of non-Buddhist teachers; sent by those heterodox masters into the Buddha-dharma to subvert and confuse it, he was clever and of sharp faculties.
Before long, he had mastered the Tripiṭaka, yet he immediately began to teach it perversely, claiming that practices which obstruct the Path do not actually obstruct the Path.
Despite his exhaustive use of wisdom and eloquence, he was unable to establish his position.

Regarding this essence of the precept: first, one is admonished with three gentle words; if it does not cease, one is then admonished through a formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) within the Saṃgha.
If, despite these three admonitions in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, one still does not desist, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If the three groups [of novices] do not eliminate their evil and heterodox views, they shall likewise be subject to expulsion through the three teachings until they are completely extinguished. 56.

The fifty-sixth matter. This is the fifty-sixth of the ninety matters; it is a common precept, and both monks and nuns commit a *pāyattika* offense for it, while the three groups [of novices] do not incur an offense.
The establishment of this precept for the bhikṣus is for the purpose of extinguishing unwholesome dharmas and for the sake of the purity of the Buddha-dharma.

As for the essence of this precept: if a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has committed an offense according to the Dharma and yet has not been expelled for his evil and heterodox views, and he nevertheless dwells with him or shares a room with him for the night, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "engaging in joint affairs," there are two kinds of affairs:
first, matters concerning the Dharma; second, matters concerning material goods.

Regarding "living together," it means living with these persons, performing the *jñapti*, *jñapti-dvitīya*, and *jñapti-caturtha* karmas, the *poṣadha* for the recitation of the precepts and the *pravāraṇā*, and the *karma* for appointing the fourteen types of officials.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu performs formal acts together with one who has been expelled—whether it be teaching the sūtras and Dharma or performing a *karmavācanā*—it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is as explained in the Sūtra, for each individual act, it is a *pāyattika*.
If explained according to individual phrases, there is a *pāyattika* offense for each phrase.
It is the same if one receives the meaning or the sūtra from a person who has been expelled.
Regarding shared property: if a bhikṣu gives robes, bowls, or even lifelong medicine to an expelled person, it is all a *pāyattika* offense.
If one takes the robes, bowl, or even the lifetime medicine from a person who has been expelled, it is all a *pāyattika*.
If one lies down together with [the expelled person] in any of the four types of dwellings and takes [their belongings], it is a *pāyattika*.
If, having risen, one lies down again, or repeatedly rises and lies down again, for each instance it is a *pāyattika*.
If one remains seated throughout the night without lying down, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The fifty-seventh item of the ninety items. This is a common precept; both monks and nuns commit a *pāyattika*, while the three groups [of novices] do not incur an offense.

Regarding this essence of the precept: if a bhikṣu knows that a śrāmaṇera has been expelled and yet keeps him, provides for him, engages in joint activities with him, or sleeps with him, it is a pāyattika offense.
As for the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu teaches the sūtras or the Dharma to an expelled śrāmaṇera, whether by verse or prose, for every verse it is a pāyattika;
if by prose, for every matter it is a pāyattika.
If explained according to individual phrases, there is a *pāyattika* for each phrase.
It is the same if one receives, studies, or recites the scriptures from a suspended *śrāmaṇera*.
If one gives robes, alms bowls, or even lifelong medicine, it is in all cases a *pāyattika*.
If one takes a bowl, takes robes, or even accepts medicine for life, it is all a *pāyattika*.
If one sleeps in any of the four kinds of dwellings together [with a nun], it is a *pāyattika*.
If, having risen, one lies down again, for every instance of rising and lying down again, one incurs as many *pāyattikas* as there were instances.
If one sits through the entire night without lying down, it is also a *pāyattika*.

If a *śrāmaṇera* harbors evil and heterodox views that are not eliminated and does not cease despite the three teachings, the *nigarhaṇīya-karman* (act of censure) of *pravāsanīya* (expulsion) shall be performed against him.
If one who was formerly a layperson dressed in white robes later returns to become a śrāmaṇera, the previous *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) remains valid.
If one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), the previous *karmavācanā* likewise remains valid.
If one’s gender changes and becomes a śrāmaṇerī, the previous *karmavācanā* also remains valid.

If one dwells together, performs affairs together, or lives together with the three groups of persons who have not eliminated their evil and heterodox views after being expelled, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Likewise, if one dwells together or performs affairs together with those who have been expelled for causing a schism in the Saṃgha, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.

58. The Fifty-eighth Matter. This is the fifty-eighth of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense, while the three other assemblies do not commit an offense.
Regarding "jewels," these include gold, silver, mother-of-pearl, agate, lapis lazuli, pearls, or gold leaf and golden images.
As for any such jeweled vessel, whoever grasps it commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one personally grasps and lifts a golden image, it is a *pāyattika* offense;
if it is lifted together with a *kappiya-kāraka*, there is no offense.
Regarding all things resembling jewels, whether grasping them or lifting them, there is no offense.
If one uses imitation jewels to make ornaments for women, holding them constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If they are made as ornaments for men—excluding spears, lances, bows, arrows, swords, and staves—and are made into saddles, bridles, whips, or belts, there is no offense in holding any of these.
If one takes up armor or any musical instrument, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one takes up money oneself, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu takes up precious objects of great value, it is a *pāyattika*.
If members of the three assemblies or laypeople are made to hold it, there is no offense.
With the exception of within a monastery or a residence, if someone leaves a treasure behind, one should take it with the following resolve:
"When the owner comes to seek it, I shall return it."
"It should be so. Regarding "within the monastery grounds" (saṃghārāma): this refers to the area within the walls, moats, fences, or enclosures.

Regarding "within the dwelling place" (āvāsa): this refers to the dwelling place where a bhikṣu resides, established according to the location of a layperson's house; this is called "within the dwelling place."

If there is someone who has forgotten a treasure in these two places, and if there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle allowable items), one should instruct them to take it up and guard it; if there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one should take it up oneself.
If the owner comes, one should ask for identifying characteristics; if they correspond, then one should give it back, but if they do not correspond, one should not give it.
If there is a dwelling place for laypeople outside the monastery’s fence or wall, one should not take [anything from it].
The sequential rules are as explained in the Vinaya text.
59. The Fifty-ninth Matter. This is a common precept: for a nun, it is a *pāyattika*; for the three groups of disciples, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding "new robes," this refers to whether they are new or old; they are called "new" simply because they were first obtained.
There are five primary colors:
yellow, red, blue, black, and white.
Yellow refers to that dyed with the root of saffron (*kuṅkuma*) or indigo;
red refers to that dyed with *urubūka* or *lākṣā*;
