blue is sometimes said to be indigo or *dai* (antimony), though others say it is a derivative of these and not the substance itself—this too is prohibited.
Others do not yet understand its basis.
Generally, regarding these five major colors, if one dyes them oneself, it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense;
if one makes a robe from them, it does not constitute a valid acceptance.
Whether one makes robes of standard measurement or non-standard measurement, none of them may be worn.
If one first obtains a robe of the five primary colors and later alters it to a color that conforms to the Dharma, then it becomes a properly maintained possession.
If one first prepares the color according to the Dharma, but later destroys it with the five primary colors, the formal undertaking is not accomplished.
Although the undertaking is not accomplished, if one applies the three-point purification, it may be worn in all circumstances.
If one makes robes from deep blue-black or dark green cloth, they do not constitute valid formal acceptance (*parigraha*).
With the exception of the three robes, for all other garments, it is without fault to wear them provided they have been purified by applying only three dots of dye.
If one makes robes from indigo wood (sao-mu-lan), all may do so and it shall be considered valid for formal acceptance and maintenance.

If it is not pure blue, but light blue or greenish-blue, it may be used as a patch for purification and made into the lining of a robe; provided that the inner layer is not visible on the outside, it may be worn.
However, if it is made into a robe where the color is visible, it must not be worn at all.
The same applies to those that are red, yellow, or white, as well as those whose colors are not pure or are large.

With the exception of *puṭa* (woolen socks) and leather shoes, all other clothing, bedding, and articles—even down to a waist-belt—must undergo the purification of the three dots (*tripuṇḍra-śuddhi*).
If one wears a garment that has not been consecrated by the *adhiṣṭhāna* rite, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense in all cases.
Any robe of improper color is not validly possessed; any robe of proper color is validly possessed.
If one wears any robe, whether its color is appropriate or inappropriate according to the Dharma, without having performed the ritual of *jìng* (purification), it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If the original markings on a robe have faded, it remains a purified robe and need not be marked again.

If one has already performed the ritual purification (*parikarma*) for a garment and subsequently patches it with new pieces—whether at ten locations or five—one need only perform a single act of purification at one location; it is not necessary to purify each individual patch, because they all constitute a single repair by means of stitching.
If the garment is merely sewn straight, one must perform the ritual purification (*pratyavekṣaṇā*) for each section.
Whether the garment is mended by patching with backstitches or mended by straight seams, if one wears it without performing the ritual purification, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are three kinds of pure dharmas:
first, clothing purified by the three points according to the Dharma; and as for all medicinal gruels that must be purified, a bhikṣu may perform the purification himself.
Second, if one obtains fruits, vegetables, or seeds of the five types, they must be purified by a novice (śrāmaṇera) or a layperson (avadātavasana).
Third, if one obtains leather sandals of two layers or more, or new boots, one must have a layperson wear them and walk five, six, or seven paces; this constitutes purification.
Regarding the three types of items—storing jewels, using various jewels, and trading goods—all such things must be purified through a layperson (*avadātavasana*).
Furthermore, there are two other kinds of purification:

first, intentional purification (*saṃketa-pariśuddhi*). This refers to fruits, vegetables, or the five types of seeds, as well as concentrated juices, which are intentionally purified by means of fire, a knife, fingernails, or water; this is called intentional purification.

Second is "purification not intentionally performed. For example, if there are five types of seeds such as fruits or vegetables, if they fall onto [the food] by themselves due to a knife or fire, this is called purification; the same applies to parrots.
If rain falls into a gruel, it is likewise called purified. This is what is meant by "purification not intentionally performed."
There are three types of dyeing for the purpose of making a cloth "defiled" (kṛta-kalpa):
first, blue; second, black; and third, madder.
If one wears a robe of lawful color that has been marked with the five primary colors, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Excluding the five primary colors, there are pure colors—namely, yellow, blue, saffron, lac, indigo, and all shades of green—which are called pure colors; these also must not be worn.
If a robe is yellow, red, or white, although it has been purified by the three dots, wearing it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

However, if one performed the purification by dots while the material for the robe was still uncolored, and later dyed it into its final color without performing the purification again, there is no fault, because it was already purified previously.
If one wears robes of five pure colors, they do not constitute valid possession; if one applies the "three-dot purification" (trimaṇḍala), wearing them constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
However, if the robe was originally of pure color and is subsequently altered by a color that conforms to the Dharma, it then becomes valid possession.
Purple grass, pear bark, barberry bark, *di-huang*, crimson dyes, and yellow *rhus* wood—all these are colors that do not conform to the Dharma.
If one re-dyes them with a color that conforms to the Dharma and covers [the former] over it, then they become properly possessed.
If a robe was originally of a permissible color, but is later dyed with an impermissible color and marked as purified, it may be worn, yet the formal undertaking of its possession is not established.

60. The Sixtieth Matter. This is the sixtieth of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense, while for the three groups [of novices], it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu bathes before the fifteenth day has passed, it is a pāyattika.
If the fifteenth day has passed or if more time has elapsed, there is no offense.
Regarding the "hot season": the remaining one month and a half of spring and the first month of summer—these two and a half months are called the hot season.
The Vinaya Master says:
"It becomes hot early in India; this is what is meant by the Indian hot season."
In this manner, whenever it is hot, whether morning or evening, one may bathe up to two and a half months in succession; bathing during that time is not an offense.
Regarding those who are ill: when illnesses such as cold, heat, or wind disorders can be cured by bathing, this is called "the time of illness."
During the time of wind, there will inevitably be dust that soils the body; this is called the time of wind.
During the time of rain, the falling rain will inevitably moisten one's clothes and defile the body; this is called the time of rain.
"During the time of work" refers to even sweeping the ground of the monastic quarters for a distance of five or six feet; this is called the time of work.
"During the time of traveling on a road" refers to traveling even half a *yojana* either coming or going.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu arrives yesterday and bathes today, it is a pāyattika.
If he departs tomorrow and bathes today, it is a pāyattika.
If one travels half a yojana on the very same day and bathes, there is no offense.
If there are no such causes or conditions, to bathe less than once every half-month constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If there is a reason [to bathe], yet one bathes without informing the other bhikṣus, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
61. The sixty-first matter. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a pāyattika, and for the three groups of followers it is a duṣkṛta.
The precepts were established for the monks out of compassion, to sever evil deeds, and to foster respectful faith.
Regarding the offenses herein, there is one *pāyattika* for taking the life of an animal: whether one takes it oneself, instructs another to take it, or sends a messenger to do so.
Generally, three factors constitute the offense of killing:
first, the perception of a living being; second, the intention to kill that living being; and third, the severing of life—these constitute a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding self-inflicted killing: if, with the desire to cause death, one uses the hand, the fist, the head, the feet, or objects capable of killing living beings such as staffs, wood, tiles, stones, knives, spears, arrows, or bows, and strikes or hurls them [at oneself] such that death occurs, it is a *pāyattika*.
If he does not die immediately, but dies later as a result of this, it is a *pāyattika*.
If he does not die immediately, nor dies later as a result of this, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Whether poison is placed in the eye, or on a part of the body, or in food, or in a place where he walks or lies down—the meaning of whether he dies or does not die is as explained previously.

If one sets a snare, trap, or mechanical device to press upon the abdomen and cause an abortion—down to the point where the fetus has first acquired two sense-faculties within the mother’s womb—with the intention that it should die, yet it does not die, the meaning is as previously explained.
If one instructs another to kill, or dispatches a messenger to kill, and the messenger kills that person instead of the intended one, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one instructs someone to come and kill, and they kill [the victim] at the time of their departure, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
These various meanings regarding killing are as explained in the *Pārājika* section;
the only difference lies in the fact that [the victim] is a human rather than an animal.

62. The sixty-second matter. This is the sixty-second of the ninety matters. This is a common precept (*sādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada*); for both monks (*bhikṣu*) and nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), it is a *pāyattika*; for the three assemblies (*trisaṃgha*), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the offenses herein, there are six causal conditions: first, birth;
second, receiving full ordination; third, transgression; fourth, interrogation; fifth, objects; and sixth, rules.
There are two ways of addressing one's birth:
first, asking another bhikṣu,
"When were you born?"
He asked:
"When did the hair grow beneath your armpits?
When did the beard grow upon your face?"
"When will the throat appear?
There are four ways of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*):
if a bhikṣu asks another bhikṣu:
“When did you receive full ordination?
“Who is your preceptor (upādhyāya) and who is your teacher (ācārya)?
Who is your instructor (śikṣācārya)?”
The third question:
"Did you receive full ordination before a group of ten or before a group of five?
The fourth question:
"Did you receive full ordination outside the boundary,
or did you receive it within the boundary?
Regarding the offense, there are four types:
First, committing an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; second, committing an offense of *pāyattika*; third, committing an offense of *pratideśanīya*; fourth, committing an offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding "questioning," it means questioning another bhikṣu:

"You walked through such-and-such a village, through such-and-such an alley, went to such-and-such a house and sat there, and conversed with such-and-such a woman at such-and-such a place; she is a woman of ill repute."
"Did you go to such-and-such a nunnery and speak with such-and-such a nun? That nun is ill-reputed.
This is called "questioning.
As for "objects," it is when a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
"Who is it that shares your intent regarding the bowl and even the lifetime medicine?
As for the rule (*dharma*): if a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Do not keep many robes;

do not eat repeatedly; do not eat separately from the community; do not enter another's house unless invited; do not enter a village at an improper time; do not enter a town or village without wearing the saṃghāṭī."
Regarding the first six matters, one who causes [a person] to be born may incur a *pāyattika*, a *dukkaṭa*, or be without offense.

If, when considering the age at birth and the duration of the three marks, the person was not yet eligible to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) when they did so, and the former person spoke these words out of a compassionate and kind heart while actually not having received the precepts themselves, there is no offense.
If one intentionally desires to cause another to feel doubt or regret, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If the other person already possesses the precepts and one wishes to vex them by causing doubt or regret, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

If, by means of the latter five matters, one speaks with the intent to cause doubt or regret, it is a *pāyattika* offense regardless of whether the preceding bhikṣu actually experiences doubt or regret.
If, apart from these six matters, one speaks of other things with the intent to cause doubt or regret, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This refers to speaking to a bhikṣu, saying:
"You sleep too much, you eat too much, you speak too much; such a person is not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, and not a son of the Śākya."

If one causes others—such as bhikṣuṇīs, the three groups of novices, laypeople who have no preceptor-monk, those who were originally monks but broke their precepts and returned to lay life, those who have "crossed over" (defected), those who dwell as thieves, those who have been expelled by formal act, the six types of offenders, those of the fivefold dharma, those with deranged minds, those with distracted minds, those with diseased minds, those who have killed an arhat, those who have defiled a bhikṣuṇī, or those who were originally impotent—to harbor doubt or regret regarding these six matters, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). All such cases constitute *duṣkṛta*.

If one ordains a novice (śrāmaṇera) who has already received the full precepts, or one who is blind, deaf, mute, or has not been seen [to be guilty], or has not been subjected to the formal act of suspension (pravāsanīya-karman), or whose evil views have not been removed, or who is undergoing the parivāsa or mānatva penances, or who is subject to the four types of formal acts such as dependence (niśraya)—in all such cases, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If one uses these six matters to dispatch a messenger to instruct another person, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

63. The sixty-third item. This is the sixty-third of the ninety items. This is a common precept; for both monks (*bhikṣu*) and nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), it is a *pāyattika*, while for the three groups [of novices], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu strikes or tickles another bhikṣu with one finger, it is a pāyattika.
If he strikes or tickles him with two, three, or even up to nine fingers, each instance constitutes a separate pāyattika.
If one strikes or tickles with all ten fingers at once, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one strikes or tickles a bhikṣuṇī, a member of the three assemblies, a person guilty of the six offenses, a person belonging to the five groups, one who is insane, mentally deranged, or whose mind is impaired, or a layperson who lacks a teacher or a saṃgha—striking or tickling such persons as these constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in every case.

Those who are blind, sightless, deaf, or mute; those undergoing *parivāsa* or *mānatva*; novice monks (*śrāmaṇera*) who have received the precepts; and persons subject to the four types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*) such as "not performing," "not seeing," "not removing evil views," or "reliance"—for all these, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one strikes or tickles with wood, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one instructs another to strike or tickle, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
As for the seventeen groups who struck and killed, they were young junior bhikṣus.

64. The sixty-fourth matter. This is the sixty-fourth of the ninety matters. This is a shared precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense, while for the three groups [of trainees], it is a duṣkṛta offense.

The reason for establishing the precepts together with the bhikṣus is to ensure the respect accorded to the Buddha-dharma, to foster and increase reverent faith, to prevent the neglect of right practice, and to cultivate correct mindfulness.
Regarding the offenses herein, there are eight kinds:

first, causing joy; second, causing pleasure; third, causing laughter; fourth, playing; fifth, splashing water; sixth, causing others to feel joy; seventh, causing others to feel pleasure; eighth, causing others to laugh.

If a bhikṣu engages in any one of the eight matters—whether splashing water, submerging head-first, twisting like a fish, floating on one arm, floating on both arms, leaping up with the body, or floating face-up—each such act that violates the rules of decorum constitutes a pāyattika offense.
Even if there is water on the rim of the bowl, or if one draws with a finger while seated on a bed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if it is for the purpose of learning to swim, or if one is simply crossing [the water].

65. The sixty-fifth matter. This is the sixty-fifth of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a pāyattika, and for the three groups of followers it is a duṣkṛta.
There are four kinds of dwellings:

those that are entirely covered and entirely enclosed; those that are entirely enclosed but not entirely covered; those that are entirely covered but not entirely enclosed; and those that are entirely covered and partially enclosed.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu stays overnight with a woman or a female animal within any of these four kinds of dwellings, it is a pāyattika.
If he rises and lies down again, or repeatedly rises and lies down again, he incurs as many pāyattikas as there were instances of doing so.
There is no offense if one does not lie down throughout the night.
However, if there is a woman staying overnight in another house, or if the dwelling has a hole large enough for a young cat to enter, and one stays overnight in such a house, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there is one woman in the room, it constitutes one *pāyattika* offense.
If there are ten women, it constitutes ten *pāyattika* offenses.
This precept is completed as an offense through bodily action (*kāyakarma*), and it is also completed as an offense with respect to the person (*pudgala*).
Lying down once constitutes one *pāyattika*; lying down ten times constitutes ten *pāyattikas*. This is called the completion of the offense through bodily action (*kāyakarma*).

If there is one woman present when one lies down, there is one downfall; if there are ten women present when one lies down, there are ten downfalls. This is called incurring the offense with respect to persons (*pudgala*).
If it is entirely covered and unobstructed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it is entirely covered but obstructed on three sides and unobstructed on one side, or even if it is obstructed on one side and unobstructed on three sides, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there are obstructions on four sides but it is not entirely covered, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it is entirely covered and entirely obstructed, regardless of its size, it is always a *pāyattika*.
If one constructs a central hall (*kūtāgāra*) or a monastery (*caitya-vihāra*), they must share the same roof and enclosure.

Even if there are various small rooms within the hall, although each room is distinct, because the hall is one, it constitutes a single unit; one must ensure that the four sides of the hall have enclosures and that the roof above is likewise unified.
If a bhikṣu closes the door of his own small room within a hall, and a woman is likewise in another small room, because the hall has a single roof over both, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.

If within the house of a layperson there are separate rooms, and a bhikṣu is in one room while a woman is in another, it is a duṣkṛta offense if the bhikṣu does not close the door of his room; if he closes the door, there is no offense.

If the walls of the rooms are connected as a continuous barrier and they share the same roof above with doors side by side, yet the points of entry and exit are distinct, then even though they are connected and share a common roof, there is no offense for a bhikṣu to close the door.
If it is under a tree, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the woman is a female animal capable of engaging in sexual intercourse, it is a *pāyattika*.

If she is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse—such as a barren woman (*śilāputrī*), one whose organs are impaired, a female spirit (*yakṣiṇī*), a celestial maiden (*devī*), or a female pigeon or sparrow—it is a *duṣkṛta*.

66. The sixty-sixth matter. This is the sixty-sixth of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a pāyattika, and for the three groups of followers it is a duṣkṛta.
Regarding the offenses within this, there are six kinds:
form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*). As for form:
if a bhikṣu assumes the color of an elephant, the color of a horse, the color of a sheep, the color of a water buffalo, or other such terrifying forms.
Question:
"This is something we see constantly; why should one fear it? Answer:
"Because it is at an improper time, it causes people to be afraid.
Whether it actually causes fear or not, in all cases it is a *pāyattika* offense.
This is called "form."
The same applies to sounds, odors, and tastes; because they occur at an improper time, they cause people to feel fear.
Regarding tastes: if a bhikṣu asks another bhikṣu, "What did you eat today?"
He replied,
"I used curd and fish.
He spoke again:
"If one eats rice with curd or fish, that person will contract leprosy or scabies.
Whether the assembly is frightened by this or not, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding such names, flavors, and textures:

as for "touch," if another person has previously spread out a hard object for sitting, one might remove that hard covering and replace it with a soft one in order to cause fear; by suddenly altering the characteristics of the object, one causes them to be startled and terrified.
The same applies to moving from softness to hardness.
Such various different tactile sensations used to terrify others are called "touch.
As for "dharma," it refers to when a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
"Do not defecate or urinate upon fresh vegetables; you shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Whether one succeeds in causing fear or not, it is an *pāyattika* offense in either case.
If a bhikṣu, by means of six matters, threatens himself or causes another bhikṣu to be threatened—whether he succeeds in causing fear or not—it is a pāyattika offense.
If, setting aside these six matters, one further terrifies a bhikṣu by means of other matters, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

That is to say, if one says, "By sleeping excessively, eating excessively, or speaking excessively, you shall fall into hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm," and thus terrifies another bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If one fears a bhikṣuṇī, the three groups [of novices], the six types of offenders, those who practice the five dharmas, those with deranged minds, those with disordered minds, those with impaired minds, laypeople, those without a preceptor, those who have left the monastic order, those who have killed an arhat, those who have defiled a bhikṣuṇī, those who were originally impotent, all non-Buddhist renunciants, or any householders, it is entirely a duṣkṛta offense.

For a śrāmaṇera who has received the precepts, one who is blind, one who is deaf, one who is mute, one undergoing *parivāsa* or *mānatva*, one who does not acknowledge [the offense], one who does not desist from evil, one who does not remove [wrong views], one who is suspended (*pravāsanīya*), and those subject to the four types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*) such as seeking dependence—[if one ordains any of these], it is a *pāyattika* offense for all.

67. The sixty-seventh matter. This is the sixty-seventh of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs it is a pāyattika, and for the three groups of disciples it is a duṣkṛta.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu hides another bhikṣu’s robe, bowl, door-latch, or leather sandals, it is a pāyattika if he cannot find them upon searching; if he finds them upon searching, it is a dukkaṭa.
If one conceals stone bowls, gold bowls, silver bowls, lapis lazuli bowls, or any such bowls made of precious materials, whether they are found or not found, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one conceals the robes of those made from the five major types of wool—namely, camel hair, cow hair, black ram’s wool, or mixed sheep’s wool—one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense in every case.

If one conceals the robes or alms bowls of a *śrāmaṇera* who has received the precepts, of one undergoing *parivāsa* or *mānatva*, of one who is blind, deaf, mute, or dependent, or of one who has not confessed their fault, has not ceased their evil conduct, or has not been expelled, one commits a *pāyattika* offense in every case.

If one conceals any of the following persons—the six types of offenders, those who have committed the five heinous acts, householders who lack a preceptor, former bhikṣus who have left the order again, those who have defected, those who dwell as thieves, those who have killed an arhat, those who have violated a bhikṣuṇī, those who were originally impotent, bhikṣuṇīs, or members of the three other assemblies—their robes and bowls all constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To conceal any of the one hundred and one types of articles constitutes a *pāyattika* offense;
if the bowl has not yet been fumigated, it is likewise a *pāyattika*.
To conceal any long robe, bowl, or bowl-fastener that has been formally purified (*pariśuddha*) for storage—even down to a needle case—constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If there is a needle in the needle-case, it is a *pāyattika*; if there is no needle, it is a *dukkaṭa*. 68. The sixty-eighth matter.
This is the sixty-eighth of the ninety matters. This is a common precept; for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *pāyattika*, while for the three groups [of novices], it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding this precept: originally, one gave a robe to another with the intent to deceive, desiring to employ their labor.
Having caused the other to form the notion that it was their own possession, one then seizes it back; this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The reason it is not considered a grave offense is that it was not given with full ownership.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, and they do not return it, yet he takes it back by force, it is a pāyattika.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Scroll Eight. Continued from the Preface to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*. Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhishou of East Chan-ting Monastery in the Western Capital. When the Hero of the World had ceased his transformative activity, the Vinaya Piṭaka branched out into various divisions, whereby the sages of India subsequently provided separate commentaries for each section.

Since the Buddhist teachings first flowed eastward, many centuries have passed, and the Vinaya and Abhidharma treatises of the Western lands have been transmitted to this region; yet, this Sarvāstivāda school specifically interprets the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Zhi-shou, whose past karmic conditions had accumulated merit, entered the monastic order at an early age. Upon first advancing to the stage of receiving the precepts, he immediately devoted himself to the study of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
He perused various vinayas and śāstras with thorough diligence, yet he often lamented that although this treatise was essential and profound, its textual explanations were incomplete.

From the regions south of the Yangtze and east of the Huai, extending as far as Guansi, I have personally inspected all existing collections of the scriptures; they were all equally decayed and few were complete.

Although I sought them with ever-increasing earnestness, the reasons for their loss remain unfathomable. I have always regretted these deficiencies, attributing them to the limitations of the translators, and whenever I reflect quietly upon this, my sorrow and lamentation deepen.

Recently, having received imperial edicts, I came to reside here in meditation. Fortunately, I encountered the Vinaya Master Baoxuan of Xishu with whom I discussed this treatise; as for its missing meanings and profound words, they are fully present in my native region.

I was not expecting to hear this news, and my joy and exultation were beyond measure; thereupon, I earnestly inquired three times about its origins and only then learned that this scripture was translated in Shu, and that according to the original text, it consists of nine fascicles.

In the past, during the Wei dynasty, when Emperor Daowu utterly destroyed the Dharma-gate, these sublime teachings were left fragmented from beginning to end. Consequently, throughout the four quarters, only incomplete versions were transmitted, while the authentic mantras in their full perfection remained preserved in Chengdu.
Zhishou then entrusted the task to travelers from Qiong and Bi, as well as reliable messengers from Jinglu; after three years of arduous travel, his wish was finally fulfilled.

In the twelfth month of winter in the second year of the Daye era (the Bingyin year), the twenty-sixth year since the Sui dynasty took control of the world, he personally obtained this manuscript and transmitted it to the capital.
With deep aspiration, Zhishou causes the waters of enlightenment to flow and the lamps of wisdom to be spread, so that his disciples may awaken and his treasury of Dharma may be replenished.

A copy already exists, which he has entrusted to the Monk Sengsha, Master of Shentong Monastery in Qizhou, to be transcribed and circulated among the various collections throughout the region between the sea and Mount Dai.

I still regret that it has not yet been circulated in the regions of Jin, Wei, Yan, and Zhao. Master Jinghong of Xiangzhou, a master craftsman of the Vinaya, was also personally instructed by Master Zhishou from his youth; I now respectfully entrust a copy of this work to him to transmit to the region north of the Yellow River.
Therefore, I have set forth this preface in full at the beginning of this volume; may the worthy readers examine it and remain free from doubt or confusion.
*Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Volume Nine.
The translator’s name has been lost; it is now appended to the records of the Qin dynasty.
69. The sixty-ninth matter: The sixty-ninth of the ninety matters.
To slander another constitutes a grave offense (sthūlātyaya).
To commit a duṣkṛta offense by slandering even a single person also constitutes an offense.
70. The seventieth matter: Regarding women traveling on the same road. The previous rule regulated *bhikṣuṇīs*; this rule regulates laywomen.
The meaning is no different from that explained above regarding nuns.
If one travels together with many women, one commits multiple offenses.
71. The seventy-first matter: Regarding traveling together with thieves. *Kāṣāya*—in the language of Qin, it means "dyed."
The fetters, cravings, and so forth are also called "defilements.
One who wears this garment causes wild animals not to fear him; for this reason, hunters delight in borrowing such clothing.
Later, when the animals see a bhikṣu from afar, they immediately give rise to a sense of fear and avoid him from a distance.
Traveling with bandits is likewise; because people see a bhikṣu traveling with bandits, they lose faith, and for this reason the Buddha established the precept.

Seventy-second: Regarding the seventy-second of the ninety matters—concerning one who is less than twenty years of age. If one is under twenty, or perceives oneself as being under twenty, and thus does not obtain the precepts, it is because one is truly not yet twenty, or even lacks nineteen years; therefore, one cannot obtain the precepts.

Regarding the fact that nineteen years according to the Hu calendar is required to receive the precepts, this is not like the system of Qin; it requires that the number of days be completed to reach a full year. As for those who receive the precepts before the year is complete, this is because the period spent in the mother's womb is included to fulfill the requirement.
Regarding "those who perform communal acts," this refers to the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and the *Karmavācanā* ceremonies.
Regarding "incurring an offense through communal residence," this occurs by staying for more than two nights; it also applies if the full year has elapsed, even if the number of days is short.
If a person is actually twenty years old and perceives themselves as being twenty, yet when questioned by the Saṃgha says they are not full [twenty], there are two possibilities:
first, if this was due to error or forgetfulness, this person obtains the precepts;
second, if it was because they did not intend to receive them and said they were not full because the preceptor forced them to do so, this person does not obtain the precepts.

At sixty years of age, one may not receive full ordination; even if a preceptor and the Sangha were to forcibly confer it, it would be invalid, because such a person is incapable of enduring the hardships of the path.
Furthermore, as their mental faculties are dull and weak, they are permitted only to remain as a śrāmaṇera.
It is also not permitted to ordain those under seven years of age; if one does so and they receive the precepts, both parties commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there is the principle of observing physical characteristics.

Those who have not yet reached twenty years of age are not permitted [to receive full ordination] because they are flighty and cannot endure cold or hardship; if they were to receive the *mahā-śīla*, many people would reproach them.
If one were a śrāmaṇera, people would not rebuke them for this reason.

As for the twelve [grounds] obtained by a bhikṣuṇī, it is because she is sent into service by her husband's family, where she must endure various sufferings and develop a deep sense of revulsion toward her former life.
73. The seventy-third matter: Regarding the seventy-third of the ninety matters, "digging the earth" refers to solid ground according to the Hu (Hui) manuscript;
"non-growing" refers to non-solid ground.

The fourth and eighth months constitute the rainy season; because the earth is continuous and saturated with moisture, capable of producing grasses and trees, it is termed by definition "productive ground" (*jāti-bhūmi*).

In other seasons when there is no rain, the ground is parched by the sun and the wind blows up the dust; because grass does not grow there, it is termed "unproductive ground" (*ajātā bhūmiḥ*) in meaning.
If one touches the dry soil upon this [ground], one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one encroaches upon damp ground, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If the wall is built level with the foundation and does not extend into the ground, there is no offense, as it is distinct from the earth.
Even if the ground has been leveled and treated, if it remains saturated with moisture, its emergence constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

Whenever one wishes to take vegetables, grass, or soil, one should speak from a distance, saying, "Bring some clean [earth] from such-and-such a place where it is good. If one goes to the edge and points it out, one commits an offense.
When an anthill is formed during rain, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅) offense, because it is not fundamental, solid earth.
If one cuts grass growing therein, touching the grass constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; covering the soil constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.
The reason it is a *dukkaṭa* is that there is a slight portion [of the ground] connected [to the living plant].
If one disturbs the ground beneath mud, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.

If grass grows upon a roof or a wall, or if there is earth or soil covering an area as extensive as an anthill, to dig it up constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense; if it is ground beneath mud, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
74. The seventy-fourth matter, the seventy-fourth of the ninety matters. Regarding the invitation for four months, the Buddha prohibited begging from those who are not relatives at improper times.

Because the group of six [monks] considered Śreṇika Bimbisāra to be a relative, they begged from him after the four-month period had ended; because they were at an improper time, acted contrary to the Dharma, and used threats to demand [gifts], he rebuked them and established this precept.
Regarding "because of repeated requests": either the host is preoccupied with official business and, unlike what was requested, invites again later;
or when the two-month period has already expired, they have further wealth and invite for another two months;
or because a wealthy person repeatedly makes such requests.
The circumstances are not always the same.

Among the three periods, one may accept [the invitation] according to the request: if requested at the beginning of summer, one accepts during the middle of summer; if requested midway through summer and the four months have not yet elapsed, it is combined with the winter period for acceptance; the same applies to other times.
Regarding "inviting separately": if one privately invites a person of great virtue, there is no offense. Seventy-fifth:

The seventy-fifth of the ninety matters concerning the establishment of common precepts. If a precept is common to both divisions [of the Sangha], it must necessarily be established within the Great Assembly of monks. Subsequently, a Great Bhikṣu is instructed to inform the Bhikṣuṇīs, because women are of inferior status and ought to receive them from the Great Assembly.

If the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts alone were established, they would fall within the two assemblies; that is, some would arise due to an incident involving a *bhikṣuṇī*, some would arise due to an incident involving a *bhikṣu*, and some would arise due to incidents involving both, with differing circumstances.
*Sūtra* refers to the four Āgamas and the two hundred and fifty precepts.
*Vinaya* means "to subdue," so called because it can subdue greed, hatred, and delusion; this refers to the various codes of discipline (*vinaya*).
The *Mātṛkā* is that which skillfully discerns the characteristics and meanings of all phenomena; it resembles the *Abhidharma*.

As for the *Vibhāṣā*, it refers to the *Abhidharma* and the *Ekottarika-vinaya*; it is so called because it elucidates the characteristics of meaning, discusses matter and non-matter, as well as the taught and the untaught, and so forth.
As for those who have entered the Vinaya-sūtras, these refer to the various places where the precepts are expounded in other sūtras.

If one explains the precepts from this sūtra to someone who has not yet received the full ordination (mahā-śīla), one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense; however, this constitutes an offense only if one intentionally disregards that person and they consequently do not come to listen to the precepts.
If their failure to come is due to other circumstances, there is no fault.

76. The seventy-sixth matter: Regarding the seventy-sixth of the ninety matters, "going to listen to a dispute," one commits an offense by being able to cause the Buddha-dharma to be destroyed and the Sangha to be split into two factions; therefore, it is prescribed that one commits an offense upon listening after a dispute has occurred.

Therefore, regarding those who listen while standing at a higher or lower level, because the matter of dispute is grave, this is not the same as the procedures for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) or formal acts (*karmavācanā*).
In this case, whether the disputing parties or others who are not disputing come to listen, and whether one speaks to others about it or not, all constitute an offense.

77. The seventy-seventh matter: Regarding the seventy-seventh of the ninety matters, concerning rising in silence during a formal monastic proceeding (*saṃghakarma*). If it is said that only the *jñapti*, *jñaptidvitīya*, and *jñapticaturtha* procedures are mentioned, it is because all one hundred and one types of formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) are included within these three categories.

For light matters, there is the *jñapti-karman*; for middling matters, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*; and for grave matters, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. When these three types of formal acts (*karman*) are being recited, if one rises and departs, one commits a *pāyattika* offense; for any other matter that is not a formal act, if one rises and departs, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
78. The seventy-eighth matter: The ninety matters, the seventy-eighth, concerning "lack of respect" (Skt. *anādara*), which in the Hu language is called "causing distress to others.
There are generally four ways of causing distress to others:

(1) Having already given an instruction or recognition, and being addressed by a teacher or a senior (*sthavira*) to refrain from doing a certain thing, one initially complies with the words but subsequently does it anyway. This is the first.
Regarding the two types of *ānantarya* offenses, they constitute a *pāyantika*;
regarding the act of harassing a junior monk, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
When one has not yet been granted formal authorization (*vyākaraṇa*), there are two matters involved, and one incurs only a *duṣkṛta*.

79. The seventy-ninth matter: Regarding the ninety matters, the seventy-ninth concerns drinking alcohol. Among the three—alcoholic fragrance, alcoholic flavor, and intoxication—if one drinks even one of these three, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding the offense of consuming *maku* (leaven): it is said that this *maku* is made by mixing barley and medicinal herbs with wine; after it has fermented and dried, one carries it about and drinks it by dissolving it in water, which is capable of intoxicating a person.
There is no offense regarding other types of yeast.

If one commits a transgression exceeding this, this wine is extremely grave; one who drinks it can commit the four *ānantarya* sins, with the exception of the sin of causing a schism in the Sangha, because a schism must necessarily involve claiming oneself to be a Buddha.
It can also destroy all precepts and other various evils. 80.

The eightieth matter: Entering a village at an improper time. Regarding those who dwell in *āraṇya* (forest hermitages), there are donors (*dānapati*) who establish residences, places for study, and *āraṇya* sites near the outskirts of a village.
If there is a fear of bandits due to residing in a remote *āraṇya*, one may establish a monastic storehouse near a village.
If the monastery is outside the village, to leave the monastery for the city gate without informing [the community] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, it is said that when entering a village, if one announces the entry to the community as a whole, one may subsequently go wherever one pleases.
If one makes a specific announcement, or if one did not previously announce it but makes an announcement upon seeing a bhikṣu from another monastery, there is no offense.

81. The eighty-first matter, the eighty-first of the ninety matters: Regarding "before and after eating," this is a formal rule (*niyama*) for bhikṣus concerning the households of donors (*dānapati*).
On account of Upananda, [the donor] provided one hundred measures of gold, one hundred measures for storage, and one hundred measures for food and drink.
This was the reason the donor invited the Buddha and the Sangha, desiring to beg for his livelihood from among the monks.
However, because he knew that [the donor] intended to beg for alms and had already arrived beforehand, while the others came later, he therefore established the precept.
When a lay patron or a monastic prepares a meal, it is not an offense for the Sangha to go there at dawn after being informed.
If one goes without having announced one's intention, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.

If one has announced one's intention, yet while on the way goes to another household to seek food, and receives and eats a formal meal (*bhojana*), one commits a *pāyattika*; if one receives supplementary food (*vighasa*), one commits a *dukkaṭa*.
If one departs with the Sangha at the same time without having announced one's intention, the one who enters first commits an offense of transgression (*pācittiya*).
If the host is to prepare food on the following day, and one goes there oneself on that very day, it is an offense of transgression, except when invited by the host.
If one leaves of one's own accord after the host has dismissed them following the meal, it is an offense of falling (pācittiya).

If one causes the host to labor over the preparation of the meal, yet arrives only after the Sangha has already reached the site, it is an offense of falling. If one departs after the meal before the *dakṣiṇā* (alms-offering) has been given, it is an offense of falling.
If other practitioners wish to travel privately, they must inform their fellow students; whether this constitutes an offense or not is the same as stated above.
Even within the great boundary (mahā-sīmā), if one visits the house of a layperson near the monastery without informing them, it is likewise an offense of falling (pāyattika).
It is a *duṣkṛta* offense to enter the city abruptly.
It is also a *duṣkṛta* offense to cause distress to the monks by returning late after having announced one's arrival.
Section Eighty-two: The Eighty-second Matter. Regarding the eighty-second section, it refers to the outer gate of the royal palace.
The "door threshold" (menkun) refers to the wooden bar placed before the palace gate; one commits an offense by passing beyond this wood.
"The treasure has not yet been stored away" means that the king has already gone outside, but the queen has not yet risen.

When he enters the inner chamber, the precious robes he wears are light and translucent, illuminating his body so that they appear externally; because he does not remove these robes when his desire arises, they are called "unconcealed jewels."
Furthermore, when the woman serves as the "jewel" for the man, if she has not yet covered her body with other garments, this is also called "the jewel not yet concealed.
Regarding the phrase "before night has dawned," the original Indic text contains two meanings:
first, that it has not yet dawned; second, that the lady has not yet arisen.
If the king and his consort have not yet departed and the precious robes have not yet been stored away, entering within the boundary of the wooden frame constitutes an offense.
If they have already departed and the robes have already been stored away, entering within the boundary does not constitute an offense.
Furthermore, if one enters by force due to the power of the king, the consort, a great minister, or a crown prince, it does not constitute an offense.
If the treasure has not yet been stored away, there is no offense for the lady;
if the treasure is present but the lady is absent, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
To enter the palace gates of devas, nāgas, or spirits constitutes an offense of wrongdoing.
Entering the gate of an empty palace is not an offense.
"A king" refers to those above the village headman. 83.

The eighty-third matter: Regarding the eighty-third of the ninety matters, "I now only know this rule for the first time," means that one commits an offense by listening to the precepts with a frivolous mind or a distracted mind.
It is said that at the initial arrival [of the instruction], one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense for violating the rules of training; once the recitation is finished, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one actually knew [the rule] beforehand but claims to have known it only now, one commits a *pāyattika* offense for lying.
This section primarily defines the offense of not listening with a focused mind.
84. The eighty-fourth matter: Regarding the needle case, because it is a minor object, it is not included among the thirty matters.
Furthermore, it ought to be discarded: if it is returned to its owner, the owner will not accept it; if it is given to another, the owner will suffer distress.
To offer it to the Saṃgha would be contrary to the Dharma; it should only be cast away.
As for "bones," these refer to the bones of elephants, horses, or dragons.
Ivory refers to the tusks of elephants and pigs.
Teeth refer to the teeth of elephants, horses, and pigs.
Horns refer to the horns of oxen, sheep, and deer.
This is an offense due to being fond of [luxury] and because it is impure.
The same applies to other items such as bowl-stands and the like.

85. The eighty-fifth matter: Regarding high and wide beds. Because they give rise to arrogance, any wooden bed that is tall or large constitutes an offense; this is the same as the eight precepts for laypeople.
"Eight fingers" means two inches per finger.
"As soon as obtained" clarifies that one incurs an offense at the very moment of using it while sitting or lying down.
The reason it is not classified under the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture) is because it has been cut short.
One must cut it to the proper measurement and confess it before the Saṃgha. If it is for a low-lying or damp place, eight inches are permitted;
if the support exceeds this, one commits an offense. 86. The eighty-sixth matter: Regarding *tūla*, this is a general term for the cotton-like down from plants and flowers.
Because it is kept by persons of high status;
because it is resented by others; and because it is prone to breeding insects.

Furthermore, if one lies upon something soft and warm, one will be unable to endure the cold or coarse textures encountered later; thus, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of begging, and as soon as the bedding is stored until it is completed, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
Generally, when one makes offerings to the Buddha, one obtains merit, yet there is no one through whom it is utilized.
Now, because the Buddha does not utilize them, whereas the Saṃgha utilizes them constantly and merit is thus constantly generated, one should protect and prepare bedding for them.
87. The Eighty-Seventh Matter: Regarding the wound-covering cloth (*vastra*). Previously, the wearing of the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) had not been permitted.
There was a certain bhikṣu who suffered from an abscess; pus and blood flowed out and soiled his *antarvāsaka* (inner robe).
The Buddha saw this and permitted the keeping of a wound-covering cloth; it may be kept for up to ten days after the wound has healed, and there is no offense.
Since the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) was permitted, when one suffers from a wound, it should be worn inside the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, with dimensions equal to that of the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*.

88. The Eighty-eighth Matter: Regarding the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat). Originally, when the Buddha was in the world, these were made small because he did not lie down on them. Later, because of Nanda, it was permitted to increase the size; by adding one span (*vitasti*) at one end from the edge of the woven cloth, they became six feet long and three feet wide, intended for the bhikṣus to lie upon.
The measurement of a monk’s bedding is four by eight *chi*.
Now, if one wishes to make a *niṣīdana*, its measurement must remain as it was originally.
It is said that because this was established first, it is included here.
Later, because thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses were established, one enters into the category of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one now acts improperly, one immediately incurs a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

89. The Eighty-ninth Matter: Regarding the making of requests for a rain-bath robe (*varṣāśāṭī*). The Buddha did not grant excessive requests; "excessive request" refers to the manner of kings and great personages who, when someone comes to them with a request, never fail to comply with their ritual obligations, granting whatever is sought—whether wives, concubines, slaves, servants, fields, or houses. If such a thing is requested, they grant it all.
Because the Buddha did not grant wishes that were contrary to the Dharma, it is said that he did not grant excessive wishes, but only granted wishes that accord with the Dharma.

It is said that whenever a bhikṣu bathes, whether in an open space or a covered room, he must not do so in the presence of laypeople or with his upper body uncovered; he must certainly wear a *kaṣāya*. This is for two reasons: first, to maintain a sense of shame, and second, because [exposing the body] gives rise to lustful thoughts in others.
In the past, there was an arhat bhikṣu who was bathing. Another bhikṣu, seeing that his body was fresh, pure, fine, and soft, immediately conceived a lustful thought.
Not long thereafter, his male organ fell away and a female organ appeared; he then abandoned the path to become a layman and fathered children.

Later, when he encountered him again, he recognized him immediately; knowing the original cause, he returned with sincere intent to seek [his help]. Upon the Arhat’s instruction to repent, he applied himself with utmost devotion and regained his male organ.
Therefore, one should not expose one's form.

It is said that the offense of committing sexual misconduct with a great bhikṣu who maintains the precepts or a śrāmaṇera is equal to destroying a stupa made of the seven precious gems; conversely, the merit of encouraging others to leave the household life and practice with diligence is equal to building such a stupa.

90. The Ninetieth Matter. Regarding the ninety matters, the ninetieth states: "The measurement of the Buddha’s robe. The Buddha’s body is sixteen feet tall, while that of an ordinary person is half of that; therefore, the width and length of the robe should both be half [of the Buddha's proportions].
The Buddha’s younger brother Nanda was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha; therefore, his robes should be reduced by one chi in length and four cun in width compared to those of medium size.

Previously, Nanda wore the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) while the Buddha wore the middle robe (*antaravāsaka*); now, it is not permitted for [Nanda’s robes] to exceed [the Buddha's] in size, but it is permitted for him to wear the lower robe (*nivasana*), which for ordinary people is the lowest of the low.
The color of the Buddha’s robe was like that of *kaṣāya* (gold-dye), and the color of the cotton cloth was likewise; therefore, Nanda’s robe should be like *pāṃsukūla*.
*Pāṃsukūla* means "dyed with earth-color" in the language of Qin; it is intended to make it identical to the robes of other bhikṣus.

7. Four Confessions. 1. The First Matter: The Four Confessions. First, this is a unique precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*); bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs do not incur an offense, while a śrāmaṇera incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept has no name for its transgression; one confesses the fault by speaking once in the presence of another person.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu who is not ill enters a village and takes root food with his own hand from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, he incurs a *pāyattika* (pratideśanīya) offense.
If one takes fifteen kinds of food at once, it constitutes one *pāyattika* offense;
if one takes them one by one, there are fifteen *pāyattika* offenses.

There is no offense if it is given to one who is ill, or to a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative, or among a great multitude in a deva temple, or at a śramaṇa’s residence, or outside the village in a bhikṣuṇī’s dwelling; in these cases, there is no offense.

2. The second matter. This is an *asādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada* (an offense not shared with other classes); there is no offense for bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, or śrāmaṇerikās, while for śrāmaṇeras it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu accepts food offered by a bhikṣuṇī who has instructed him to give it, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense; for every such acceptance, he incurs a corresponding *pāyattika*.
If two groups of the Saṃgha are seated together, if even one person within one group speaks to that bhikṣuṇī, the second group is also said to have spoken.
If they enter separately, sit separately, eat separately, and depart separately, the bhikṣu who enters the donor’s gate should ask the departing bhikṣu:
"Which bhikṣuṇī instructed the donor here to give food to the bhikṣus?"
He replies, “I am so-and-so.
One should then ask:
"Have you issued the instructions? He replied,
"I have already issued them."
This entry for a bhikṣu is also called "injunction.
When there are bhikṣus exiting through a city gate, if there is a bhikṣu entering, one should question the one exiting.
If one has gone out without having given instructions, the one who enters should give instructions;
if one has gone out having given instructions, the one who enters is likewise considered to have received the instructions.
Third Matter: This precept is shared with the bhikṣuṇīs, but not with the other three assemblies.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, in a family under training (*śaikṣa-kula*), after the Saṃgha has performed the formal act of *karmavācanā* for that family, takes staple food with his own hand on his own initiative without having been previously invited, he incurs a *pratideśanīya* offense.
If one takes fifteen kinds of food at one time, one incurs one offense.
If one takes them separately at different times, one incurs fifteen *pāṭidesanīya* offenses.
The fourth matter: this is a unique precept (*asādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada*) for which the four assemblies are not at fault.

Regarding the offense herein: if a monk has not been appointed by the Saṃgha, and that person takes root food with their own hands outside the monastery grounds, but takes it inside the monastery grounds, they incur a *pāṭidesanīya* offense.
If a bhikṣu has received the formal authorization (*saṃgha-karman*) and knows that a thief has entered therein, he should bring a pure person (*śuci-puruṣa*) and stand within it.
If he sees someone among them who resembles a thief, he should take that food and say to those carrying the food:
"Do not come in; there is someone here who resembles a thief."
"If the person carrying the food comes by force, there is no offense.
The Vinaya Master said:
"The person for whom the *karmavācanā* is performed must necessarily be brave, strong, and capable of repelling robbers."
If they cannot drive them away, the entire Saṃgha should go to the place where the robbers are.
If that is still not possible, they should inform the lay donors of the village and have many people provide protection.
5. The First of the Many Trainings (Saṃvara-śikṣāpada). This is a common precept.

Regarding those monks who wear the *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* (undergarment) excessively high: these are not the five original bhikṣus, nor are they Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his companions, nor Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, nor the *svāgata* (welcomed) bhikṣus; for the most part, they are those who received full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
For example, among the thousand members of the Śākya clan who renounced the world simultaneously, many of these people frequently violated the rules of decorum.
Because these Śākya bhikṣus originally came from noble lineages, due to their former habits, they wore their inner robes (nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī) low.
The various Brahmins and non-Buddhists who had gone forth within the Buddha-dharma wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robes high;
the group of six bhikṣus, however, wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robes unevenly.
Question:

Within the five categories of precepts, why did the Buddha specifically enjoin the wearing of the *nivāsana* and the three robes (*tricīvara*), and instruct one to contemplate the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as the Śuddhāvāsa deities?
He replied:
"The Buddha established the five categories of precepts; all should be observed by contemplating the Buddhas of the three periods and the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
However, because many years have passed, the texts have been lost, such that these [contemplations] are absent from the other categories and exist only in this one."

Furthermore, regarding the compilation of the five categories of precepts (*pañca-pārājika*), this [first category] was established at the very beginning; however, those who compiled the later collections arranged it toward the end because this category serves as the thread that runs through the beginning. For this reason, the other categories are not discussed here.

Furthermore, regarding those precepts that are minor compared to others in this section, future disciples might fail to give them due respect; therefore, the Tathāgata, having observed with his Buddha-eye the Buddhas of the past and future as well as the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, subsequently established these rules so that sentient beings of future generations would not incur the fault of arrogance.

Furthermore, the precepts established by the Buddhas of the three periods of time may be the same or different; among the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*), they are not necessarily identical in all respects. However, this practice of wearing the *nivāsana* (undergarment) and the *kāṣāya* (robe) is entirely the same for all Buddhas of the three periods. For this reason, when observing this precept, one contemplates the Buddhas and the Śuddhāvāsa devas, whereas other categories of offenses do not require such contemplation.
Question: "Since these rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma) were established at the beginning, why do they appear here at the end? Answer:
"The Buddha established the precepts at the beginning, and those who later compiled the Dharma-piṭaka arranged them in subsequent order. Why is this?

Although the names of the offenses are the same, there are five degrees of gravity; heavy precepts are placed first and light precepts are placed last. Since this precept is the lightest among the five categories (pañcāpatti), it is therefore placed at the end."

Furthermore, one is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and the other is a prohibitory offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*); since the natural offense comes first and the prohibitory offense follows, [the former is listed first].
Moreover, one is an offense without remainder (*anavaśeṣa*) and the other is an offense with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, it is like a scorched and rotten seed, or like a tāla leaf; therefore, that which is weightier is placed first, and that which is lighter is placed later.
He asked: “In the other sections of the precepts, it is not stated that one ‘should train,’ yet why is this precept alone so?”
He replied:
"Other precepts are easy to maintain yet carry heavy offenses; if one violates them, the offense is established, and one must repent before the assembly or in the presence of another.
This precept is difficult to maintain yet carries a light offense; should one happen to violate it, by repenting in one's heart and resolving to train, the offense is immediately extinguished."
"Because the precepts are difficult to maintain and easy to violate, one should always train with careful mindfulness so as not to incur an offense; this is simply stated as 'one should train.
Regarding "wearing the inner robe too high or too low": it should be one span above the ankle; if it extends above or below that, it is called "high or low."
If a bhikṣu or śrāmaṇera comes from a long journey, it is permitted for [the robe] to extend two spans above the ankle up to below the knee.
For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs, at all times it must be one span above the ankle; even when walking or coming, it must not be made higher than that.
3. It is not uneven.
4. It is not like the head of a woodcutter’s axe.
5. It is not like a tāla leaf.
Sixth, it is not like an elephant’s trunk.
Seventh, it is not like a lump of flour.
Eighth, it does not have fine pleats.
9. Not to wear [the robe] with a tufted fringe.
10. Not to fold both edges together.
11. Not to wear an undergarment made of fine thread.
12. The twelve points regarding the wearing of the three robes (*tricīvara*) include four matters:
as for the height and width, they should be four finger-breadths above the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*.
The three [sides] are not uneven;
the four sides are even.
There are forty-one matters regarding entering the house of a layperson, and twenty-seven matters regarding receiving food:
1. Receive the rice with a single-minded focus.
2. Receive the soup with a single-minded focus.
3. Do not receive the soup or rice so that it overflows the bowl.
4. Eating with soup and rice;
5. Not being restricted by the amount of rice and food;
6. Not gathering up the rice and food.
7. Not to take large mouthfuls of food;
8. Not to hold food with the hand;
9. Not to open the mouth in anticipation of food.
10. Not speaking with food in the mouth.
11. Not biting off half a morsel of food.
12. Not making a slurping sound while eating.
13. Not making noise while chewing food.
14. Not swallowing food before it has been tasted.
15. Not sticking out the tongue while eating.
16. Not eating with the nose wrinkled.
17. Not eating while licking the hands.
18. Not wiping the bowl with the fingers while eating.
19. One should not eat while shaking one's hand.
20. One should not discard half a mouthful of rice from the chopsticks.
21. One should not grasp a drinking vessel with greasy hands.
22. When not ill, one must not seek out soup or rice for oneself. 23.
One must not cover the soup with rice in order to expect to receive more.
24. One must not look at the bowl of the person sitting beside one.
25. One should gaze steadily at the bowl.
26. One should eat all the food in successive order until it is finished. 27.
If there is rice in the water used for washing the bowl, one should not discard it inside [the monastery] without asking the master.
There are nineteen matters regarding preaching the Dharma to others; three matters regarding excreting feces or urine and spitting or sneezing; and one matter regarding climbing trees. 8.
The Seven Methods for Settling Disputes. 1. The First Matter: The Seven Methods for Settling Disputes. First, the method for settling disputes through self-accusation.

Matters concerning the five groups of persons, as well as matters regarding whether there has been an offense or no offense in relation to the five classes of precepts, are all settled by the method of settling disputes through self-avowal (*sammukhavinaya*).
Regarding the settling of disputes through self-avowal, there are ten kinds that are contrary to the Dharma and ten kinds that are in accordance with the Dharma.
The ten unlawful matters are as follows: if a bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense but claims he has not committed one,
and the Saṃgha asks him,
"Do you yourself say that you have committed it or not?"
To claim for oneself that one has not committed an offense when one has, is called "unlawful.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta offense, yet claims for himself that he has not committed it.
The assembly of monks asked him, "Do you yourself say that you have committed an offense?
He replied, "I myself say I have not committed one. This is called the fifth unrighteous [proceeding].
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has not committed a pārājika offense but says of himself,
"I have committed one," and the Saṃgha asks him,
"Do you yourself say that you have committed it?"
To say of oneself, "I have committed an offense," when it is not so, is called *adharma* (unlawful).
There may be a bhikṣu who has not committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *duṣkṛta* offense, yet says of himself, "I have committed one."
The assembly of monks asked,
"Do you yourself say that you have committed an offense?
When he himself says, "I have committed one," this is called the tenth unrighteous [proceeding].
Regarding the ten points of accordance with the Dharma: Suppose there is a bhikṣu who has committed a pārājika offense and says of himself, "I have committed it.
The Saṃgha asks him, "Do you yourself say that you have committed it?"
To say of oneself, "I have committed an offense," is called acting in accordance with the Dharma.
There may be a bhikṣu who has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta offense, and says of himself, "I have committed an offense."
The assembly of monks asked, "Do you yourself say that you have committed an offense?
He replied, "I myself say I have committed one. This is called the fifth [case] of being in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who has not committed an offense of pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta, declares himself to have committed no offense.
The assembly of monks asked, "Do you yourself say that you have committed an offense? He himself said, "I have not committed an offense.
This is called the tenth *yathādharma* (act in accordance with the Dharma).
2. Regarding the second matter: there are two types of non-Dharmic and two types of Dharmic ways to settle a dispute through presence (*sammukha-vinaya*).
As for the two non-Dharmic ways: there is a non-Dharmic Saṃgha; to command this non-Dharmic Saṃgha to subdue [the offender] and grant settlement through presence is non-Dharmic.
There is an unrighteous Saṃgha that commands three, two, or one unrighteous person to submit and grants them the *pratyakṣavinaya* (face-to-face settlement).

Even down to an unrighteous individual who commands another unrighteous individual, a Saṃgha, three, or two persons to submit and grants them the *pratyakṣavinaya*—this is called the first type of unrighteous *pratyakṣavinaya*.
There is an unrighteous Saṃgha that commands a righteous Saṃgha to undergo subjugation, and grants it the *saṃmukhavinaya*.
There is an unrighteous Saṃgha that commands three, two, or one person of the righteous [Saṃgha] to undergo subjugation, and grants them the *saṃmukhavinaya*.

Even if there is but one person who acts contrary to the Dharma, he may command another person who acts in accordance with the Dharma—whether it be a Saṃgha, three persons, or two persons—to subdue him and grant him the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement before the assembly).
These are called the two types of *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of) that are contrary to the Dharma.

Regarding the two types of *sammukhavinaya* that are in accordance with the Dharma: there is a Saṃgha that accords with the Dharma, which instructs the Saṃgha to act in accordance with the Dharma so as to subdue [the offender] and grant them *sammukhavinaya*.

Furthermore, as with the Sangha acting in accordance with the Dharma, it may instruct three, two, or one person who acts in accordance with the Dharma to subdue [the offender] and grant them the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (face-to-face discipline).

Likewise, even a single person acting in accordance with the Dharma may instruct one, three, or two persons who act in accordance with the Dharma to subdue [the offender] and grant them the *pratyakṣa-vinaya*. This is called the first type of *pratyakṣa-vinaya* in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, as when a *saṃgha* acting in accordance with the Dharma commands an *asaṃgha* not acting in accordance with the Dharma to submit, and grants them the *pratyakṣavinaya*;

or as when a *saṃgha* acting in accordance with the Dharma commands three persons, two persons, or one person not acting in accordance with the Dharma to submit, and grants them the *pratyakṣavinaya*.

Even if there is one person acting according to the Dharma who instructs another person, a monk, three persons, or two persons who are not acting according to the Dharma, causing them to be subdued and granting them the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (face-to-face discipline).
These are called the two kinds of *yathādharma-pratyakṣa-vinaya*.
Third matter, third matter: this is the *saṃvara-vinaya*; it is granted as *smṛti-vinaya* to all three assemblies, and it is granted as *smṛti-vinaya* for all five categories of offenses.

Regarding the granting of the *smṛtivinaya*, it must be granted through a formal procedure of fourfold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). This may be performed either in the presence of the assembly or in their absence; specifically, while the monks and nuns are present, the three other assemblies are not present.
If a bhikṣu, having attained mindfulness, subsequently lowers his precepts and becomes a śrāmaṇera, he immediately regains that prior mindfulness.
If, after returning to lay life from the monastic order, he goes forth again—whether as a śrāmaṇera or receives full ordination—he immediately regains that prior mindfulness.
If one whose faculties have transformed becomes a bhikṣuṇī, they immediately regain their former mindfulness.
If a śrāmaṇera regains his former mindfulness and subsequently receives full ordination, he likewise immediately regains his former mindfulness.
If, after returning the precepts and re-entering lay life, one goes forth again—whether as a *śrāmaṇera* or receives full ordination—one immediately recalls the previous [ordination].
If one’s faculties change and one becomes a *śrāmaṇerī*, one likewise immediately recalls the previous [ordination].
If a bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, or śrāmaṇerī has attained mindfulness, they shall proceed through the successive stages according to the rules for bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras.
There are three kinds of *dhāraṇā-vinaya* that are contrary to the Dharma, and three kinds of *dhāraṇā-vinaya* that are in accordance with the Dharma.

Regarding the three kinds that are contrary to the Dharma: there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense without remainder (*anavaśeṣa*), yet he himself declares that he has committed an offense with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*).
If this bhikṣu requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants this bhikṣu the *smṛtivinaya*, this is called an illegal [act]. Why is that?
This person should be expelled because they ought to be suppressed.

Furthermore, it was like the bhikṣu Śreṇika, who, due to a deranged and deluded mind, frequently committed impure acts, unrighteous deeds, and practices that were not in accordance with the Path or the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
When this person has recovered their original mind, they constantly recount their previously committed offenses to the Saṃgha, or to three people, two people, or one person.
If this person requests the *smṛtivinaya* (the discipline of mindfulness) from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants the *smṛtivinaya* to this person, this is called an illegal act.
Why is this? Because such a person should be granted the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the disciplinary act for one who was not insane).

Furthermore, it is like the bhikṣu Akhata, who, lacking shame and dread of blame, committed offenses regarding transgressions of precepts, views, or doubts; this person first said, "I have this offense," but later said, "I do not have this offense."
If the Saṃgha grants this person the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection), it is called illegal.
Why? Because this person should instead be granted the *tattvavinaya* (settlement by investigation of the facts).
These are called the three *adharma-smṛti-vinaya* (unlawful legal procedures based on memory).

Regarding the three *dharma* (lawful) procedures: for example, when the bhikṣu Dharmapāla was falsely accused of a groundless *pārājika* offense by the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyaṇī, if the Saṃgha, or three persons, or two persons, or a single person constantly speaks of this matter [in his defense].
If this bhikṣu requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants him the *smṛtivinaya*, this is called being in accordance with the Dharma. Why is that?
This person should be granted the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection).
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu commits an offense; he confesses this offense and, according to the Dharma, performs repentance so that it is eliminated.
Yet, if a saṃgha, or three persons, or two persons, or even one person still speaks of this matter [as if it were still present].
If this bhikṣu requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants him the *smṛtivinaya*, it is called "in accordance with the Dharma. Why?
Because this person is one to whom the *smṛtivinaya* ought to be granted.

Furthermore, it is as when a bhikṣu has not yet committed an offense but is certain to do so; on account of this matter, if a Saṃgha, or three persons, or two persons, or one person declares that he has committed this offense.
If this bhikṣu requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants him the *smṛtivinaya*, this is called being in accordance with the Dharma. Why is that?
Because this person should be granted the *smṛti-vinaya*, these are called the three lawful forms of the *smṛti-vinaya*. Regarding the practice of the *smṛti-vinaya*:

other monks should not point out his transgressions, should not cause him to remember them, should not request an audience from him, nor should they accept a request for an audience from another monk. If one requests an audience from him, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one accepts a request for an audience from another, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
If he does not listen, or if one causes him to confess his offense, or if one causes him to remember it, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
This fourth matter is the protection of the *vinaya*; the five assemblies all receive the *amūḷhavinaya* (the discipline for those who are no longer insane).

Regarding the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who is no longer deluded), it must be conferred through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations). It may be conferred either in the presence of the assembly or not in their presence; that is, with monks and nuns present, while the other three groups of disciples are not present.
If a bhikṣu, having received the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the disciplinary act for one no longer insane), subsequently lowers his status to that of a *śrāmaṇera*, he retains that prior *amūḍha-vinaya*.
If he renounces the precepts and returns to lay life, and later goes forth again—whether as a *śrāmaṇera* or receives full ordination—he likewise retains that prior *amūḍha-vinaya*.
If one whose faculties have changed becomes a bhikṣuṇī, it is then the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of non-delusion) as before.
If a śrāmaṇera, having received the *amūḷhavinaya*, subsequently receives full ordination, it is then the *amūḷhavinaya* as before.
