If one who has reverted from the precepts and returned to lay life subsequently leaves the household life again—whether as a *śrāmaṇera* or by receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*)—this constitutes the *pūrvāparicittaviparyāsa-vinaya*.
If one’s gender changes and becomes a *śrāmaṇerī*, this likewise constitutes the *pūrvāparicittaviparyāsa-vinaya*.

If a bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, or śrāmaṇerī has received the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the disciplinary procedure for one no longer insane), the successive procedures shall follow the rules for bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras.
Regarding the *amūḍha-vinaya* (settlement for one no longer insane), there are four kinds that are contrary to the Dharma and four kinds that are in accordance with the Dharma.
As for the four kinds that are contrary to the Dharma: suppose there is a bhikṣu who, though not insane, manifests the appearance of being mad and deluded. The community of bhikṣus asks him:
"Do you remember what you did while you were insane and deluded?"
He replied,
"Venerable sir!
I recall that I did it out of delusion."
"Others instruct me to practice two recollections;
in dreams, I practice three recollections;
being naked, running east and west, and standing while defecating or urinating—this is the fourth."
If this person requests the *amūḍha-vinaya* from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants this person the *amūḍha-vinaya*, these are called the four illegal [procedures].
As for the four legal [procedures]: there is a bhikṣu who is actually insane, whose mind is deranged, and who manifests the appearance of insanity. The other bhikṣus ask him:
"Do you remember what you did while insane?"
He replied:
"I do not recall anyone instructing me to do it; I do not recall doing it in a dream; I do not recall running here and there naked; nor do I recall standing while defecating or urinating."
If this person requests the *amūḍha-vinaya* from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants this person the *amūḍha-vinaya*, these are called the four lawful *amūḍha-vinayas*.

Regarding the procedure for the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of non-delusion): other bhikṣus should not point out his faults or offenses, should not cause him to remember them, should not request a formal hearing from him, nor should they accept a request for a formal hearing from another bhikṣu.
If one solicits another for permission and receives it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if one receives a solicitation for permission from another, one also incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the other does not grant permission and one nevertheless departs, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; if one causes [the other] to recall [the matter], one also incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

5. The Fifth Matter. This is the *tshad-pa'i dbyen* (vinaya of subduing). For all five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*), the *yathābhūta-mṛgya-vinaya* (vinaya of seeking according to reality) is applied; for all five classes of monastics (*pañca-saṃgha*), this vinaya is applied.
When the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs are present, but the three other groups [of disciples] are not present, one grants it through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
Regarding the *yathābhūta-mṛṣā-vinaya*, there are five kinds that are contrary to the Dharma and five kinds that are in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding the five kinds of illegal [procedures]: if a bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense, yet first says he did not commit it and later says he did;
if the Saṃgha then grants this person a *yadbhūyaḥparyeṣaṇā-vinaya* (seeking the truth of the matter), this is called illegal.
Why is this? Because such a person should be subject to the penalty of *pravāsanīya* (banishment).
There are monks who have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta* offense, yet first claim they did not commit it and later claim they did.
If the Saṃgha grants this person the *yadbhūyaḥparyeṣaṇā-vinaya*, it is called illegal. Why?
Because this person should be disciplined according to the offense actually committed.
The fifth case of being in accordance with the Dharma: Suppose there is a bhikṣu who commits a pārājika offense, yet first says he has committed it and later says he has not.
If the Saṃgha grants this person the *yadbhūyaḥparyeṣaṇā-vinaya* (the legal procedure of searching for the truth), this is called being in accordance with the Dharma.
Why is this? Because such a person should be investigated according to the facts.
If a bhikṣu has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta offense, yet first says he has committed it and later says he has not.
If the Saṃgha grants this bhikṣu the *yadbhūyaḥparyeṣaṇā-vinaya*, it is called "in accordance with the Dharma. Why?
Because this person deserves to be granted the *yadbhūyaḥparyeṣaṇā-vinaya*.

Regarding the practice of the *yadbhūyaḥ-vinaya* (the discipline of seeking the truth): A bhikṣu who has received this [disciplinary measure] must not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; he must not receive dependence (*niśraya*) from others; he must not keep new or old śrāmaṇeras; he must not teach the Dharma to bhikṣuṇīs; if the Saṃgha performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to instruct bhikṣuṇīs, he must not accept it; he must not again commit the offense for which the Saṃgha granted him the *yadbhūyaḥ-vinaya*; he must not commit any offense similar to or greater than that offense; he must not criticize a formal act of the Saṃgha nor those who perform the formal act; he must not request permission from others; he must not obstruct the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*; he must not obstruct the conferral of ordination; he must not obstruct the *pravāraṇā*; he must not proclaim the faults or offenses of an innocent bhikṣu; and he must not engage in communal affairs with others.
One should discipline one’s mind and conduct so as to accord with the will of the community of bhikṣus.
If one does not practice according to this dharma, one shall not be released from this *karma* for as long as one lives.

6. The Sixth Matter: Regarding *yadbhūyaiṣīya-vinaya*. It is called *yadbhūyaiṣīya-vinaya* because it seeks out many causes and conditions for a decision; although the matter has not been settled in many places, it is decided by the majority, and is thus named *yadbhūyaiṣīya-vinaya*.
When distributing voting sticks (*śalākā*) or when settling a legal matter, the entire Saṃgha must assemble; the taking of *chanda* (consent) is not permitted. Why?
Because many bhikṣus might speak what is contrary to the Dharma.
This is called the procedure for distributing voting sticks (*śalākā*).
In this matter, no bhikṣu should accept a proxy vote (*chanda*), just as in the procedure for distributing alms bowls (*pātra*).

If [the dispute] cannot be settled, then even if there is only one bhikṣu in that monastery who is learned in the Tripiṭaka and esteemed by the fourfold assembly, he should go to that place and speak to that one bhikṣu, recounting the entire matter in the proper sequence as previously described.
That virtuous bhikṣu should speak thus:
"It is impossible for two people to argue with each other and both be victorious; between them, one must necessarily be the victor and the other the vanquished."
To speak in such a manner is called speaking according to the Dharma;
to speak otherwise is called speaking contrary to the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu, after a matter has been settled in accordance with the Dharma through these various formal procedures, should again raise it, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If one merely censures them, saying that the legal decision was not in accordance with the Dharma, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

As for *tālaṭṭhila*: *tāla* means "earth" and *ṭṭhila* means "abiding. It refers to one whose wisdom is supreme and who dwells unshakably within the True Dharma, like a person standing on the earth who cannot be overturned.

Regarding those who should be excluded from the period [of instruction]: fearing that the matter may become entangled and difficult to sever, one should say, "I have received instructions that are partial," for this also serves to prevent the other person from seeking to reach one's own level.

Regarding "that which should be relinquished and entrusted to the Saṃgha": because it originated from within the Saṃgha, and since it could not be extinguished [by the individual], it is appropriate that it be returned to its original source.

Regarding "the Saṃgha being present before one": this clarifies that once the Saṃgha has assembled, if there are those capable of objecting who do not do so, then the Saṃgha is in harmony; this is termed "being present before one."
Regarding "Avihā-Kūla": *Avihā* means non-duality, and *Kūla* means equality; the mind is without duality and its evenness is like a scale.
Now, it must be that these two persons possess five qualities.

Regarding the five qualities: because he does not follow personal attachment, he abandons what is culpable; because he does not follow anger, he punishes the innocent; because he does not fear others, he does not violate the Dharma; because he is not deluded, he does not fear committing an offense or adjudicating matters with unjust leniency; and because he knows when to decide and when not to decide, he is called an *avahārika*.

Regarding the granting of consent (*chanda*) by departing to a distant place: this is because one fears that there may be mutual assistance within the Saṃgha, which would inevitably make it impossible to terminate the proceedings.
The reason for taking the consent is to ensure that those who might have provided assistance will not speak further on the matter later.

Furthermore, regarding the appointment of an *avavādaka* (a teacher of instruction), as disputes increased, there was concern that they might cause a schism in the Sangha and obstruct the practice of the Path.
Therefore, another person capable of skillfully adjudicating matters was appointed; it was not necessary for this person to possess the five specific qualities.

Regarding the dispatching of a messenger to a nearby monastery: if one were to go to another location, the matters would inevitably increase and be difficult to resolve; therefore, a messenger is sent.

Once the messenger has arrived, if someone capable among them says, "The seven-day period has ended and the *anvāgama* has been broken," this is because the thirty-nine-night period has not yet been opened.

Regarding the phrase "from such-and-such a place up to those who uphold the Mātṛkā": there are two pillars of the Buddha-dharma that can sustain it, namely, meditative cultivation (dhyāna) and scholarly inquiry (śruta). Therefore, one seeks out such individuals.
Furthermore, there may be virtuous persons among them who cause the matter of dispute to become shameful and difficult to resolve.

As for the person who transmits the matter and adjudicates it, this is because he fears that if it reaches another location, it will be difficult to extinguish; he also hopes that by going to another location, the Sangha there will feel shame and accept his admonition.
Furthermore, due to the exhaustion of sitting in meditation over a long distance, and because evil matters are extinguished for the sake of attaining goodness, one establishes a fixed period.
Since the undertaking of the matter begins from the summer retreat, one excludes the three months of the summer retreat and takes the remaining nine months to clarify the matter.
If it cannot be severed, one should devise a skillful means to ensure it is severed, so that it does not recur during the summer retreat.
If this can be accomplished, entrust him with the duties of transmission and let him return.
The reason for requiring the assembly to be complete outside the boundary (*sīmā*) is to clarify that four persons must be dispatched outside the boundary to effect the resolution.
This is because, as the matter is grave, it must be settled so that it will certainly not recur in the future.
For five reasons, one establishes a person to distribute voting tallies (*śalākā*) and to swiftly suppress [disorder].
There are three types of the powerful:
first, those who possess physical strength themselves; second, those who rely on those with physical strength; and third, those who possess the power of wealth for coming and going.

Regarding "moving from one dwelling place to another": this clarifies that the matter has persisted for a long time; having passed through many locations without interruption, the entanglements of the matter have become firm and knotted.
This is because that person lacks shame and dread of blame, and their mind has become increasingly crafty and deceitful.

As for the reason for casting lots: since the matter is difficult to resolve, if one were to declare something right or wrong, it would inevitably increase the malicious intent of others. Therefore, by casting lots before the assembly, likes and dislikes naturally subside, and the principle remains impartial.

Regarding the distribution of voting sticks (*śalākā*): because the mind of the person distributing the sticks is that of one who acts contrary to the Dharma, they expect to receive many votes from those who likewise act contrary to the Dharma.
This is because, if one assists those who act contrary to the Dharma within a field of clear knowledge, one will be attached to taking up voting sticks that are contrary to the Dharma.
"Those who have made a pact" refers to those who have entered into an agreement together; "those who are intimate with one another" refers to those who have formed such an agreement.

When the entire Saṃgha takes up the voting sticks (*śalākā*), it is because this matter is of great importance that everyone assembles for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the invitation to confession (*pravāraṇā*).

Although they are essential, there are still some who do not come; this is because one wishes to ensure that those who assist will have no further complaints later, and also out of fear that those who accept invitations might take an excessive number of illegal voting sticks (*śalākā*).

Regarding those who are respected by the fourfold assembly: because they take up two kinds of tally-sticks (*śalākā*) and remain impartial, such that their judgment cannot be severed; and because among virtuous people, there is no one whose word is not followed by the assembly; those who do not comply feel shame and are mocked by others. Thus, they must accept the instruction. When transmitting matters, people generally speak of the facts rather than the person; likewise, a monk of great virtue speaks directly of the right and wrong of the matter itself, without speaking of the person.
When there is a matter, if the two parties each internally acknowledge it and remain silent, then victory and defeat will manifest themselves.
Regarding the re-initiation of a *pāyattika* offense, it is marked by two offenses so that neither party may speak further thereafter; thus, the offense is established.
7. The Seventh Matter. Why is the seventh matter called the *tṛṇaprastāraka-vinaya* (the settling by covering with grass)?
It may happen that at a certain residence, various bhikṣus take pleasure in quarreling and engaging in mutual recrimination.
Once these bhikṣus have gathered together in one place, they should reflect thus:
"Venerable elders!
We have suffered a great loss and not a gain; a great decline and not a benefit; a great evil and what is unwholesome."
Out of faith, we have left the household life to seek the Way within the Buddha-dharma; yet now we delight in quarreling and speaking ill of one another.
If we were to seek the root of this matter, it would be that within the Saṃgha, disputes that have not yet arisen would arise, and those already arisen could not be extinguished.
Having formed this thought, he informs the Saṃgha:
"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; this matter shall be settled through the *bhūtagrāsa-vinaya* (the settlement by covering over as with grass).
This is called the formal motion (*jñapti*)."
The bhikṣus should divide themselves into two groups. Among them, if there is a senior elder, he should say to one group:
"We have suffered a great loss rather than a gain; we have met with great decline rather than benefit; we have encountered great evil rather than what is wholesome."
Out of faith, we have left the household life to seek the Way within the Buddha-dharma; yet now we delight in quarreling and speaking ill of one another.

If we were to humble our own wills, then regarding the offenses we have committed—excluding *sthūlātyaya* offenses and those associated with laypeople—we shall confess and repent them before you without concealment.
"If not even a single bhikṣu among them objects to this matter, they should go to where the second group of the assembly is; if there is an elder or senior monk there, they should say to him:
'We have suffered a great loss rather than a gain, a great decline rather than a benefit, and a great evil rather than a good.'"
Out of faith, we have left the household life to seek the Way within the Buddha-dharma; yet now we delight in strife and mutual recrimination.

If we were to investigate the root of this matter, there would be those within the Saṃgha who would initiate disputes that have not yet arisen, and those who could not extinguish disputes already arisen.

Now you all should humble yourselves; regarding the offenses we have committed—excluding those of *sthūlātyaya* and those associated with laypeople—we shall now, for our own sake and for theirs, openly confess and repent before you without concealment.
The bhikṣus said,
"Do you see your own fault?
He replied:
“I see my fault.
“Repent according to the Dharma; do not let it arise again.
The second assembly spoke in the same manner.
This is called the *tṛṇaprastāraka-vinaya* (the method of spreading grass).
All matters concerning disputes, slanders, offenses, and reconciliations are subsumed under the *sammukha-vinaya* (the method of presence).
Only the four lower categories of offenses are extinguished without remainder by means of the seven preceding methods of discipline (*vinaya*).

All wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [actions], as well as the fourteen causes of schism in the Saṃgha and the six origins of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), are collectively termed "disputes" (*vivāda*). When these reside in individuals, they are called "disputes"; when they reside in the Saṃgha, they are called "matters" (*vastu*). They are extinguished by means of the three *vinaya* methods: presence (*sammukha-vinaya*), majority decision (*yadbhūyaḥ-sammatā*), and the covering over with grass (*tṛṇaprastāraka*).

Arising from the roots of seeing, hearing, or suspicion, it is declared a transgression whether the act was committed or not; it is generally termed a "matter" (*adhikaraṇa*), which is called a "person" when residing in an individual and a "matter" when residing in the Saṃgha. It is extinguished by means of the four *vinayas*: presence (*sammukha-vinaya*), recollection (*smṛti-vinaya*), non-delusion (*amūḍha-vinaya*), and investigation according to the facts (*tatsvabhāva-aiṣīya*).

Arising from bodily action, vocal action, or both bodily and vocal action, it is collectively termed an "offense" (*āpatti*). Its preliminary stage is called the "preparatory offense" (*prayoga-āpatti*); its completion is called "breaking" (*bhaṅga*); and its non-confession is called "transgression" (*vyañjana*). It is extinguished by means of two *vinayas*: *saṃmukhavinaya* (presence) and *pratijñāvinaya* (admission).

Regarding the performance of the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā* through the *jñapti*, *jñapti-dvitīya*, and *jñapti-caturtha* procedures, fourteen persons are appointed; from the Saṃgha down to the individual, these constitute the basis for formal acts (*karmavastu*), which are collectively termed "formal acts," and they employ the *vinaya-pratyakṣa* (the presence of the Vinaya).
The Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā, Fascicle Nine.
